text: $PEP Q3 2026 earnings: PepsiCo's sales grow faster, but it cut its profit forecast PepsiCo sold more snacks and drinks abroad, but its North American business earned less and forced a lower profit outlook. Underlying sales, which strip out acquisitions and currency moves, grew 3%, the fastest pace since late 2023. Profit per share excluding one-offs rose 2%, and by our math tariff refunds supplied all of that gain. Finance chief Steve Schmitt said North America needs more time. • Sales growth without acquisitions and currency: +𝟯.𝟭% (+2.4% last quarter) • Revenue: $𝟮𝟱.𝟯𝗕 (+5.6% from a year ago) • Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟮.𝟯𝟰 (+2% from a year ago; about −2% without tariff refunds, by our math) • Full-year profit-per-share growth outlook, excluding one-offs and currency: 𝗖𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗼 +𝟭% 𝘁𝗼 +𝟮% (was the low end of +4% to +6%) ⚖️ 𝗩𝗲𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁: 🔴 Bearish The story got worse because PepsiCo cut this year's profit growth outlook by more than half while sales sped up. The company spends more on lower prices and advertising in North America, and profit there fell. The good news: international sales grew 8%, with higher margins. The question now is whether North America's price cuts and extra advertising will bring back profitable growth. Either snack volumes keep rising and profit recovers, or PepsiCo has bought volume that earns less. Fourth-quarter North American profit and February's 2027 outlook will tell. Full article with charts - link in bio 🐂 𝗕𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲 🟢🟢 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝗮𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗚𝗿𝗲𝘄 𝟴%, 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝘀 PepsiCo runs four businesses outside the US and Canada, and they sell snacks and drinks in markets such as Mexico, India and Turkey. Chief executive Ramon Laguarta credited the quarter to "the scale and resilience of the international business", and the numbers support him. Underlying international sales, which strip out acquisitions and currency moves, grew about 8%. Laguarta called it the fastest pace since early 2024. Customers also bought more units in three of the four businesses, so higher prices did not carry the growth alone. • Asia Pacific Foods volume: up 11%, led by India • International Beverages Franchise, which sells drink concentrate to bottlers abroad: volume up 5% • International profit excluding one-offs: up 16% • International profit margin: 20.9%, up about 1 percentage point This matters because the international group now brings in 44% of revenue and has a higher profit margin than North America. One caution: in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, prices added 7 points of growth and volume only 1. Several of that region's markets have very high inflation. What to watch: international volume in the fourth quarter, which PepsiCo reports in February. Continued volume growth would show that demand, and not only price increases, supports the region's sales. 🟢 𝗡𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗔𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗦𝗻𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗩𝗼𝗹𝘂𝗺𝗲 𝗜𝘀 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗴𝗮𝗶𝗻 PepsiCo Foods North America sells Lay's, Doritos, Cheetos and Quaker in the US and Canada. The unit lowered prices and launched new products this year to win back shoppers, and Laguarta said those efforts "have resonated well with consumers". Shoppers bought about 0.5% more from the unit this quarter, after no growth in the second quarter. Savory snacks did better than the rest, and the company said it gained share of US potato chip volume. • Savory snack volume: up 1%; other foods: down 4% • Multipacks of small portions: more than $3.5 billion of yearly revenue, with volume growth • Snacks the company calls "Permissible options", such as Baked and Sun Chips: about $3 billion of yearly revenue What to watch: whether the unit's sales in dollars grow next quarter. Volume growth with flat dollar sales means lower prices still pay for every extra bag, so dollar growth would show real demand. 🟢 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻'𝘁 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁 Three strengths of the PepsiCo case came with descriptions but without figures this quarter, so the results neither confirmed nor weakened them. • Cost savings: executives again credited productivity savings in every business and gave no dollar amount; a yearly savings figure would test the claim. • Energy drinks sold with partner Celsius: the brands hold nearly 20% of the US category, but PepsiCo does not disclose its revenue from them. • Sales in restaurants, gyms and workplaces: the company reported "good net revenue growth" and no size; a revenue figure would show how much this channel matters. 🐻 𝗕𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲 🔴🔴 𝗟𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗮𝘅𝗲𝘀 𝗛𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝘁 𝗖𝘂𝘁 PepsiCo measures its yearly target as growth in profit per share, excluding one-offs and currency moves. It lowered that target this quarter, and finance chief Steve Schmitt blamed margin "pressures we expect in the North America business". Two items make the cut larger than the headline figures suggest. • Profit-per-share growth target: 1% to 2%, down from the low end of 4% to 6% • Expected tax rate: about 21%, down from 22%, which adds about 1.3 points of growth by our math • Tariff refunds in the quarter: $178 million, or about $0.10 of profit per share by our math • Operating profit excluding one-offs: up 3% with the refunds, down about 1% without them by our math • Selling, advertising and overhead costs: 37.5% of revenue, up 0.8 points from a year ago First, a lower tax rate lifts profit per share without any change in the business. So by our math the operating outlook fell by nearly 4 points, more than the target shows. Second, the US government returned tariffs that PepsiCo paid last year, and that money comes only once. Without it, third-quarter profit per share fell about 2% by our math. What to watch: fourth-quarter profit per share excluding one-offs, which arrives in February. The new target implies a small fall by our math, and a larger one would mean PepsiCo enters 2027 with shrinking profit and no refunds. 🔴🔴 𝗡𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗔𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗦𝗻𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝘁 𝗙𝗲𝗹𝗹 𝟭𝟮% PepsiCo Foods North America, the unit behind Lay's, Doritos and Quaker, earns more than any other PepsiCo business. Its profit excluding one-offs fell 12% this quarter, and Laguarta said North America "performed below our expectations". • Profit margin excluding one-offs: 21.2%, down 2.8 points from a year ago • Selling, advertising and overhead costs: up 2.4 points of revenue • Cost of making the products: up 0.4 points of revenue • Underlying sales: down 0.2% by our math, after a 2% fall last quarter Schmitt named three causes: lower prices, more advertising and a gain from an asset sale a year ago that did not repeat. The filing puts that gain at 4 points of the decline, so most of the fall comes from the business itself. He expects North American margins "to remain under pressure in the fourth quarter". What to watch: the unit's profit margin in the fourth quarter, and any target for it in February. PepsiCo gives no profit target for this business, so a number would let investors measure the recovery that Schmitt says needs more time. 🔴🔴 𝗕𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗔𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗮 𝗖𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗔𝗰𝗾𝘂𝗶𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 PepsiCo Beverages North America sells Pepsi, Mountain Dew and Gatorade in the US and Canada. The unit's revenue grew 5%, but acquisitions and new distribution deals supplied about 6 points. Without them and without currency moves, sales slipped 0.3% by our math. • Volume: down 3%, against a 3-point gain from prices and product mix • Soda volume: down 2%; non-carbonated drinks: down 3% • Value of the future payment tied to poppi's targets: $12 million, down from $278 million in December Laguarta said the company's sodas "trailed category performance". Management also said poppi, the prebiotic soda brand it bought in 2025, "delivered improved results". The accounts are less hopeful. PepsiCo owes poppi's sellers $300 million "if certain performance milestones are achieved by the third quarter of 2027", and it now values that promise at a small fraction of the sum. That markdown and related items added $96 million to reported operating profit this quarter, although the lower value signals weaker prospects for the brand. Profit excluding one-offs leaves the gain out. What to watch: the unit's underlying sales in the next two quarters, as last year's distribution deals enter the comparison. Growth without help from deals would show that the core drinks have stopped shrinking. 🔴 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗸𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻'𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿 Five standing risks received little or no new information this quarter. Each one has a specific reading that would change the picture, and none of those readings arrived. • Ingredient and energy costs: Laguarta cited "rising input cost inflation" without a figure; a stated cost increase for 2027 would size it. • Currency: exchange rates added 0.7 points to revenue, down from 2 points last quarter; a weaker Mexican peso would remove that help. • Russia: 6% of revenue but 20% of cash; any new limit on moving money out would matter more than the revenue share suggests. • Weight-loss drugs and healthier eating: executives did not mention the drugs; data on snack demand among users would show the effect. • Retailers' own brands: the filing again warns that store chains favor them on the shelf; share figures against those brands would measure it. 👓 𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗣𝗲𝗽𝘀𝗶𝗖𝗼 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗖𝘂𝘁𝘀, 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗮 𝗙𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗲 Laguarta said "Additional structural cost reduction actions are being identified and will be implemented in the coming months". His examples include "reductions in corporate costs", and he gave no savings target. Severance charges already rose to $148 million this quarter from $46 million. The filing expects about $500 million of further restructuring charges before year-end. PepsiCo claimed refunds and said it "received substantially all of the refunds of such tariffs". The administration has since introduced new tariffs, so the group's import costs remain uncertain, and the refund will not repeat. — • — • — 💲 𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗞𝗣𝗜𝘀 𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗵 𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄 (𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲): $𝟱,𝟴𝟱𝟳 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 ⇗ accelerating Cash left after capital spending rose 81% from $3,241 million a year ago. Operating cash flow grew because profit rose and payments to suppliers drained less cash. PepsiCo also made its final payment, $965 million, under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, so that outflow now ends. Five of the six businesses spent less, and only Europe, the Middle East and Africa spent more. Lower spending explains part of the stronger cash flow. PepsiCo replaced a range with one figure, the middle of the old range. By our math, that leaves about 3.6% underlying growth for the fourth quarter, above this quarter's 3.1%. The comparison gets harder, because last year's fourth quarter grew faster than last year's third. Exchange rates should now add about 1.5 points to revenue and profit-per-share growth this year, up from 1 point. The benefit is shrinking, though: currency added only 0.7 points to third-quarter revenue. The Mexican peso supplied most of this year's gain, according to the filing. Acquisitions and distribution deals from 2025 should now add about 1.5 points to revenue growth, up from 1 point. They added 1.7 points this quarter, almost all in North American beverages. The outlook covers only deals from 2025, so the boost ends next year. 𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗻𝗲𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵: 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘅𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗹𝘆 +𝟲% ⇘ decelerating 🠅 raised from +4% to +6% Raised to the top of the earlier range. The whole increase comes from currency and acquisitions, because the underlying sales outlook did not move. By our math, the plan leaves about 4.5% growth for the fourth quarter, below this quarter's 5.6%. Revenue grew 6.7% in the first nine months. The nine-month rate was 21.5%. A lower rate lifts profit per share: by our math it adds about 1.3 points to this year's growth, and that softens the cut to the profit target. The plan now has profit per share, before one-offs and currency moves, growing 1% to 2% this year. Growth reached 2% in the first nine months, so by our math the fourth quarter adds almost nothing. PepsiCo held this target for two quarters, pointed to its low end last quarter, and has now lowered it. Including currency, the plan has profit per share excluding one-offs growing about 3% at the middle of the range, to roughly $8.38. By our math, that leaves about $2.23 for the fourth quarter, 1% below a year ago. Nine-month growth was 5%, so the plan implies a clear slowdown at year-end. Nine-month spending ran at 3.2%, well inside the limit, so PepsiCo has room for a heavier fourth quarter. Last year's fourth quarter took 6.5% of revenue by our math. text: India has joined Washington’s campaign against excess manufacturing capacity—even as Washington investigates India for the same issue. That is the central theme for India in the Joint Ministerial Statement USTR announced on October 7, 2026. India and 14 other economies have agreed to coordinate against government-supported overproduction that distorts markets and threatens domestic industries. The initial focus: automobiles and EVs, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors and solar panels. No target country is named, although China appears to be the principal implied focus. But India’s position deserves closer attention. On March 11, 2026, USTR launched a Section 301 investigation into structural excess capacity across 16 economies. India, the EU, Japan, Mexico and South Korea are now both subjects of that investigation and signatories to the new declaration. They will help shape a collective response while their own industrial policies remain under US scrutiny. For India, USTR cited expanding capacity and potential export-driven oversupply in solar modules, steel and petrochemicals. It noted that India’s solar-module capacity was nearly three times annual domestic demand. The deadline for final findings is March 11, 2027. The Joint declaration itself imposes no tariffs, quotas or sanctions. It creates sectoral platforms to exchange information and explore coordinated defensive measures, with a technical meeting planned before December 2026. Any US remedies under Section 301 would follow a separate process and may impose new tariffs as the investigations on forced labour did. Yet the political question is already clear: will India’s participation help protect its manufacturers—or give Washington greater legitimacy to challenge their expansion? There is also a question of consistency. Participating economies are coordinating against market distortions without confronting the US over its own trade-rule violations during the past two years. India needs room to expand manufacturing, build supply chains and compete in export markets. Capacity exceeding current domestic demand cannot, by itself, establish harmful overproduction. That way any exports can be defined as surplus capacity. Signing the declaration must not become an admission that India’s manufacturing ambitions are part of the problem.

text: Japanese companies are retreating from China at a historic rate as a cooling economy and deepening diplomatic friction force corporations to reevaluate their presence in the world’s second-largest economy. According to Japanese corporate credit research firm Teikoku Databank, the number of Japanese firms operating in mainland China dropped to 10,118 as of June—the lowest count since tracking began in 2010, down 22% from June 2024 and 30% below its 2012 peak. The corporate exodus is being driven by shrinking profit margins, heightened U.S. tariff risks, escalating labor and manufacturing expenses, and aggressive competition from domestic Chinese competitors. Bilateral relations deteriorated sharply after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi stated in parliament last November that Japan could become militarily involved in the event of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. Beijing retaliated by restricting exports of critical minerals to Japanese companies and urging its citizens to avoid traveling to Japan. Jeremy Chan, an analyst at Eurasia Group, noted that while Japanese companies were already seeking to trim their footprint, the geopolitical tailspin has injected acute urgency into their withdrawal plans. Over the past two years, a record 4,137 Japanese firms completely pulled out of China, while only 1,221 entered through subsidiaries, factories, or offices—the lowest influx on record outside the COVID-19 pandemic. To offset the downturn, Japanese businesses are diversifying into alternative hubs like India and redirecting capital toward the United States. Topix-listed companies have seen the share of profits generated in China fall to under 15% this year, down from 23% in 2020, while the share originating from the U.S. climbed from 25% to 35%, according to estimates by Jesper Koll of Monex Group. Koll pointed out that while Washington is actively courting Japanese manufacturers to bolster domestic re-industrialization, Beijing has increasingly prioritized a self-reliant “made in and made by China” model. Deepening corporate anxiety, Beijing's detention of several Japanese nationals this year—including executives held in August over alleged dual-use export violations—has made companies wary of sending personnel across the border. “Japanese firms and their employees increasingly feel unwelcome and unsafe in China,” Chan said, reinforcing findings from the Japan External Trade Organization that show businesses are broadly unwilling to expand. In response to the mounting departures, Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng told a visiting Japanese trade delegation that China “always welcomes” Japanese investment, urging Tokyo to maintain the correct course on historical issues to preserve commercial ties. Analysts expect automakers, parts suppliers, and export-oriented manufacturers to lead the continued pullback, while specialized firms in precision machinery and medical equipment with deeply localized operations are more likely to remain.

text: Starlink is licensed in India. It got its GMPCS licence in June 2025. IN-SPACe cleared it in July 2025. Trial spectrum came in September 2025. Twenty gateways are built. The one thing it does not have is security clearance from the Ministry of Home Affairs — and under the DoT's draft spectrum rules, a licence is not permission to start: an operator awaiting security clearance for its equipment gets spectrum only after that clearance, and cannot connect to public telephone networks without explicit approval. So the question is not "who is blocking Starlink." It is why the last gate stays shut when four opened. The answer is in the record: • Iran. Roughly 50,000 Starlink terminals reported operating in Iran without authorisation by early 2026, used during protests after the state cut national connectivity. Reported terminal use during the Iran conflict is what Bloomberg reported in June 2026 as the trigger for the Home Ministry withholding clearance. If a network operates in a country where it is unlicensed, an Indian licence guarantees very little. • The operator has switched service on and off before, unilaterally. In 2023 Musk refused Ukraine's request to activate coverage over Sevastopol for a drone strike on the Russian fleet, saying he would not be "explicitly complicit in a major act of war." One private owner decided what a sovereign state's military could do on its own soil. In Brazil in 2024, when the Supreme Court moved against X, Justice Moraes froze the accounts of X and Starlink together; Starlink told regulator Anatel it would not block X until its accounts were unfrozen. That one only ended when money moved out of one company to settle another company's fine. • Licensing is coercible, and everyone watched it happen. In 2025 State Department documents obtained by The Washington Post showed US embassies pressing tariff-hit countries to clear Starlink's regulatory path, with the Secretary of State directing the push. Within two weeks of 50% US tariffs on Lesotho, that country licensed Starlink for the first time; a State Department memo recorded Lesotho "hopes that licensing Starlink demonstrates goodwill." None of that is a conspiracy of Indian telecom bosses. It is a regulator asking a fair question: can a foreign-owned, border-agnostic network, whose owner has refused shutdown orders elsewhere, be made to obey an Indian order in a crisis? South Africa has been asking an ownership version of the same question for four years — its 30% black-ownership rule — and Starlink still has not launched there.

text: Why India's Amines Industry Is Suddenly Interesting — And Why Today's Rally Needs a Closer Look | Detailed Amines are not a glamorous part of the chemical industry. But they sit quietly inside some very important products - from pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals to polyurethane foams, water treatment and specialty chemicals. And this week, the sector suddenly came into focus after the US started trade proceedings against certain amine compounds imported from China. The market's immediate interpretation was simple: China could become less competitive → Indian manufacturers could gain share. But the real story is more nuanced. First, what exactly are amines? Think of amines as chemical building blocks. They are used either directly in products or as catalysts that help other chemicals react in the right way. One interesting application is polyurethane (PU). PU is used in things like insulation, refrigerators, construction materials, mattresses, automobile components and spray foams. Certain amines act as catalysts that control how the polyurethane reaction takes place. So these chemicals may be small in quantity, but they can be critical to the manufacturing process. Why is China suddenly relevant? US producers have initiated anti-dumping and countervailing-duty proceedings against certain Chinese amine compounds. The important word is “certain.” This is NOT a blanket action against every amine exported from China. The proposed scope is product-specific, based on chemical characteristics and specifications. That distinction matters enormously for investors. A headline saying “US imposes duties on Chinese amines” could make the entire Indian amines sector look like an immediate beneficiary. But actual earnings benefit depends on: Which products are covered → Who manufactures them in India → Existing US sales → Available capacity → Customer approvals → Incremental orders. So who could benefit? The obvious names being discussed are: Balaji Amines, Alkyl Amines and Indo Amines. Balaji and Alkyl are major Indian amines players, so investors are naturally extrapolating a China-substitution opportunity. But there is an important reality check. The US proceedings do not automatically mean these companies will receive large new orders. At this stage, the earnings impact is not established. Indo Amines is particularly interesting because its product portfolio includes polyurethane catalysts such as Bis-DAPA, DMDPTA and DMDEE. That gives it a more direct product-level connection to the PU catalyst opportunity. But even here, we don't yet know the exact US revenue exposure, capacity available for exports or how much of its portfolio falls within the final legal scope. This is where investors need to be careful The market often jumps from: Trade action → China substitution → Indian capacity → higher earnings. There are several steps missing in between. The actual chain is: US trade case ↓ Final product scope ↓ Duties actually imposed ↓ Chinese competitiveness changes ↓ US customers seek alternatives ↓ Indian suppliers qualify ↓ Orders increase ↓ Capacity utilisation rises ↓ Margins improve We're currently much closer to the beginning of that chain. So today's stock-market reaction should be treated as a potential structural catalyst, not yet as a confirmed earnings upgrade. What makes the theme interesting beyond today's rally? The larger structural story is China's dominance in chemicals versus India's opportunity to become an alternative manufacturing base. If Western customers increasingly want: China + 1 then Indian specialty-chemical companies with the right products, quality certifications, manufacturing capability and customer relationships can potentially capture incremental volumes. But this will not happen simply because a tariff is announced. What should investors watch now? For the amines companies, I would focus on five things: 1. Exact product overlap - Which Indian products actually fall inside the US case? 2. US revenue exposure - How much are companies already selling into the US? 3. Capacity availability - Can they take additional orders without major capex? 4. Customer qualification - Are existing Chinese customers actually approaching Indian suppliers? 5. Realisation and margins - Is China substitution creating sustainable pricing power—or simply more volume? The bigger investment lesson Today's rally is interesting. But the opportunity is not the headline. The opportunity, if it develops, will come from actual product substitution and incremental volumes. That's why I would not treat every Indian amines company as an automatic beneficiary. The next few months should tell us much more. US trade action → product-level overlap → customer enquiries → orders → utilisation → earnings. Until that chain starts becoming visible, the right approach is to separate sector excitement from company-level fundamentals. Because in specialty chemicals, being in the right industry is not enough. You need to be making the right molecule, for the right customer, at the right cost. #Amines #SpecialtyChemicals #BalajiAmines #AlkylAmines #IndoAmines #Chemicals #Investing

text: OK, I've done business in the US, EU, UK, Japan, India, Bangladesh, Kenya and a few others. The UK is not a high-regulation country. The UK is not a high-tax country. The UK is a high-cost country. That's a problem, but the only way to fix that is to collapse the property market and undo a great deal of damage done to our energy supplies over many decades. Of course you can personally move to Dubai or Monaco. No developed country can compete with those right now (although Dubai is moving towards taxation now, and Abu Dhabi will eventually tire of footing the bills). Why aren't tech companies starting-up in the UK or Europe? Well, a lot of it has to do with the capital structures, and the general dollarisation of the world. Sterling has little competitive benefit these days, and the EU is not fully getting behind the benefits of the Euro. Some of it is to do with bankruptcy laws - the lack of Chapter 11 hurts us a great deal, and especially hurts lenders. If I lend to a high-growth company, I'd like to see the shareholders wiped out but the upside potential of the company retained, rather than the arrangements we have in the UK. Lenders can't use the growth potential as security, so instead have to take physical security, which in turn limits lending. Some of it is to do with market access. The US is the large, English-speaking elephant in the room. It is also politically unstable - your foreign market access can be cut off in a heartbeat (and often is). So if you want to access that market you have to be based there. The same is no true in reverse - we don't regulate overseas digital businesses remotely enough in the UK or EU meaning there's no market imperative to be based here. Some of it is to do with language - it is easier to deal in English than with a Tower of Babel of European languages. Some of it is to do with FX risk. Rightly or wrong, the dollar is perceived as safer, certainly than GBP. If the Pound slides 10%, that wipes out a lot of growth in the underlying business. But it is almost entirely not to do with taxation. The actual costs of US companies employing staff is often higher than in the UK, for instance. text: Indian bearing makers: the slowdown had outside causes, and they are fading Bearings let one part of a machine rotate smoothly against another. Cars, two-wheelers, trains, motors and wind turbines all use them. From FY24 to FY26, growth at most Indian bearing companies stalled. Most of the damage came from outside the companies, and those pressures have now eased. Bearings are harder to make than they look. Clean steel, precise heat treatment and smooth finishing are essential, and a vehicle maker may test a supplier for two to three years before approving it. After that, the supplier usually stays for the full life of the model, which keeps new entrants out. Four shocks hit the sector together: weak tractor demand after a poor monsoon, order cuts from European customers, a steep jump in US duties on some Indian parts, and higher steel and copper costs. Each one has turned. The GST (Goods and Services Tax) cut boosted vehicle sales, US duties on Indian bearings are now below those on China, exports are recovering, and railway wagon orders and wind installations are strong. Many companies added capacity during the downturn, so these plants can fill up quickly. Global bearing majors are also moving production to India over time, which benefits local suppliers of rings and cages such as Rolex Rings and Harsha Engineers. On valuation, NRB Bearings appears the most reasonable among companies that design their own products. Harsha stands out as a business with few peers in India. Multinational names such as SKF and Schaeffler already trade at high multiples. There are risks too. US tariff rules have changed four times in 18 months, and specialised bearings for EVs (electric vehicles) still come from abroad. Three things to track: 1Pace at which new plants fill up, especially Timken's Bharuch facility 2Wagon orders and wind installations 3Any quality rule on imported bearings A general takeaway: when a sector slows, separate internal problems from external ones. External problems that reverse can bring a recovery faster than expected. Source: Newspaper and SOIC article on Bearing

text: Global turmoil is testing every emerging economy: $100+ crude, wars disrupting energy routes, rising US yields, foreign capital outflows and a stronger dollar. Yet India enters this storm from a position of strength and that is where Modi govt's economic management needs to be praised or criticised. • Q1 FY27 GDP growth: 7.8% • Forex reserves: ~$766 billion • Current Account Deficit: just 0.5% of GDP • PSB profits: record ₹1.98 lakh crore • PSB Gross NPAs: historic low of 1.93% • PSB capital adequacy: 16.6% • Moody’s has upgraded FY27 growth forecast to 7% This resilience wasn’t created after the crisis began. Years of bank clean-up, fiscal consolidation, infrastructure-led capex, formalisation, stronger tax collections and building external buffers created the shock absorbers India is using today. The rupee is under pressure. Oil is expensive. Foreign investors are pulling money from emerging markets. But India is still growing near 8% with strong banks, massive reserves and a manageable external deficit. Before blaming Nirmala Sitharaman for every global shock, at least look at the numbers India is carrying into this turmoil. Inflation? CPI was 4.82% in August 2026 despite global energy and geopolitical pressures. Fiscal discipline? The Centre’s fiscal deficit is budgeted at 4.3% of GDP in FY27, down from 4.4% in FY26, while capital expenditure continues at massive scale. Taxes on ordinary consumption? Take common household products as an illustration: before GST, ₹100 of products such as toothpaste, shampoo and hair oil could carry roughly ₹31 of combined indirect taxes. That fell to ₹18 after GST and, following the latest rationalisation, many such essentials are now taxed at just 5%. Income tax? In 2013-14, the basic exemption for a normal individual was only ₹2 lakh, with 10%, 20% and 30% slabs thereafter. Today, under the new regime, an individual with taxable income up to ₹12 lakh can have NIL income-tax liability through the rebate; for salaried taxpayers, the ₹75,000 standard deduction can effectively take that to ₹12.75 lakh of salary. And look at the banking system. Public-sector banks posted record PROFIT of ₹1.98 lakh crore in FY26. That is not a cosmetic change. It means cleaner balance sheets, better-capitalised banks and greater capacity to lend when the world economy turns hostile. Oil shocks, wars, US yields, tariff battles and foreign capital flows are not controlled from North Block. The Finance Minister’s job is to ensure India enters those storms with fiscal space, manageable inflation, healthier banks and stronger domestic demand. Whether one likes Nirmala Sitharaman politically or not, those are the numbers that should be part of any serious assessment of her record.

text: India-US trade talks hit a plateau: FM Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said India-US trade talks have reached a plateau, and further give-and-take may now be very difficult. Talks are still on, but an early deal is not imminent. The main sticking point is the trade gap the US wants cut. She said the imbalance is being pushed through other means, as tariffs are now used as leverage, not just a bargaining tool. She added that if imbalance is the test, the same logic should apply to China. India is lining up new trade partners and expects bilateral investment treaties with at least three more countries, including Canada, by December or early next year. A treaty with Saudi Arabia was signed last week. New Delhi has also warned that any US tariff threat over Russian oil buys must not hurt India’s energy security.

text: Farai, your first principle is correct - diplomacy must serve domestic economic interest. Where you collapse is the maths. *Let's use real 2024-2026 numbers, not slogans:* *1. YES, the West is life support for VALUE-ADDED jobs. You are right on this.* - EU is SA's biggest trading bloc: *€46 billion (R880bn) total trade in 2025*, 23% of all SA trade in goods, 43% of all FDI in SA. 1,700 EU companies employ 500,000 direct jobs + 1.6m indirect. [EU Commission 2025] - AGOA: *R68bn in 2024 alone*, R300bn between 2019-2024, 22% of all SA exports to US use AGOA. SA is 54% of ALL AGOA exports since 2000. About 500,000 jobs linked. Automotive 22% of SA exports to US ($1.88bn). Citrus, wine, steel. [DTIC / Solidarity] - When Trump put 30% tariffs in Aug 2025, NAAMSA said it would kill the Eastern Cape auto industry. That is not ideology, that's factories. 718381b3 So if we lose AGOA eligibility in November 2026 review, it's 70,000 direct + 430,000 indirect jobs gone. No one serious denies this. *2. BUT your "Russia and China will not buy our cars and citrus" - China ALREADY buys more than the US.* - *China is SA's largest SINGLE export destination:* $13.5bn in 2025 vs US ∼$10bn. - In June 2026 alone: China ZAR24.1bn, US ZAR14.6bn, Germany ZAR14.1bn exports. [OEC] - China + India + Thailand + Saudi + UAE = 49.5% of SA imports. Asia has already overtaken Europe as leading import source.[TradeInt] 0f229b05 The problem is STRUCTURAL: We export ores to China (iron, chrome, manganese - 2/3 of exports) and import finished goods (machinery, phones, EVs at HS 8517). We export cars and fruit to EU/US and import machines. That is the colonial division of labour you want to preserve. China just offered *duty-free access for all African nations* in 2025 - precisely to replace AGOA if US leaves. That's not grandstanding, that's hedging. *3. BRICS is not about replacing the West, it's about not being held hostage by one market.* Lamola's real failure is NOT pro-BRICS. It is failing to convert BRICS into beneficiation. The smart policy is: Keep AGOA + EU EPA (98% duty-free under SADC EPA) for high-value jobs, while using BRICS CTIP deal signed Nov 2025 to force China to buy finished goods, not raw ores. EU signed its own Clean Trade Partnership with SA for the same reason - to secure critical minerals. Ramaphosa's hedging is not indecision - it is the classic middle-power strategy: Don't pick a side when you are a debtor nation. Indonesia, India, Brazil all do it. Non-alignment pays. The moment you pick Washington fully, you lose Beijing's R200bn import market. Pick Beijing fully, you lose 500k AGOA jobs. Your critique of Transnet and ports is correct - that's the real reason we have no leverage. Not ICJ. We can have the best diplomats, but if rail can't move cars to Durban, EU and China both go elsewhere. So the market verdict is not "West vs BRICS". The market verdict is: - If we lose AGOA in Nov 2026 because of ICJ posturing without a backup plan, that's economic illiteracy. - If we lose China because we want to please Washington for 4% of total exports (AGOA is <4% of SA total exports), that's also economic illiteracy. Farai, you are warning about ideological vanity on the left. I am warning about ideological vanity on the right - thinking the West will save us out of goodwill. The West will cut us the same second we are not useful - as they did with 30% tariffs. Realpolitik = Keep EU + Keep AGOA + Force China to buy beneficiated goods. Not one or the other.

This is NOT the same as saying “the trade deal is dead.” But the room for further give-and-take appears to have become very limited. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said both sides have reached a “plateau” beyond which further concessions could be “very, very difficult.” Talks are still ongoing. So what is actually stuck? ↓ 🇺🇸 US wants to reduce its trade deficit with India. 🇮🇳 India wants a balanced agreement without giving away too much on sensitive areas. And tariffs have increasingly become a tool to pressure trade partners. Sitharaman's point was interesting: Earlier: TRADE IMBALANCE ↓ NEGOTIATION ↓ MARKET ACCESS ↓ GIVE & TAKE Now: TRADE IMBALANCE ↓ TARIFF PRESSURE ↓ NEGOTIATION She described this shift as tariffs becoming “weaponised.” There is another important angle. The US is India's largest export destination, so the stakes are meaningful for Indian exporters. At the same time, India also has a massive trade deficit with China. Sitharaman's argument: If trade imbalances are the problem, the answer should ultimately involve NEGOTIATION and RECIPROCAL CONCESSIONS. Not simply tariffs. For investors, this is the part to watch: India–US trade deal + Tariffs + Russian oil issue + Export competitiveness + Supply-chain relocation can directly affect several sectors. IT services → relatively different exposure Pharma → US market dependence Textiles → tariff-sensitive Engineering goods → tariff + competitiveness Chemicals → global sourcing advantage matters Electronics → China+1 opportunity vs tariff risk The key takeaway: ❌ Deal is NOT dead. ❌ Deal is NOT imminent either. ⚠️ Negotiations appear to have reached a difficult bargaining point. And until the tariff structure becomes clearer, DON'T BUILD AN INVESTMENT THESIS AROUND AN UNFINALISED TRADE DEAL. Watch the policy. Watch the tariff. Then watch the company's actual numbers. POLICY → ORDERS → REVENUE → EARNINGS. That's the chain that matters.

text: Taleb, Game Theory — and Why the Tata Boardroom Is a Better Example Than the Prisoner’s Dilemma Nassim Taleb recently called game theory a “vuuuge scam” — typical Taleb provocation. But beneath the insult is a serious criticism: game theory works beautifully when the world is small, the players are known, the rules are stable and the payoffs are visible. Real life is rarely like that. Stephen Wolfram makes a similar point using the famous Tit-for-Tat strategy from Robert Axelrod’s Prisoner’s Dilemma tournaments. Tit-for-Tat is wonderfully simple: Cooperate first. If the other side defects, retaliate. If they return to cooperation, forgive. It performed brilliantly in Axelrod’s tournaments and became almost a moral lesson: cooperation can emerge even among self-interested players. Wolfram’s objection was uncomfortable: Tit-for-Tat won against the strategies humans happened to submit. What happens when you search a vastly larger universe of possible strategies? Suddenly there may be no universal winner. And that takes us from the laboratory to the boardroom. Consider the Tata conflict This may actually be a wonderful contemporary case study in why real-world “games” become impossible to reduce to neat payoff matrices. At one level, you could describe it simply: Tata Trusts owns roughly two-thirds of Tata Sons. Noel Tata represents the controlling shareholder. N. Chandrasekaran leads Tata Sons. Trustees and directors have differing views over governance, listing and control. Easy game-theory problem? Hardly. The current dispute involves Chandrasekaran’s leadership, Tata Sons’ potential listing, the Trusts’ relationship with Tata Sons, regulatory questions, and disagreements among trustees themselves. Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh have challenged actions associated with Noel Tata and taken complaints to Maharashtra’s charity regulator; Noel has in turn sought greater scrutiny of Tata Sons board processes. Now ask a game theorist to define the players. Noel? Chandra? Venu Srinivasan? Tata Trusts? Tata Sons? The Shapoorji Pallonji shareholder? The RBI? The Charity Commissioner? The Government? They are not even playing for the same prize. One player may optimize for corporate value. Another for shareholder control. Another for institutional independence. Another for preservation of the Tata philanthropic structure. Another for regulatory compliance. Another for liquidity. And each move alters the game itself. That is Taleb’s “large world.” Geopolitics is the same phenomenon, only with armies. Take India–Pakistan. A textbook model might say: Pakistan cooperates → India cooperates. Pakistan attacks → India retaliates. Pakistan de-escalates → India de-escalates. Tit-for-Tat. Except: who exactly is “Pakistan”? The civilian government? Military? Intelligence establishment? A militant organization? A splinter group? Now add China, Kashmir, elections, nuclear deterrence and domestic public opinion. An attack occurs. Before choosing the optimal response, India first has to answer a much harder question: Who actually made the move? US–China gets worse. “Tariff for tariff” looks like Tit-for-Tat. But neither country is merely maximizing next year's trade surplus. The game contains Taiwan, semiconductors, AI, rare earths, naval power, supply chains, alliances, domestic employment and technological sovereignty. Something economically irrational over three years may be strategically rational over twenty. So what exactly is the payoff? GDP? Military superiority? Regime stability? Technological independence? National prestige? There is no single scoreboard. The Middle East almost breaks the model completely. Imagine a proxy militia attacking Israel. @nntaleb @TataCompanies

text: US-India trade negotiations appear to have reached a difficult point, with senior officials on both sides signaling that an agreement may not be close despite months of intensive discussions. Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the talks have effectively “reached a plateau,” suggesting that both countries have already made significant concessions and that finding additional areas for compromise could be challenging. Her comments came shortly after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the negotiations were in their final stages but that a deal was not imminent. The two countries have been working toward a broader trade agreement after reaching an interim arrangement earlier this year, but disagreements over tariffs, market access and the overall balance of trade continue to complicate the negotiations. A major obstacle is the difference between Washington’s demands and New Delhi’s priorities, particularly over tariff levels, access to India’s protected markets and India’s continued purchases of Russian oil. US officials want to reduce America’s trade deficit with India and have maintained pressure on New Delhi to address issues surrounding Russian energy imports, while Indian officials are seeking assurances that India will receive competitive tariff treatment and will not face additional penalties after an agreement is reached. Washington’s newly expanded authority to impose potentially severe tariffs on countries that continue buying Russian oil has added another layer of uncertainty. Despite the impasse, both sides continue to negotiate and officials have indicated that discussions remain active, leaving open the possibility of a breakthrough if negotiators can resolve the remaining sticking points. - World Business News.

text: Trade talks with US are at an impasse – India Further concessions would be “very difficult” for both sides to make, although talks are ongoing, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman says Published 5 Oct, 2026 (FULL) India-US trade negotiations have hit a “plateau,” making further concessions “very difficult,” Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday, days after Washington said a deal is not imminent. India and the US have been negotiating a Bilateral Trade Agreement since February last year, covering market access, tariff and non-tariff barriers, digital trade, and supply-chain resilience. The finance minister’s comments, despite repeated assertions by both sides in the last few months that a deal is near completion, is the first clear indication that the talks have hit an impasse. “Both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which, giving, or taking, might be very, very difficult,” Sitharaman said at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi. She said the talks are continuing, and left open the possibility of movement if either side finds additional negotiating space, describing the proposed agreement as “hard and very rigorously negotiated.” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said last week, following talks with Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, that the two countries have identified the remaining sticking points, but that an agreement is not imminent. Among them are US demands for wider access for its farm and dairy products, a politically sensitive subject for New Delhi. Goyal struck a more optimistic note last month, saying the deal was almost “done and dusted.” He added, however, that implementation depends on India securing a competitive tariff advantage over rival exporters in the US market. US goods imports from India reached $103.8 billion last year, compared with $45.4 billion in exports, leaving the US with a $58.4 billion goods trade deficit. Total goods and services trade between the two countries stood at an estimated $239.6 billion. The balance is in India’s favor and Washington wants to reduce the gap, Sitharaman said. The failure to reach a deal “would not stop trade or raise tariffs” automatically, the founder of New Delhi-based think tank Global Trade Research Initiative, Ajay Srivastava, told RT. However, he said the tariff uncertainty would make pricing, contracts, and investment decisions harder. “The bigger risk is fresh US tariffs over Russian oil purchases or alleged excess manufacturing capacity. Signing a trade deal may not remove that risk.” A new law signed by President Donald Trump last month gives him authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue significant purchases of Russian energy. India, the second largest importer of Russian oil, has warned that the tariffs could hurt bilateral ties. Greer, however, has not publicly identified Russian oil as one of the unresolved issues in the trade negotiations

text: In my two decades of following the global economy and markets, I have rarely seen such despondence about the India story. To be fair, a spectrum of opinions continue to exist but the overall texture cannot be ignored. 2008 and 2020 were rightly seen as global problems, not unique to us. 2013 was more India-specific but seen as a macro adjustment not a doubt about the long-term story itself. Today with US Big Tech going all in on AI and with the rise of China, some are doubting India's convergence itself. Can we innovate, build, rise? I strongly disagree with this despondence. Not as an emotional or cocky reaction, but as an empirical and conceptual one. And as an analyst not an activist. As in what-is-likely-to-happen, not what-should-happen, which is a separate lens (for which I have written separately). Yes, a snapshot today is stark. The global trading system is under assault and so is the energy logistics system. If last year was all about tariffs, this year has been about Iran. The rupee is constantly weakening. The pandemic's after-effects linger. We are still of course relatively poor. Judicial-police-bureaucratic corruption and delays still haunt us, our cities and villages are not very liveable if you are not well off and our politics can still be cynical. Yet through it all, India's growth has been strong. Railroads are being laid rapidly. Human capital is improving annually and is likely to be rich-word-equivalent by the middle of the century. Tax reforms and tech are creating a 1.5 billion market. Our banks are in great shape, entrepreneurs and innovators are raising risk capital, companies are deleveraged, inflation is low and trade is booming yet more balanced and diversified. There is largely peace and stability. India is being stitched together across regions, languages, castes, sects, even classes. An incredible churn which lowers our legendary capacity for self-sabotage. As somebody who is obsessed with history - economic, financial, political, cultural - it is difficult to impress how unique this moment is. My fundamental starting point is that human beings are basically similar, if not same, across large numbers. An Indian has the same potential to be creative and take risks and change the world as an American or Chinese (or African or European), if the right nurture is provided. The bedrock of Indian society is its family structure, which despite many much-needed ongoing changes (especially from a woman's perspective) largely remains a healthy institution that teaches deferred gratification. What is new is the Indian state, which has finally been able to begin to organise this gargantuan latent scale. It is the pluralist yet rooted nature of India which has ensured that Indians have taken to democracy like fish to water, which in turn ensures this scale. To understand the importance of scale, see how Europe - despite its prosperity - is unable to respond to various changes effectively. It became dependent on American security, Russian energy, Chinese markets and Middle Eastern migrants because the centre did not hold. Structurally, the European Union wants to be what India has already become. Yes, India is poorer but that is rapidly changing by historical standards. Political changes - be in Europe or China - are perhaps more difficult. Till the 2040s, India has an incredible demographic transition tailwind, and its growth will surprise most. Many (not all) of the worries you probably flagged a decade or so ago have been solved or ameliorated. We have rightly moved on to worrying about a new cohort. And that constant worrying is part of the reason why India will succeed. There is no large, liquid, diversified story which is structurally more sound than India yet cyclically more depressed in terms of its currency or markets. More on this very soon. #LongIndia

Sitharaman’s remarks point to that transition. The discussion is no longer centered only on tariff schedules or product categories but on Washington’s broader objective of reducing a deficit that is politically visible in the United States. That changes the character of the talks. Trade deficits are influenced by consumer demand, competitiveness, supply chains and investment patterns, many of which cannot be quickly altered through a single agreement. If deficit reduction becomes a primary benchmark, the range of acceptable compromises narrows. India appears increasingly willing to absorb delay rather than accept terms it sees as limiting future policy flexibility. That stance suggests New Delhi believes its bargaining position has strengthened compared with the early stages of the negotiations. text: THE SALAMANDER OF LISIEUX VI Sculpted above the group of the man with the griffin, we notice an enormous grimacing head adorned with a pointed beard. Its cheeks, ears, and forehead are stretched out to the extent that they take on the appearance of flaming expansions. This blazing mask, with an unfriendly grin, seems crowned and provided with horned, ribboned appendices which are resting on a twisted cord in the background of the cornice (Plate IX). With its horns and its crown, the solar symbol takes on the meaning of a genuine Baphomet; in other words, of the synthetic image in which Templar Initiates had assembled all the elements of high science and tradition. Truly a complex figure under its apparent simplicity, an eloquent figure, pregnant with teaching in spite of its rude and primitive aesthetic. If we recognize at first the mystic fusion of the natures of the Work, symbolized by the horns of the lunar crescent placed on the solar head, we are no less surprised by the strange expression, reflection of a devouring ardor emanating from the inhuman face, specter of the last judgment. Even the beard, hieroglyph of a luminous and fiery beam projected toward the earth, justifies the exact knowledge of our destiny that the scientist possessed. Could we possibly be facing the dwelling of some affiliate of the sets of the Illuminati or of the Rosicrucians, descendants of the old Templars? The cyclical theory, concurrent with the doctrine of Hermes, is so clearly exposed here, that except for ignorance or dishonesty we could not suspect the knowledge of our Adept. As for us, our conviction is firm; we are certain not to be mistaken in front of so many categorical assertions: we indeed have before our eyes a baphomet, renewed from the one of the Templars. This image, about which we possess but vague indications or simple hypotheses, never was an idol, as some believed, but rather a complete emblem of the secret traditions of the Order, especially used outwardly as an esoteric paradigm, a seal of chivalry, and a sign of recognition. It was composed of an isosceles triangle, its apex pointed down, hieroglyph for water, first created element, according to Thales of Miletus, who maintained that "God is the Spirit which has formed all things from water" (1). A second similar triangle, inverted in relationship to the first, but smaller, was inscribed in its center and seemed to occupy the position reserved for the nose on the human face. It symbolized fire and more precisely, fire enclosed in water, or the divine spark, soul incarnate, life infused in matter. On the inverted base of the large triangle of water, there was a graphic sign similar to the Latin letter H or Greek [*158-1] (eta), but wider whose central bar was cut with a median circle. This sign in hermetic steganographiy indicates the universal Spirit, the Creative Spirit, God. Inside the large triangle, slightly above and on each side of the triangle of fire, one could see on the left the lunar circle with an inscribed crescent and on the right the solar circle with a visible center. These small circles were arranged in the manner of eyes. Finally, welded to the base of the small inner triangle, the cross, placed on the globe, thus realized the double hieroglyph of sulphur, active principle, associated to mercury, passive principle and solvent of all metals. A longer or shorter segment often located at the apex of the triangle was carved with lines of a vertical tendency where the layman could recognize not the expression of luminous radiation but a sort of goatee. Thus presented, the baphomet assumed a gross animal form, imprecise and uneasy to identify. This would probably explain the diversity of descriptions it inspired, where the baphomet is seen as a haloed death head or a bucrane, sometimes the head of the Egyptian Hapi, of a goat, and, even better, the horrifying face of Satan himself! Simple impressions, far removed from reality, but images so unorthodox that they, alas, contributed to spread the accusation of demonology and sorcery upon the learned Knights Templar and became one of the foundations of their trial, one of the causes of their condemnation. We have just seen what the baphomet was; now we must try to discover the meaning hidden behind this name. In the pure hermetic expression corresponding to the labor of the Work, Baphomet comes from the Greek roots [*158-2] (Bapheus), dyer, and [*159-1], standing for [*159-2], the moon; unless we want to use [*159-3], [*159-4], in the genetive case, mother or matrix, which leads to the same lunar meaning, since the moon is truly the mother or the mercurial matrix which receives the tincture or seed of sulphur, representing the male, the dyer --- [*159-5] (Bapheus) --- in metallic generation. [*159-6] has the meaning of immersion and of tincture. And it can be said, without revealing too much, that sulphur, father and dyer of the stone, fertilizes the mercurial moon through immersion, which brings us back to the symbolic baptism of Mete, expressed again by the word baphomet (2). It appears as the complete hieroglyph of science, represented elsewhere in the personality of the god Pan, mythical image of nature in full activity. The Latin word Bapheus, dyer, and the verb meto, to gather, collect, harvest, also indicate the special quality possessed by mercury or the moon of the sages, of collecting the tincture gradually as it emitted during the immersion or the king’s bath, and which the mother keeps in her bosom for the required time. It is the Grail containing the eucharistic wine, liquor of spiritual fire, vegetative liquor, living and vivifying, introduced into material things. As for the origin of the Order, its lineage, the knowledge and beliefs of the Templars, we could not do better than to literally quote a fragment of the study which Pierre Dujols, the erudite and learned philosopher, devotes to the brother knights in his Bibliographie Generale des Sciences Occultes (3). "The brothers of the Temple", says the author, "--- and we could no longer uphold the opposite view --- were truly affiliated to Manichaeism". Furthermore, Baron de Hammer’s thesis conforms to this opinion. For him, the sectarians of Mardeck, the Ismaelians, the Albigensians, the Templars, the Freemasons, the Illuminati, etc., depend on the same secret tradition emanating from this House of Wisdom (Dar-el-hickmet) founded by Hakem in Cairo around the 11th century. The German academician Nicolai concludes in the same sense and adds that the famous baphomet, which he derives from the Greek word [*159-7] (Baphometos), was a Pythagorean symbol. We will not spend any time with the divergent opinions of Anton, Herder, Munter, etc., but we will dwell for a moment on the etymology of the word baphomet. The idea of Nicolai is acceptable if we admit, with Hammer, this slight variation: [*160-1](Baphe Meteos), which could be translated as "baptism of Mete". Precisely a rite of this name has been established among the Ophites. Mete was an androgynous divinity representing naturing Nature. Proclus says verbatim that Metis, also called [*160-2] (Erikarpaios) or Germinating Nature, was the hermaphroditic god of the Snake worshippers. We also know that the Greeks venerated Prudence, designated by the word Metis, as Jupiter’s wife. In a word, this philological discussion indisputably confirms that the Baphomet was the pagan expression of Pan. And like the Templars, the Ophites had two baptisms: one, exoteric, the baptism of water, the other esoteric, that of the spirit, or fire. The latter was called the Baptism of Mete. St Justin and St Irenaeus called it illumination. It is the Freemasons’ baptism of Light. This purification --- the word is truly appropriate here --- is found on one of the Gnostic idols discovered by Monsieur de Hammer, which he illustrated. It holds in its lap --- mark well the gesture as it is very revealing --- a fire-filled basin. Tungsten: Small Volumes, Outsized Criticality Tungsten is a dense, hard, high-strength metal with the highest melting point of any metal (about 3,422°C), which makes it hard to substitute in extreme-heat, wear and high-density uses. It is a strategic input for cutting tools, defense, aerospace and semiconductors, yet roughly 80% of global supply sits in China, which has tightened exports since 2025. Tungsten's value rests on its density (close to gold's) and exceptional hardness, and two of its derivatives matter most commercially. The first is tungsten carbide, formed by combining tungsten powder with carbon. It has hardness approaching that of diamond and is usually sintered with a cobalt binder into cemented carbide. This is the largest end use, at roughly half or more of demand by most industry estimates, and it goes into cutting tool inserts, drill bits, mining and oil and gas tooling, dies and wear parts that underpin modern machining in autos, aerospace and general engineering. Cobalt is a second input in this chain, and carbide scrap recycling is a meaningful secondary source of tungsten. The second is tungsten hexafluoride, a gas made by reacting tungsten metal with fluorine. It is far smaller in volume but critical in semiconductors, where it is the precursor for chemical and atomic layer deposition of the thin tungsten films used for contacts, vias and plugs in logic chips and for wordlines in 3D NAND and DRAM. Ultra-high-purity WF₆ has no easy substitute in these processes, so chipmakers depend on a reliable supply of high-grade tungsten metal. Beyond these two, tungsten also goes into tool steels and superalloys, heavy alloys for defense, counterweights and radiation shielding, X-ray targets and filaments, and emerging uses such as fusion reactor components. text: History Share New chat What is the likely outcome of the Cannadian and American debacle Thought for 8s The current Canada–U.S. “debacle” is the trade and political rupture that followed the collapse of negotiations in August 2026. It is a commercial conflict with sovereignty rhetoric attached, not a security crisis, and the most likely path is a prolonged, uneven decoupling rather than either a quick return to the old free-trade status quo or an outright break. After months of talks, a near-deal fell apart in late August. The Trump administration then imposed 50 percent tariffs on roughly $20–28 billion of Canadian goods (about 5 percent of Canadian exports to the United States), using a 1930 Tariff Act provision. Prime Minister Mark Carney matched them dollar-for-dollar with Canadian tariffs of 15–50 percent on about C$27.6 billion of U.S. goods, effective early September, plus a support package for affected industries. Washington escalated further with outright import bans, effective 29 September, on selected Canadian alcohol, dairy products (including whey), and motorcycles—covering on the order of $1 billion, or roughly 0.25 percent of Canadian exports to the U.S. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said the administration sees no urgency to settle, while warning of possible further tariffs on autos, parts, and steel. Trump has described Canada as “very bad” and “being taught a little lesson,” alongside earlier 51st-state comments and an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” (which does not change existing treaties or statutes). The economic effects so far are concentrated, not economy-wide. Two-way goods trade remains on the order of $800–900 billion a year; energy, potash, and much agricultural trade continue. The bans and the 50 percent tariffs hit politically sensitive sectors (dairy, liquor, steel, autos, motorcycles) more than overall GDP. Canadian goods exports to the United States had already fallen from about 77 percent of the total in early 2024 to about 68 percent in the first half of 2026. Canadian travel to the United States dropped sharply in 2025 and has only partly recovered. Polling after the latest tariffs found roughly 41 percent of Canadians describing the United States as an “enemy country.” Likely near-term outcome (through late 2026 and into 2027): Continued standoff is the base case. Analysts tracking the dispute put the odds of further material U.S. trade or procurement restrictions in the 70–85 percent range and additional Canadian retaliation in the 55–70 percent range, with only a low teens probability of a serious strategic-resource or sovereignty confrontation and a very low probability of military or extraordinary national-security measures. A limited, face-saving deal remains possible—especially if U.S. midterm results in November constrain the administration—but USTR comments and Carney’s refusal of terms he called sovereignty-limiting (including restrictions on Canada’s other trade agreements) make a full restoration of the prior USMCA framework unlikely soon. Canada will keep trying to diversify (EU, India, critical minerals) and shield auto, steel, and dairy interests. That reduces leverage for Washington over time but does not eliminate Canada’s structural dependence. Longer-term, the deeper outcome is already visible in both capitals and in Canadian public opinion: the post-1980s project of ever-closer North American economic integration is treated as damaged or finished, even if a narrower commercial accommodation is eventually reached. Trust and the assumption of automatic partnership are the main casualties; the bulk of energy and commodity trade is more durable than the political relationship around it.

text: Steel Sector Likely to Witness Several 'Good' Quarters: Domestic Prices at Premium to Import Parity, Restocking Ahead of Busy Season The Outlook Commodity traders and analysts believe the domestic steel sector is likely to see several good quarters Domestic hot-rolled coil (HRC) prices are at small premiums to import-parity prices Low inventory and high demand should lead to re-stocking going into the busy season spanning October to March This comes as infrastructure building and construction gain pace following the end of the monsoon Price Trends Indian steel producers have taken price hikes driven by higher input costs Coking coal prices are high, but mine restarts in China should reduce prices due to supply expansion In the July-September quarter (Q2), domestic steel realisations are overall expected to soften due to monsoon-led seasonal weakness Domestic rebar prices have recovered on tightening supply and low inventories; auto sector contract price revisions in Q1 will partially offset any softness In September: per tonne domestic HRC and primary rebar prices rose to ₹61,700 and ₹57,300, respectively; rebar was rebounding from ₹48,000 a tonne in July In August, domestic rebar prices were up 10% MoM (after falling for three months) and up 12% YoY HRC prices increased 2% MoM and 19% YoY; the rebar increase was due to planned maintenance shutdowns, lower inventories and good demand Stainless steel prices also strengthened, up 3% MoM and 17% YoY Global and Input Cost Backdrop In the UK and the Netherlands, steel prices are expected to improve in Q2 and Q3 (October-December) European coking coal costs will also rise; HRC prices in the US are up over 30% from August levels, while China's export HRC prices are stable Iron ore is soft, with NMDC cutting prices in August in response to softer global ore price; but coal is up In September, NMDC raised lump ore prices by ₹150 per tonne but kept ore fines unchanged Currently, given geopolitics, global demand is being driven more by concerns around potential supply-chain disruption than prices; security of supply is a high priority, and the US market has absorbed 50% tariffs on steel and aluminium Company Views Tata Steel and JSW Steel have high capacity of flat products and lower exposure to external coking coal SAIL has high exposure to coke prices Jindal Steel and JSW Steel may be strong plays on improving volumes, with possible upsides to consensus estimates of ferrous metal realisations for FY27 SAIL has the highest operating leverage and exposure to recovering rebar prices Tata Steel looks more attractive in the near term from a valuation standpoint, with an improving earnings outlook for European operations For the medium term, Jindal Steel and JSW Steel offer strong combinations of volume growth and pricing leverage Investors should be selective and monitor domestic supply-demand and raw material costs; the recovery in steel prices has already led to a positive re-rating across the sector, and the key question is whether realisations have started to recover after hitting rock-bottom levels Q1 Results Snapshot Tata Steel: consolidated Ebitda in line with consensus at ₹9,264 crore (up 25% YoY, down 6% QoQ); consolidated revenue ₹60,794 crore, up 14% YoY, down 4% QoQ, ahead of consensus; PAT ₹2,664 crore (up 21% YoY, down 18% QoQ) SAIL: adjusted revenue ₹26,555 crore (up 3% YoY, down 14% QoQ); adjusted Ebitda ₹4,462 crore, up 72% Y-o-Y, which comfortably beat consensus; PAT ₹1,644 crore, up 121% YoY Coal India: consolidated revenue ₹46,255 crore, up 8% YoY; adjusted Ebitda ₹10,238 crore, down 9% YoY and 17% QoQ, in line with estimates; reported Ebitda ₹12,069 crore, a miss versus consensus; net profit ₹8,852 crore, up 1% YoY, down 18% QoQ, ahead of consensus due to high other income Core Theme With domestic HRC trading at small premiums to import parity, inventories low and the October-March busy season ahead, analysts expect several good quarters for steel, helped by recovering rebar prices (₹57,300 per tonne in September from ₹48,000 in July), with JSW Steel and Jindal Steel favoured for volume and pricing leverage, SAIL for operating leverage and Tata Steel for valuation, though investors are advised to stay selective as sector re-rating has already begun and input costs remain a watch point.

text: A Byproduct of Gas Processing Became a Record U.S. Export in the First Half of 2026 The United States shipped an average of 2 million barrels of propane abroad every day in the first half of 2026, the highest level on record. The Energy Information Administration published the figure on October 1. It is 11% above the average for January through June of 2025. April set the monthly record at about 2.1 million barrels per day, and the agency said shipments after April stayed well above the five-year average. The agency tied the growth to record domestic production. Propane is a byproduct of natural gas processing and crude oil refining, so output rises with gas and oil production whether or not Americans burn more of it. Supply that domestic customers do not buy moves to export terminals on the Gulf Coast. Buyers in India and other South Asian countries took more of those cargoes, the agency said. The research compiled for this piece attributes part of that demand to importers replacing Middle Eastern supplies disrupted by regional instability, and to American propane selling below Asian prices. China moved the other way. Beijing placed a 10% tariff on U.S. propane in February 2025, raised it to 125% in April of that year, and returned it to 10% in May. U.S. propane exports to China fell 28% in 2025 compared with 2024. They fell a further 19% in the first half of 2026 against the same months a year earlier. Total exports still set a record, which means other buyers absorbed more than China gave up. Two physical limits now bear on further growth. The first is terminal capacity. Enterprise Products is expanding its Houston Ship Channel and Nederland terminals in Texas, a project the agency said would add 300,000 barrels per day of export capacity and is expected to finish this year. The second is the Panama Canal, where drought has cut the number of daily transits and raised the cost of the route from the Gulf Coast to Asia. More recent figures suggest the pace held into autumn. Weekly agency estimates cited in the research report put exports at 2.08 million barrels per day for the week ending September 11, 2.2 million for the week ending September 18 and 2.07 million for the week ending September 25. Weekly estimates are preliminary and are not directly comparable with final monthly data. Those three figures were not rechecked for this piece. Prices abroad have been rising. Reuters reported on October 1 that Saudi Aramco raised its October propane benchmark by $55 to $680 per metric ton, according to the research report. That price applies to international contracts and does not by itself show what American households will pay. The winter heating season begins within weeks. The agency's report does not say whether record exports will tighten domestic supply this winter. That depends on how production, inventories and regional delivery capacity compare with what leaves the country, and the report gives no forecast for any of them.
