text: 📗The road to Mad Max? - Fuel, scarcity and imminent collapse📗 Constantin von Hoffmeister The road to Mad Max begins long before the first armed convoy appears on the horizon. It starts when tanker trucks stop running, refineries close, fuel tanks run out, and machines that supply cities and move armies begin to run out of fuel. First comes the price impact. Then the queues. Then the black market. And then the question that every government fears: what happens when the system still exists on paper, but the fuel that keeps it alive no longer arrives? Diplomacy suddenly acquired an urgency. Sergey Lavrov and Marco Rubio met in New York. US and Iranian representatives held indirect talks outside the United Nations General Assembly. Kirill Dmitriev traveled to the United States to meet with members of the Trump administration. Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit, where Trump personally received him at Andrews Air Force Base. These meetings revolve around different wars, powers and interests, but all develop in the same context: energy. Halford Mackinder taught that global politics is ultimately based on physical space control, communications and resources. States can speak the language of law, values and diplomacy, but ships still need fuel, diesel trucks and armies, supply lines. Therefore, the current diplomatic turmoil can be interpreted, in part, as a reaction to a tangible fact that no communication can erase: the global fuel supply system is under immense pressure. Alfred Thayer Mahan immediately understood the origin of the danger. The modern economy still depends on a handful of sea routes that geography has become irreplaceable. The Strait of Hormuz is severely affected, Bab el-Mandeb remains dangerous and the East-West Saudi pipeline has been temporarily shut down after several attacks. It’s not just about lines drawn abstractly on a map. They are the arteries through which crude oil and refined products flow from the producer to the consumer. When several of these arteries narrow simultaneously, the entire system begins to compete for the remaining available routes. There may be considerable amounts of oil underground, but that matters little if it cannot reach a refinery, if the refinery cannot obtain raw materials or if refined diesel cannot be transported to its market. Mahan wrote about the dominance of the seas in military terms. Today, it also means the control of oil routes, export terminals and insurance policies that allow cargoes to sail. Nicholas Spykman argued that power is concentrated along the great coastal strip of Eurasia. Just look at the diesel crisis to understand its magnitude. Russia restricted its diesel exports following repeated Ukrainian attacks that damaged its refining capability. Routes across the Middle East were disrupted. Asian refineries must compete for crude oil and decide how much fuel they can reserve for foreign buyers. As a result, the United States has become even more important as an exporter, even as U.S. consumers themselves are paying record prices: the national average price of diesel has exceeded six dollars per gallon this month. Global reserves are so low that, according to Reuters, shortages could drag on well beyond early 2027. Therefore, the problem is no longer limited to a single war. The pressure extends from Russia to the Persian Gulf, the Persian Gulf to Asia, from Asia to Europe and Africa, and then from foreign demand to the U.S. domestic market. Spykman regarded Eurasia as an interconnected strategic belt. The diesel market demonstrates the same thing through pipelines, refineries and tankers. Next, the problem of sanctions arises, and here Carl Schmitt proves to be more useful than most economists. Schmitt insisted that political power is more clearly manifested in the ability to decide when ordinary rules cease to apply. On September 18, Trump signed the Lindsey O Act. Graham of Sanctions to Russia and Iran. Among other provisions, this law authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and natural gas. This represents considerable legal power. But power in theory and power in practice are two distinct things. China and India remain key buyers of Russian energy, while Russian crude oil continues to supply refineries serving global markets. Enforcing the law with the utmost rigor could therefore penalize Moscow and, at the same time, increase the pressure on the fuel market that Washington is trying to stabilize. The paradox is essentially Schmittian: the greater the exceptional power that is deposited in the hands of the executive power, the greater the caution with which it determines when it can actually exercise it. Friedrich List would have immediately understood the fundamental problem. A country is not economically sovereign simply because it can buy something cheap abroad. Sovereignty requires productive capacity. Some states produced much more refined fuel than they consumed, while others allowed their refining capacity to stagnate because imports were cheaper. This system seemed efficient because the sea routes were open, the exporters were reliable and the political risks seemed manageable. This world is disappearing. Russian exports have been restricted, refining capacity and shipping in the Middle East have been paralyzed by the war, and Asian refineries are adjusting their production to meet their own needs. Even China, which has recently increased its exports of refined products, treats them as a variable that can restrict or expand depending on their internal situation. The old List distinction between wealth and the ability to produce wealth seems suddenly less obsolete. A fleet of tanks filled with imported diesel represents wealth. A refinery capable of replacing these imports represents power. Karl Polanyi would have added that markets never exist independently of society. On a trading screen, diesel appears as one more commodity; but outside the stock market, it drives virtually everything that keeps industrial society alive. The shortage of gasoline causes inconvenient to motorists and quickly becomes a political problem. The shortage of diesel has a much greater reach. Trucks carry food. Tractors cultivate the fields. Excavators open mines and construction sites. Fishing boats bring protein. Backup generators keep hospitals, factories and telecommunications in operation. When the price of diesel rises sharply, the increase is not limited to gas stations. It extends to the freight, food, construction, mining and electricity sectors. Therefore, the current shortage is more significant than a regular increase in commodity prices. A modern society can tolerate a rise in the price of a luxury item. He finds it much more difficult to cope with an increase in the cost of transporting, producing and distributing virtually anything. Reuters today describes inventories in several major markets as historically low, while refining margins in Asia have reached extraordinary levels. Polanyi said economic crises end up becoming a social crisis. Diesel provides an exceptionally direct transmission mechanism. Fernand Braudel would have urged us to stop focusing solely on the presidents and instead to examine the structures that underpin them. Africa offers a paradigmatic example. For decades, much of the continent exported crude oil and imported refined petroleum products. The tankers arrived at the coastal ports, the fuel was unloaded and then fleets of tanker trucks carried it hundreds, even thousands, of kilometers inland. This system relies on cheap shipping, operating ports, accessible refineries and enough foreign currency to purchase the products. If an item is deleted, the network becomes more expensive. If several are removed at a time, the network may collapse. The huge Dangote refinery in Nigeria is significant precisely because it alters this ancient structure by creating a large-scale refining capability within Africa. Its operators predict that global fuel tensions will persist beyond the ongoing war in the Middle East. Braudel wrote history by studying the material foundations, slow and deep, underlying transcendental political events. Refineries, ports, and fuel tanks belong to this deeper layer. Immanuel Wallerstein’s global systems approach helps us understand why poorer importing states suffer the most serious consequences. An industrialized and wealthy country facing high diesel prices can turn to its reserves, subsidize consumers, adjust taxes, overcome the offers of poorer competitors to monopolize shipments or redirect some of the demand to other forms of energy. A poor country that imports almost all of its fuel has fewer resources. Participate in the same global auctions with less money. When the offer is contracted, the best bidder not only receives a better service: another runs the risk of not receiving any shipments. Current tensions in Pakistan’s energy sector have already led the government to restore energy-saving measures, such as restrictions on fuel consumption in utilities and reduced business hours. In a crisis of this magnitude, the crucial dividing line is not simply between East and West, nor between the North and the South, but between States with sufficient financial, industrial and logistical capacity to absorb a crisis and those whose economies depend on an uninterrupted flow of imported essential goods. Ibn Khaldun would have understood what is happening next, considering that the political order was based on material cohesion rather than on the government ceremony. When the tanker truck stops coming, the crisis spreads throughout society. The irrigation pump runs out of water. The tractor remains inactive next to the field. The flour mill reduces its production. The delivery truck cannot make its routes. Food is made more expensive. The power supply becomes less reliable. Anger, initially directed at the price of fuel, begins to spread to all the grievances already existing in society. Governments in fragile states rarely fall for a single commodity, but shortages can reveal previously hidden weaknesses. Therefore, the shortage of diesel deserves as much attention as fertilizers and cereals. Agriculture depends on all three. If fertilizers are removed, yields decrease. If cereal imports are eliminated, food prices rise. If diesel is removed, even the available grain may not reach cities. Giovanni Arrighi would have placed this phenomenon in the broader context of the redistribution of economic power under way. Energy exporters exert influence because the industrial system simply cannot function without substantial flows of physical raw materials. Therefore, Russia, Iran and the Gulf producers occupy positions that cannot be understood solely through GDP figures or financial market valuations. At the same time, consumers like China and India are gaining influence because they can absorb huge volumes that were previously sent elsewhere. Russian crude can be shipped to the east, refined in Asia and then returned to global markets in another way. Therefore, sanctions reconfigure trade rather than simply eliminating it. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have imposed real costs on Russia, including internal scarcity and reduced refining capacity, but have also contributed to reducing international supply of diesel. This does not demonstrate the existence of a deliberate Russian strategy to provoke a global shortage. However, it does mean that the shortage of raw material can increase the trading value of the remaining Russian reserves. Jean Thiriart conceived geopolitics in terms of continental blocks, rather than small isolated states, and the current fuel crisis demonstrates the importance of the continental scale. Europe is once again discovering that energy security is intrinsically linked to geography. The United States can count on an immense domestic oil production. Russia has vast reserves of hydrocarbons. China has a huge industrial and refining capacity. India has built some of the largest refineries in the world. Europe, on the other hand, combines high consumption with a considerable dependence on imported energy and refined products. Therefore, record fuel prices in several European countries are more than just a problem for consumers. They reveal the cost of occupying a rich but resource-dependent peninsula at the western end of Eurasia, while relations with its main energy supplier in the east are broken. Whether Europe will respond by further diversifying its supply sources, rebuilding its refining capacity, accelerating electrification or possibly reopening certain channels with Russia is a political issue. Geography, however, has not changed. Alexander Dugin’s multipolar language offers another way of interpreting diplomatic effervescence. The world is becoming more difficult to organize around a single center capable of setting rules for everyone else. Washington may sanction Russia, but it must take into account the reactions of China and India. Russia may redirect its energy to the east, but China and India may demand refunds. China can harness its industrial power, but it remains heavily dependent on energy sea routes. Gulf monarchies possess oil and refining capacity, but a war could close their export routes. Iran may threaten the Strait of Hormuz, but any disruption also threatens the Asian allies with whom Tehran wishes to maintain relations. No actor is sovereign over the whole system. Each has some important strengths and several weaknesses. In practice, multipolarity resembles less a harmonious congress of civilizations than a ruthless market where power dynamics, geographical advantages and needs are exchanged. The current negotiations take on their full meaning from this perspective: the powers negotiate because none of them can control all the consequences of a continuous escalation. Arnold Toynbee wrote that civilizations are forged from their responses to challenges. The next few months could represent a very real test of brutality. The global diesel system is already under pressure: U.S. prices The U.S. has exceeded six dollars per gallon, refining margins in Asia have reached record levels, European consumers face exceptionally high fuel costs and analysts predict that depletion of reserves will remain a problem until 2027. However, the markets are also adapting. China can export more refined products. New refining capacity can be launched. Demand can decrease. The Strait of Hormuz can be fully reopened. text: The Atlantic has published a major article by Anne Applebaum titled “MAGA Is Making the World Safe for Corruption.” It is a very important piece about what she believes U.S. foreign policy is becoming: a mix of an ideological far-right revolution, private business, personal connections, and U.S. state power. “Far-right ideologues have turned American foreign policy into a tool for private enrichment and anti-democratic reaction.” In 2025, the Trump administration imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, revoked the visas of eight Supreme Court justices, and imposed sanctions against Justice Alexandre de Moraes and his family. According to Applebaum, the reason was not economic. The court was hearing the case against Jair Bolsonaro, and de Moraes himself had clashed with Elon Musk. At the time, Trump publicly called the case against Bolsonaro a “witch hunt,” while Steve Bannon referred to Bolsonaro’s supporters — who stormed government buildings after the election — as “freedom fighters.” The article explicitly documents a new U.S. policy: American economic and diplomatic power is no longer being used to pressure a dictatorship, but to interfere in the domestic politics of a democratic state in favor of an ideologically aligned politician. At the same time, official channels are not functioning. A Brazilian official explains: “All the official channels that we have, they just suddenly went out of touch. And what happened is that myriad informal actors just started knocking at our doors.” Lobbyists, people with access to Mar-a-Lago, MAGA influencers, and businesspeople are emerging — all offering political services while simultaneously seeking to advance their own commercial interests. One investor, for example, offered to arrange a meeting for the Brazilians with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in exchange for access to critical minerals. The America that allies once knew, according to Applebaum, is disappearing: “American power is no longer deployed solely by trained diplomats and reliable officials, working through state channels.” Instead, an increasingly prominent role is being played by “informal envoys, private companies, online grifters, and hardened ideologues.” Moreover, Applebaum categorically refuses to label MAGA an isolationist movement. On the contrary, her argument is that it is an international revolutionary project. She compares it not to classical American conservatism, but to previous revolutionary movements that sought to reshape not only their own country but also the world around it. “They believe they represent something much greater: the vanguard of a movement that will alter not just America, but the world.” The new American foreign policy no longer rests on the premise that the United States’ allies are democratic states. Allies now include ideologically aligned politicians and parties within those states, as well as those who pay handsomely for that friendship. Last year in Munich, Vance accused Europe of straying from its “fundamental values.” This year, Marco Rubio spoke of an “unprecedented wave of mass migration that threatens the cohesion of our societies” and called on Europe and the U.S. to unite around “a shared history, Christian faith, culture, heritage, language, ancestry.” There is not a single mention of democracy, the rule of law, or transparency in this list. The U.S. National Security Strategy already explicitly speaks of the need to “help Europe correct its current trajectory” and combat “civilizational erasure.” It is precisely this logic that underpins meetings between U.S. officials and the AfD, support for Viktor Orbán, contacts with the European far right, and the transformation of CPAC into an international touring platform for MAGA’s political allies. The U.S. is no longer working neutrally with the governments of allied countries. Part of the U.S. administration is effectively choosing who it would like to see in power in these countries. And money follows ideology. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller articulated the worldview of this system: “We live in a world, in the real world that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world.” If the rule of law, institutions, and self-restraint no longer matter, then state power becomes simply another resource that can be converted into political or financial gain. At a meeting with European leaders in Paris, Steve Witkoff said he is already discussing energy and mineral agreements with Russia for American companies that could be implemented after the war ends. There, he also spoke about BlackRock’s potential role in Ukraine’s reconstruction. And this fits very well with what we’ve already seen in The New Yorker’s in-depth feature on Jared Kushner: diplomacy, peace negotiations, investment funds, real estate, energy, and private capital are increasingly finding themselves at the same table. In the article, Applebaum poses a simple question regarding the Board of Peace created by Trump: “Is this organization designed to make peace, or make money?” She asks the exact same question regarding Gaza. Kushner is participating in the negotiations while simultaneously proposing “New Gaza” as a large-scale real estate development project. Applebaum mentions a deal for tungsten mining in Kazakhstan, which is backed by approximately $1.6 billion in U.S. federal funding and involves business entities linked to the Trump family and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. According to The New York Times, Trump earned about $2.2 billion during the first year of his second presidential term, a significant portion of which came from cryptocurrency projects. Former official at the U.S. National Security Council Fiona Hill described Trump’s inner circle during his first term as follows: “They seemed to believe they were representing American interests, but they were also representing their own.” Applebaum believes that this is no longer a side effect but a system. She illustrates this particularly well through the Trump administration’s war against the European Digital Services Act. Formally, Washington calls this a fight for free speech. But this very law creates regulatory challenges for American tech giants. The U.S. government is pressuring Europe over its digital legislation. American tech billionaires are pushing for deregulation. And those same billionaires and politicians support European parties that want to weaken the EU itself. In 2018, he wrote to Jeffrey Epstein about the success of far-right parties in Europe and predicted that after their representation in the European Parliament increased: “We’ll be able to shut down any crypto legislation or anything else we want.” Epstein replied: “Roger that.” Trump refers to Canada as the 51st state, imposes tariffs, and Mark Carney articulates his government’s position very directly: “He’s trying to break us, so that America can own us.” At the same time, separatism in Alberta is gaining momentum in the American media landscape. Representatives of the separatist movement are meeting with State Department officials. Finance Minister Bessent calls Alberta “a natural partner of the U.S.” and specifically mentions its vast natural resources. Applebaum describes the possible logic in the harshest terms: “Pressure the economy, break up the federation, pick up the pieces.” And she adds: “And no, it is not a joke.” In Greenland, it’s roughly the same mix: American political emissaries, oil companies, tech investors, people from Trump’s inner circle, talk of mineral resources, data centers, and the territory’s possible annexation by the U.S. A local politician describes the consequences of such pressure: “They are destroying the trust and the respect in society, in institutions, but also in people.” And even more bluntly: “They f*ck with people's brains.” Against this backdrop, Applebaum lists an entire infrastructure for exporting MAGA: direct funding for allies, political endorsements, MAGA podcasts, CPAC, restructured humanitarian programs, contacts through Congress, and the dismantling of traditional democracy-support programs. Argentina receives $20 billion in aid on the eve of the election, with Trump effectively tying the aid to a victory for Javier Milei’s party. In Germany, Vance meets with the AfD. In Hungary, he supports Orbán. In Poland, Trump meets with Karol Nawrocki during the presidential campaign and later boasts that he “won” the election for him. In Romania, George Simion visits Bannon and declares: “We totally bashed the globalists here in Romania.” Voice of America and Radio Free Europe have been nearly destroyed. USAID has been dismantled. The Fulbright programs have been subject to political interference. According to Applebaum, State Department Human Rights Reports may now describe Germany as a more repressive country than El Salvador. In other words, the very structure of American soft power is changing. Previously, it promoted — at least formally — democracy, freedom of speech, human rights, and the American model. Now, as State Department official Sarah Rogers says, grants should go to those who are capable of: “Advancing American priorities.” And Applebaum asks a perfectly logical question: “What are 'American priorities' if the American government is run by people who use its instruments not on behalf of citizens, but on their own behalf?” Meanwhile, the rest of the Western world is beginning to draw conclusions. Canada is signing defense agreements with the EU and negotiating with Australia. The EU is concluding new trade agreements with India and Australia. In the first half of 2026, 26 world leaders visited China. The French government is gradually removing Windows, Teams, and Zoom from government computers. Similar processes are beginning in Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, as well as in banks and universities. France’s Minister for European Affairs put it as precisely as possible: “We cannot leave the security of Europe in the hands of voters in Wisconsin every 4 years.” This, in my opinion, is the main takeaway of the article. Applebaum isn’t just writing about Trump, nor is she merely writing about MAGA. She describes the collapse of the system that has underpinned American influence for nearly 80 years. The U.S. was the world’s most powerful nation not only because it had the largest army, the dollar, and aircraft carriers. Its strength also lay in the fact that countries voluntarily chose to remain allies of the U.S. America had created the system and, within that system, had limited its own use of force. Now that system has been destroyed.

text: Orchid Pharma Concall Analysis Q1 FY27 Industry Structure Severe Cyclical Headwinds in Core Franchise: Financial Year 2026 represented one of the most challenging operating environments for the global cephalosporin market in 15–20 years, characterized by a 15% to 20% contraction in both volumes and realization across key products. Persistent Industry Overcapacity: The generic API ecosystem continues to face structural overcapacity, resulting in aggressive pricing competition, particularly in Rest of the World (ROW) and non-regulated markets. High Concentration in Key Raw Materials (7-ACA): Global merchant supply of 7-Aminocephalosporanic Acid (7-ACA)—a vital cephalosporin intermediate—is concentrated among 3 to 4 Chinese manufacturers (Sinopharm Weiqida, Zhuhai United, Yili Pharmaceuticals, and Lizhong Pharma). Stabilizing Chinese KSM Pricing: Unlike Penicillin G (Pen-G) where prices experienced sharp volatility, 7-ACA prices have remained stable around a weighted average of ~$60/kg over the last 10–12 years. Chinese suppliers have largely transitioned toward private-enterprise profitability models rather than destructive price dumping. Divergent Strategic Positioning: Competitors in the domestic cephalosporin space remain focused on high-volume, low-margin generic bulk APIs (typically 3–4 products). In contrast, Orchid operates a value-focused, highly diversified portfolio of 20–25 products while vertically integrating into raw materials and forward-integrating into complex injectables. Financial Performance Restatement Post-Merger: Following the legal merger with Dhanuka Laboratories (effective July 10, 2026, with an appointed date of April 1, 2024), FY25, FY26, and Q1 FY27 financial figures are presented on a restated, combined basis. FY26 Full-Year Baseline (Restated Combined): Revenue from Operations: INR 1,233 crores compared to INR 1,398 crores in FY25. Gross Margin: Moderated by ~400 bps YoY to 32% (vs. ~36% in FY25) due to product mix compression and pricing erosion. Operating Expenses: Employee and other operating expenses were held strictly flat at INR 353 crores. Q1 FY27 Performance Turnaround: Revenue from Operations: INR 304 crores, representing ~15% YoY growth compared to INR 263 crores in Q1 FY26. Gross Margin: Expanded by ~300 bps YoY to 33% (up from ~30% in Q1 FY26). EBITDA: Rebounded substantially to INR 25 crores in Q1 FY27 vs. INR 10 crores in Q1 FY26. Segmental Financial Highlights: Antimicrobial Stewardship (AMS) Division: Reduced quarterly EBITDA drag significantly to ~INR 50 lakhs on sales of ~INR 5 crores (led by ORBLICEF and domestic brand sales). Non-Penicillin Non-Cephalosporin (NPNC) Synthetic Business: Generated ~INR 21 crores in revenue during Q1 FY27 (operating at a steady ~INR 20–25 crores/quarter baseline). Growth Guidance Annual Growth Guidance: Management deliberately declined to provide specific full-year numerical revenue percentage guidance for FY27 (e.g., declining to validate a 20% growth target), citing unpredictable non-regulated market dynamics. Sequential Outlook (Q-o-Q & H2 Trajectory): Management expects progressive sequential growth quarter-over-quarter, with H2 FY27 projected to be stronger than H1 due to seasonal winter demand in regulated markets. Long-Term Revenue Drivers & Timeline: EXBLIFEP (Enmetazobactam): Maintains long-term peak lifetime sales potential guidance of USD 1.1 billion to USD 2.0 billion. Russia EXBLIFEP Licensing: Signed agreement with an estimated 10-year long-term potential value of ~USD 178 million. 7-ACA Jammu Project: Commercial revenue contribution is scheduled to commence in FY28 following initial batch commissioning in March 2027. Cefiderocol Platform: Indian commercial launch and revenue generation are expected in Q3 FY28 (6–9 months following December 2026 plant readiness, subject to DCGI regulatory approvals). Margin Guidance Non-Linear Recovery Path: Management cautions that margin recovery will be progressive rather than a straight-line expansion due to lingering competitive pricing in core commodity APIs. Margin Expansion Drivers: Product Mix Realignment: Higher proportion of regulated market sales in H2 FY27 carrying superior realization. Merger Synergies: Initial cost and operational integration savings from the Dhanuka Laboratories merger will begin crystallizing in FY28. Backward Integration Spreads: Captive sourcing of 7-ACA from Jammu will insulate margins against KSM price fluctuations once fully operational. Operating Leverage: Fixed overhead cost discipline maintained across expanding volumes. Strategic Customer Pipeline & Volume Visibility EXBLIFEP (Cefepime-Enmetazobactam) Commercialization: Western Europe: Commercialized by ADVANZ PHARMA across the "Big 5" markets (Germany, France, UK, Spain, Italy). Vial volume expanded along a J-curve trajectory: 300% Q-o-Q growth in Q3 FY26, 175% in Q4 FY26, and 50% in Q1 FY27. B2B partnerships are being formed for Eastern Europe. Russia & CIS: Dossier submission and regulatory launch timeline estimated at 1.5 to 2 years under a USD 178M 10-year deal. Other Global Regions: Out-licensing negotiations are in advanced stages across South America, Mexico, Philippines, Thailand, Morocco, and Australia, with candidate discussions ongoing in the US and China. Supply Chain Model: Initial global orders are fulfilled through a contract manufacturing organization (CMO) in China (acquired via Allecra). Orchid will transition to direct in-house supply after site validation and registration in ~2 years. Orchid manufactures in-house for the Indian market via Cipla and its proprietary brand ORBLICEF. Cefiderocol Access Project (GARDPPartnership):GARDP has initiated a global RFP process across 135 entitled countries. Orchid is finalizing global distribution agreements and will file for WHO Prequalification (PQ) (timeline: ~2 years). India will serve as the initial launch market. US Generic Injectables Strategy (Vision 2030):Identified key pipeline molecules including Ceftaroline (ORBLICEF/ORTARO family), Ceftazidime-Avibactam, and Ceftolozane-Tazobactam (under R&D), alongside older generics (Cefepime, Ceftriaxone, Cefazolin). Generics will be manufactured out of the new Cefiderocol facility post-2028 following USFDA inspection and ANDA approvals. 7-ACA B2B Customer Ecosystem: Planned output allocation: 80% captive in-house consumption / 20% third-party merchant sales. B2B Collaboration: Rather than competing in end-market sterile APIs, Orchid plans to supply non-sterile bulk 7-ACA/intermediates to major Indian domestic producers (e.g., Aurobindo and others) who currently rely on Chinese imports. Capacity Utilization Now and in Future Existing API Manufacturing: Operational focus remains on restoring volume throughput following the FY26 market contraction. 7-ACA Jammu Mega-Project:Capital Outlay: Total budgeted capex of INR 750 crores. Scale-up Requirements: Pilot plant has achieved a 20x scale-up; commercial production requires a further 800x scale-up to the Jammu facility. Commissioning Timeline: First commercial batch targeted for February–March 2027. Ramp-Up & Utilization Trajectory: Capacity utilization will start gradually due to customer GMP site approval cycles, with guidance targeting 80% to 100% utilization by the end of Year 1 (FY28). Output will be 100% captive initially before opening to third-party sales. Cefiderocol & Complex Injectables Facility:Capital Outlay: USD 20–25 million. Timeline: Facility mechanical completion targeted by December 2026, followed by validation and initial batches during January–March 2027. Noticeable Trends Strategic Pivot from Volume to Value: Systematic transition away from low-margin commodity cephalosporins toward proprietary, high-barrier antimicrobial platforms (EXBLIFEP, Cefiderocol, Ceftaroline). De-Risking Supply Chain via In-House Fermentation: Establishing India’s largest 7-ACA fermentation facility to achieve cost leadership and national self-reliance in core cephalosporin KSMs. Collaborative Industry B2B Model: Instead of creating redundant global sterile API capacity, Orchid is positioning itself as a primary non-sterile bulk intermediate supplier to domestic peers with established global formulation registrations. Rationalization of Chinese KSM Suppliers: Chinese producers of fermentation intermediates are increasingly adhering to commercial profitability rather than destructive price cutting. Risks Biological Scale-Up Complexity: Fermentation at an 800x scale-up carries execution and yield stabilization risks inherent to large-scale biological synthesis. Competitive Pricing Actions from Incumbent Chinese Suppliers: Risk of predatory pricing responses from the 3–4 dominant Chinese 7-ACA producers attempting to defend market share. Geopolitical & Supply Chain Interruptions: Ongoing Middle East conflicts have delayed commercial rollouts in GCC markets. Equipment imports for Cefiderocol required re-routing from China through Italy, illustrating execution complexities. Regulatory Trial Waiver & WHO Approval Dependencies: Indian launch timelines for Cefiderocol depend on securing a clinical trial waiver from DCGI SEC. Global RFP execution requires WHO Prequalification, which involves a ~2-year timeline. PLI Scheme Timeline Slippage: Due to project delays, Orchid will likely only be entitled to 2 years of PLI benefits under current rules, with extension requests planned post-operationalization. Commodity Pricing Pressure: Products like Cefixime continue to face severe margin and spread compression in ROW generic markets. Management Tone Grounded, Realistic & Execution-Oriented: Managing Director Manish Dhanuka and Whole-Time Director Mridul Dhanuka maintain an honest, objective tone. They explicitly caution investors against expecting a "straight-line recovery" and decline to issue speculative annual percentage targets. High Conviction in Structural Economics: Management exhibits strong confidence in the location-specific cost advantages of the Jammu 7-ACA plant (low power tariffs, abundant water, and cheap agricultural-waste boiler fuel) and its long-term AMR innovation pipeline. Transparent Communication: Candidly acknowledged the operational severity of the FY26 sector downturn while demonstrating disciplined fixed-cost control and clear milestones for capital projects.

text: #Atlantaelectricals Why the market might be re-rating Atlanta Electricals? Atlanta Electricals Limited has reached a defining structural inflection point. This has created a severe bottleneck, with transformer lead times globally stretching out to 104 to 156 weeks (2 to 3+ years). The Export Vacuum: Global utility grids face an acute equipment deficit driven by the replacement of aging infrastructure and grid modernisations in the US and Europe. With Chinese manufacturers heavily constrained by tariff walls and rigorous supply-chain scrutiny, qualified Indian manufacturers are stepping in to fill the supply vacuum. Atlanta is actively executing a premium 15% revenue export target for the mid-term. Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS): The rapid deployment of massive battery energy grids to stabilize renewable power generation requires complex step-up transformer topologies. Atlanta has already logged high-voltage engineering requirements tied directly to BESS architectures. 3. Improving the Quality of Growth: The Shift to Private Sector Realization Historically, the primary risk to Atlanta’s valuation multiple was the Quality of Growth. Serving domestic state electricity boards (SEBs) subjected the business to extended, volatile working capital cycles (often 90 to 120+ days). Even as net income grew, substantial cash was locked up in trade receivables, naturally compressing the company’s Return on Equity (ROE) and limiting its market multiple. The ongoing operational shift toward private hyperscale data center developers and strict international export contracts changes this dynamic. Export orders are de-risked via absolute Letters of Credit (LCs) and structured advance milestones, while private tech developers operate with high liquidity and tight construction deadlines. BESS Commercialization Acceleration: Track volume expansion and incoming tender wins for specialized BESS grid-stabilization contracts. Export Order Book Trajectory: Monitor the progression of international order bookings against management’s stated 15% revenue blend target. Summary Conclusion Atlanta Electricals stands at the ultimate convergence of two powerful financial trends: an operational inflection point driven by fully pre-funded, underutilized capacity, and a fundamental upgrade in the quality of its growth as it transitions toward private enterprise infrastructure. With a record-high unexecuted order book of ₹3,116 Crores de-risking its near-term execution path, the market's ongoing re-rating of the stock marks the beginning of a sustained structural transformation. text: 🚨 INDIA’S ECONOMIC PRESSURE IS REACHING CRISIS LEVELS. The war is hurting economies around the world, but some countries are getting hit much harder than others. India is now one of them. Start with the rupee. It is having its worst year against the US dollar since 2022, down around 6% so far in 2026. At the same time, Indian stocks have fallen for 8 straight weeks, the longest losing streak since the dot-com bubble burst. Indian stocks have also dropped to a record low relative to global equities. And foreign investors are selling aggressively. FIIs sold around $12.8 billion in March, followed by roughly $7.3 billion in April, $5.8 billion in May, $5.1 billion in June, and $4.6 billion in September. From January through September, foreign investors sold roughly $42 billion worth of Indian equities in the cash market. And now the bond market is getting hit too. India’s 10-year government bond yield has crossed 7.20%, a 2.5-year high. Then comes inflation. Retail inflation jumped from 4.45% to an 8-month high of 4.82% in August. Wholesale inflation has climbed to 9.92%. And oil could make all of this even worse. India’s average crude purchase price reached $116.04/barrel in September, the highest since the US-Iran war began. The Indian crude basket even crossed $120/barrel in late September. India imports around 85-90% of its crude, and every sustained $10 rise in oil can add roughly $12-15 billion to its annual import bill. In August alone, India’s crude import bill jumped 18% to $11.7 billion, even though import volumes actually fell 3%. Oil companies are already estimated to be losing around ₹530 crore every day. That includes roughly ₹8/litre on petrol, ₹9/litre on diesel, and ₹300 per LPG cylinder. India has also already seen around 4 rounds of petrol and diesel price hikes since February, taking prices up by roughly 7-8%. And getting cheaper oil is becoming harder too. India had been buying discounted Russian crude, but the new US sanctions law gives the president authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil. Venezuelan supply is falling as well. Shipments to India dropped from roughly 297,000 bpd to 253,000 bpd in September. Now add food to the problem. India’s monsoon rainfall came in 12.6% below normal, the fourth-lowest since 2001. That matters because agriculture still contributes around 16-18% of GDP, supports roughly 42-46% of the workforce, and around 50-55% of arable land still depends heavily on monsoon rainfall. India’s foreign minister has already warned about a possible major food crisis in the coming months because of wars, grain disruptions, fertilizer shortages, and climate pressure. So look at what is happening at the same time: Rupee: worst year since 2022. Stocks: the longest losing streak since the dot-com crash. FIIs: roughly $42 billion sold. Indian stocks vs. global stocks: record low. 10Y yield: 2.5-year high. Retail inflation: 8-month high. Crude: $116.04/barrel. Oil companies: losing ₹530 crore a day. Cheap Russian oil: under threat. Monsoon: fourth-worst since 2001. Food crisis risk: rising. One of these problems alone is manageable. The scary part is that India is now dealing with almost all of them at once, and each one can make the next one worse.

text: The World Is Changing and India Must Expand Its Economic Options Dr Mayank Chaturvedi When interest rates in a major economy begin to redirect global capital, and the trade policies of a powerful country start affecting several nations across the world, it becomes a real test for every country that must both keep its economy running smoothly and ensure that its economic foundations remain strong. India, too, is currently passing through a similar phase. The biggest economic challenge before the country is to ensure that its rapidly growing economy continues to strengthen its resilience, competitiveness and strategic autonomy alongside its growth. The Economic Survey presented by the Ministry of Finance has pointed towards this changing global scenario, noting that the period when the development gains achieved after Covid could be taken for granted has come to an end. Geopolitical polarisation, global interest rates, capital flows, supply disruptions and inflation are continuously testing economic decision-making. In such circumstances, India must move beyond a trade-friendly system towards the creation of a competition-oriented economy. In reality, this is where the essence of India's next phase of economic journey lies. The growth rate tells us about the speed of an economy, but it does not provide a complete picture of its overall strength. Sustainable economic power requires better governance, faster decision-making, innovation, productivity, world-class infrastructure and a stronger presence of Indian companies in global markets. The Economic Survey has also identified enhanced state capacity and better governance as key conditions for building a competitive economy. This means that India's economic policy must focus on institutional capacity, with energy security emerging as one of the most sensitive aspects of this challenge. It is well known that a substantial portion of India's energy requirements is met through imports. Any disruption to maritime routes or a sharp rise in crude oil prices affects transport, industry, electricity, consumer markets and inflation. Excessive dependence on a single source can therefore increase economic risks. Diversification of energy supplies and the development of alternative supply routes must become a permanent component of economic policy. The same approach extends to export markets. It must be acknowledged that the United States remains an extremely important market for India. Demand there for Indian pharmaceuticals, textiles, gems and jewellery, as well as a range of manufactured goods, is directly connected with Indian industry and employment. Its impact extends to production centres, small enterprises, workers and local economies. This is precisely where the importance of export diversification becomes evident. Given the way the United States has continued to exert pressure on countries across the world, including India, through tariffs, it has become essential for India to identify and pursue the maximum possible number of export opportunities. In this context, the European Union offers opportunities in high-value markets. ASEAN is important because of geographical proximity and manufacturing linkages. The Gulf region opens up opportunities for India in trade, investment and infrastructure. Africa is emerging as a rapidly expanding consumer market, while Latin America presents new opportunities for Indian automobiles, pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals and information technology. The purpose of such diversification is not to distance India from any particular market, but to spread Indian trade across multiple markets so that a shock in one region does not reach a point where it can destabilise the entire export structure. The BRICS grouping is also important for India in this context. Trade in goods among BRICS countries has increased 13-fold over the past two decades, reaching $1.17 trillion. The need now is for cooperation that moves beyond declarations and delivers practical progress in customs reforms, trade finance, logistics, digital documentation and the participation of small enterprises in global value chains. India's MSME sector can play a decisive role here, although Indian enterprises still have considerable ground to cover in terms of their presence in global markets. In this regard, India needs to learn from China, which makes dedicated efforts to help its entrepreneurs succeed overseas and to expand the reach of Chinese goods to as many as 192 countries. India, too, is moving forward in this direction, but its approach has yet to acquire the same degree of aggressiveness and scale that China has demonstrated. India's global economic capacity will truly expand when small and medium-sized enterprises become permanent participants in international supply chains. Barriers related to finance, technology, market access and certification need to be reduced, while these enterprises must be connected with global production networks. This can strengthen employment, exports and local production capacity simultaneously. At the same time, technology is becoming a central pillar of economic competitiveness. India's digital public infrastructure, digital payments, information technology and start-up capabilities should be integrated more extensively with global partnerships. Some efforts have begun in this direction in recent years, but in reality they cannot yet be described as satisfactory. India today has several important platforms and partnerships, including the United States, the European Union, ASEAN, the Gulf, the G20, the Quad and BRICS. Rather than viewing these relationships through mutually exclusive frameworks, India can develop them as complementary economic opportunities in accordance with its national interests. Here too, there is a need to accelerate efforts at every possible level. The next decade will be important for India precisely on this account. Global economic instability may continue. Trade policies may change. The direction of capital flows may shift. Energy markets may experience fluctuations. Amid each of these changes, India's success will ultimately depend on how quickly its economy can adapt to changing circumstances. Development is India's achievement today. Competitiveness is its next test. Diversification is its security, and expanding its economic options will represent its real economic independence. Therefore, in a changing world order, this is the approach that can take India beyond being a power that merely responds to circumstances and towards becoming an economic power capable of influencing them. It may be hoped that the Narendra Modi government at the Centre is already working in this direction. Even so, the market-access challenges facing the country's small and medium-sized enterprises require urgent attention. text: After trade war, capital war? Whether the AI bubble bursts or the borrowing binge continues, India will need to strengthen its defences by T N Ninan In the retreat from globalisation, the world has already seen multiplying restrictions on the cross-border movement of people. Since Donald Trump’s return to the US presidency and the advent of tariffs as a coercive instrument of policy, the global trade in goods and services has also taken a hit. What may come next are restrictions by rich countries on the international movement of capital (capital controls have long been the norm in developing countries). The primary provocation for such a radical move (unthinkable till just the other day) lies in the United States (US), where the irresistible force of growing corporate borrowings is up against the immovable object of the US budget deficit. The big corporations leading the tech and artificial intelligence (AI) race were until recently financing their capital budgets out of their earnings. No longer, as investment plans have ballooned. Now they are borrowing in the market, and borrowing big as corporate bond issuances in the US have grown 80 per cent in two years. At the same time, the federal deficit has grown to 7 per cent of gross domestic product, and shows no sign of coming under control. US savings aren’t anywhere near enough to feed these hungry beasts, which is why the US has been for decades the world’s biggest borrower. But its growing need for capital from other countries is up against the fact that almost all large countries are turning away from US securities. China has halved its US holdings in the last few years, while Japan (now the largest holder of US securities) has started moving away too. The total foreign holdings of marketable US Treasuries are down to 30 per cent of the total, from 50 per cent in 2015. Even as central banks reduce their dollar holdings, they have increased the share of gold in their reserves. Last year, gold replaced US government bonds as the largest reserve asset; the price of gold has increased by 25 per cent in a year (and Indians are still big-time buyers!). With increasing dollar-debt issuances in the face of fading appetite for such debt, the inevitable has happened — interest rates have gone up. US Treasury rates are now the highest in two decades, and climbing. Yet international bidders for fresh US debt now account for a smaller part of the market than before. Five-year Treasury interest rates have gone up by 0.64 per cent in just one month. The US Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, has spent the past few weeks trying a variety of gambits to talk the market down, to no effect. If, despite higher rates, the US doesn’t get the capital that it wants from other countries, it could simply print dollars, cause inflation as more money chases the same goods, and thereby reduce the debt burden in real (ie inflation-adjusted) terms. India has done this for decades. In fact, as Western country debts have grown, inflation in the last five years in the US has been more than twice as high as in the previous decade, in Europe three times as high, and in Japan five times as high. Inflation wars to control debt, you might say. There is also the possibility (still remote but real) that the US might turn coercive on capital, as it has on trade. Already, Mr Trump has made investment commitments a part of some of his bilateral trade deals. Today, he is coercing inflow. Tomorrow he may squeeze outflow. In anticipation, some countries have started taking defensive measures. The Netherlands moved 78 tonnes of gold from New York to London in the last few months. The explanation was possible “geopolitical unrest”. Shortly before that, France moved all its gold out of the US. There are calls in Germany to do the same. Unthinkable as it may have been not long ago, trust in the continued openness of the US capital market has begun to erode at the margins. Meanwhile, expert voices in Europe have called for disincentivising the movement of European capital to the US, since Europe needs to invest in itself. Any such move by Europe will almost certainly be met by a counter-move from Washington. A headline in the Financial Times said in early September that “The capital wars are coming”. All this should be of serious concern to India. Portfolio capital has been moving out of the country for the last couple of years, and the rupee has taken a tumble, falling 13 per cent in value despite active Reserve Bank intervention, even as rising energy prices affect the trade balance. It is no coincidence that the main stock market indices are back to where they were two-and-a-half years ago. The last time the market disappointed investors over an extended period was in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. The biggest Reserve Bank initiative in the face of these trends was to offer a huge free lunch to non-resident Indians: Deposits at attractive interest rates along with currency protection. It may have overplayed its hand, because the scheme brought in twice as much money as was expected, over $130 billion. Non-resident Indians (NRIs) can obviously recognise a free lunch when they are offered one. The cost of the scheme to the RBI will depend on how currency rates move, and could be between $10 billion and $20 billion over the course of the scheme. Naturally, there have been critics who have made two arguments. First, the foreign-exchange reserves position is comfortable, which was not the case when attractive deposit terms were offered to NRIs in the past, through the Millennium Bonds and Resurgent India Bonds. Second, the terms of the offer were needlessly generous. The second argument holds more water than the first, because the uncertainty and tensions in international capital markets warranted a precautionary move of some kind. Consider that, in the six months between the end of February (when the US attacked Iran) and the end of August, the RBI’s foreign exchange reserves went up by a little over $50 billion, though about $130 billion came in as foreign currency non-resident (bank), or FCNR(B), deposits during this period. Neither the current account deficit nor net capital flows can fully explain the missing $80 billion. It is obvious that the RBI has spent a lot of dollars shoring up the rupee as capital has gone out of the country. So getting some extra dollars as a cushion can do no harm. Two scenarios are now possible. If the AI investment bubble bursts, there will be a global tsunami, since the US stock market accounts for more than two-thirds of global market capitalisation. If not, and the borrowing binge by governments and companies continues, there will be unprecedented competition for capital, leading to possibly higher inflation and/or restrictions on cross-country capital flows. It makes sense, therefore, to shore up reserves, increase economic security by reducing the budget deficit and government debt, and make the country more attractive to investors. The additional reserves can be used to fight currency volatility, and to fund any capital outflows. They can also be used to boost confidence in the economy’s external solvency at a time when no one knows how exactly the cards will fall. text: Trump Is Not the Whole Problem The belief in some quarters in India that U.S.-India relations will return to normal once Donald Trump is no longer president ignores the structural shift in American policy toward India. The shift began in the latter half of the Joe Biden presidency and has accelerated under Trump. Washington no longer views India’s rise as entirely benign and is determined, as U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau bluntly stated on Indian soil, not to repeat its China mistake with India. When Indian Foreign Minister Jaishankar earlier this week called out Washington’s “lack of empathy” over India’s terrorism concerns and pointed to U.S. tariff shifts as a source of “bumps,” Modi responded with a phone call to Trump. The Indian leadership is seeking to maintain a warm working relationship with the Trump administration for strategic reasons while ensuring that its official voice clearly records India’s discontent on sensitive issues. It is also addressing the political necessity of blunting critics at home who accuse the government of being overly compliant with Washington. That effort has been reinforced by the public outcry over the government’s recent release of American covert operative Matthew Aaron VanDyke and his six Ukrainian accomplices following an intervention by Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The seven had been arrested by India’s National Investigation Agency, which accused them of terrorist conspiracy and waging war against the Indian state. New Delhi must face up to a difficult reality: Simply waiting for Trump’s departure will not restore the old U.S.-India relationship. The underlying shift in Washington’s view of India predates Trump and is likely to outlast him. New Delhi will have to adjust to an American policy that increasingly sees India's rise not simply as a strategic opportunity but also as a source of economic and geopolitical friction.

text: 🚨India Shows Who Is is the Boss: Demands Sunset Clause & Forward MFN Before Signing US Trade Deal India is making one thing clear in its negotiations with the United States: a trade deal cannot be built on one-sided uncertainty. India is seeking both a sunset clause and a forward-MFN provision before finalising the agreement, two mechanisms designed to protect India if US trade policy changes in the future. The message is straightforward: India is not negotiating merely for a lower tariff today; it wants guarantees that the deal will remain fair tomorrow. A forward-MFN clause would mean that if USA later offers another country a better tariff for products covered by the provision, India could receive equivalent treatment. The sunset clause, meanwhile, would provide a mechanism to revisit the agreement if circumstances change substantially. This matters because US tariff policy has become increasingly dynamic, with tariffs and sector-specific measures being altered over time. For Indian exporters, securing market access is only half the battle. Maintaining a competitive position against countries such as Vietnam, Bangladesh, Thailand and Malaysia is equally important. India's position therefore represents a broader shift in the negotiations: market access for India cannot come without safeguards against future tariff discrimination. The same principle is visible in India's approach to Russian crude. While India can adjust its purchases based on market conditions and strategic requirements, New Delhi has maintained that its energy policy cannot simply be dictated by external pressure. The emerging message from India is unmistakable: if Washington wants a long-term trade partnership, New Delhi wants long-term predictability in return. The deal, if concluded, will not merely determine today's tariffs. Its real significance will lie in the rules governing what happens when those tariffs change tomorrow.

text: 🚨Tamil Nadu lost ₹1,606 crore in GST collection in 5 months. Biggest fall of any large state in India. Everyone's asking WHY? I took GSTN's official tables apart to find WHERE. Here's what the data shows 🧵 1. First, this is NEW. Apr–Nov 2025: TN +7.3% India +5.8% TN was BEATING India. Apr–Aug 2026: TN −2.9% India +5.3% A 10-point swing in under a year. That's a shock, not a slow decline. 2. Finding 1: it's not SGST. Of the ₹1,606 cr fall: SGST: −₹408 cr CGST + IGST: −₹1,198 cr 75% of the loss is in CGST + IGST. 3. Why that matters: IGST is the tax on goods LEAVING Tamil Nadu, to other states and exporters. By our estimate it's the fastest-falling piece, at about −4.6%. TN's problem isn't selling to Tamil Nadu. It's selling OUT. 4. Finding 2: it's the small businesses. Taxpayers handled by TN's own tax department: −3.4% (−₹1,045 cr) Taxpayers handled by the Centre: −2.3% (−₹567 cr) 65% of the loss sits with state-handled taxpayers. Most MSMEs sit there by rule. 5. 🚨Compare that with other states, same category: Haryana +24.0% Karnataka +12.1% UP +12.1% Gujarat +9.9% Tamil Nadu −3.4% Their small-business base grew. Ours shrank. 6. Finding 3: businesses didn't leave. They're paying less. GST registrations in TN: +5.5% GST collection: −2.9% More taxpayers. Less tax. Per registered business, TN now collects less than the national average. 7. Finding 4: this is the damning one. Of India's 14 biggest states, TN is the ONLY one negative on all 5 measures: ❌ Total ❌ SGST ❌ CGST+IGST ❌ Central taxpayers ❌ State taxpayers Not one sector. Not one big taxpayer. The whole supply base. 8. But here's the twist 👀 IGST settled TO Tamil Nadu (from what TN residents buy from other states and abroad): +47.9% Third-fastest among big states. That's why TN's treasury still grew 16%. 9. So the real picture: 🟢 Tamil Nadu as a CONSUMER: strong 🔴 Tamil Nadu as a PRODUCER: weakening The treasury is protected for now. The industrial base that built it is not. 10. What it cost: If TN had grown at India's pace, it would have collected: Apr–Aug: ₹4,541 cr more Apr–Sep: ₹6,086 cr more That's gross collection, not all of it TN's revenue. But it's the size of the hole in TN's tax base. 11. Which sectors? Honest answer: GSTN doesn't publish it. The leading suspects: • Textiles: Tiruppur exports −4.9% in FY26 • US tariff hit to exporters • Rate cuts on TN's core products Only TN's Commercial Taxes Dept has the data to confirm. text: Where Do We Stand in India–US Relations? India–US relations are at their lowest point since Donald Trump returned to the White House. It began with unnecessary tariffs imposed on Indian and other exporters, despite India accounting for only about $60 billion of US imports. Worse, a proposed trade deal aimed at expanding balanced two-way trade toward $500 billion a year was repeatedly delayed. Then came the Pahalgam terrorist attack in Kashmir. Instead of showing solidarity with India, Trump pressured New Delhi to halt its retaliation against Pakistan, reportedly using the threat of 200% punitive tariffs. His subsequent effort to win Pakistan’s support for the Iran war, including giving Pakistan’s General Munir a high-profile White House welcome, further irritated India. This was viewed in New Delhi as an unfriendly act that diplomacy alone cannot easily erase. Now India has been singled out for a 100% tariff over its imports of Russian oil under legislation backed by Trump. At the same time, sanctions and disruption involving Iran have tightened global oil supplies, pushing prices higher and adding to the burden on India and other importers. The result is clear: India–US relations have gone downhill and are now on slippery ground. Prime Minister Modi is unlikely to yield to every Trump demand. Moreover, India has been diversifying its trade relationships. Agreements with Australia, New Zealand, Europe, Canada and others are helping offset losses in the American market, while India continues to target strong economic growth. Trump’s cultivation of Pakistan’s military leadership may also become a liability if the Iran war remains unresolved. Pakistan, already financially distressed, is seeking billions of dollars in additional IMF support ($7 billion), while the United States has separately approved $600 millions in military assistance. Against this backdrop, Trump’s friendly phone calls to Modi and his ambassador’s conciliatory media comments are unlikely to repair the relationship by themselves. What would change the equation? Trump would need to demonstrate political strength at home, bring the Iran conflict to an end, and reassess whether Pakistan is an asset or a liability. The stalled India–US trade agreement could then be revived, Modi could be invited to Washington for a high-profile signing ceremony, military deals could be expedited, and the punitive Russian-oil tariff could be reconsidered. Much of the damage done to the relationship can be reversed—but it will require political will, including congressional action where necessary. The relationship is on slippery ground. The time to start repairing it is now.

I have spent a life in love with words crafted into elegant sentences and beautiful stories woven with these string of pearls. Sometimes I read just because skill-full authors are like musicians. They can create rhythm and melody that give you joy. My day job, however, has always only dealt with numbers. Data is the only source of truth. Rest all are stories I am paid to ignore. To any colleague who says she feels, thinks, hypothesises, is of the view…I point to the writing on the wall. Show me the data. In my world, the only valuable story is told by numbers, the rest is entertainment. English language has just 26 alphabets in which 21 consonants are strung together into words by five vowels but with it an author can make us cry, laugh, think, question, reflect, marvel, uplift, depress, entertain, make us sombre, angry, pensive and so many more emotions. To a student of economics, markets or finance, data has a similar ability to unleash emotions. Trouble is no data independently makes any sense. It is the interplay that one needs to read but in that there are differing opinions but then if everyone is on the same side of the trade there would be no market! Consider a few numbers. Nifty PE right now is about 19.5. In Covid at its lowest it was 18.5. If you look at this data alone you would want to sell your house and buy stocks but another data says that US 10 year bond which is the cost of money was 0.6% in Covid which is now 5.28% and rising. Also if you see Price Earnings to Growth India is still super expensive compared to even hot markets like Taiwan, Korea or US. Nifty earnings are currently 5.2% in rupee terms while the US 10 year is 5.28% in USD and on top of that their Hyper-scalers and AI companies are delivering growth better than what Indian markets delivered at their peak. On top of that, consider currency depreciation and the fact that INR is the Dog currency right now. We have imposed capital gains tax which is paid by FIIs for their gains in INR but when they take it back actually they could end up paying tax on what ended up as their capital loss in their home currency. When STT was brought in the stated objective of the Finance Ministry was to replace Capital Gains Tax, by retaining STT and bringing Capital Gains Tax back by their own admission its double taxation and should go. Also, Nifty companies have been in the doghouse. Action in India has shifted to smaller companies and smaller towns. For FIIs India was a bet on services (Banking and IT) and due to their own reasons both these sectors have disappointed. This isn’t surprising. The Nifty companies are focusing on their quarterly profits. Where are the investments in Greenfield, brownfield, R&D, new product launches. Institutional money chases the large caps as thats where liquidity is available. In 2014 62.3% of market cap was Nifty 50 companies. In 2026 that number has slipped to 39%. If you add all these together you get answers to two questions. Why are the FIIs leaving? and Why is the stock market debating that they can't feel the 7.8% GDP growth. Also linked to that is another factor. Ask anyone who has spent time in the markets and they will tell you that it has never happened before that we see Spring in the Primary Markets while there is Winter in the Secondary Market! Listed entities are being ignored even as new ones are being lapped up. A lot of these companies are new age ones and even in existing sectors the new listings are promising faster growth which is what the market is seeking. There has been exuberant selling of Mutual Fund SIPs with active folios crossing well over 100 million. The sales pitch was Nifty delivers 12-15% return over 10 year period. Unfortunately this may not be entirely true. Since the last four years a vast majority of SIPs, specially those in large caps have underperformed Fixed Deposits and while most likely markets will reward the patient, not everyone has the luxury of being patient. The XIRR of SIP Investors in Nifty assuming starting on the first trading day of each year has been 6.64% in 2021, 5.34% in 2022, 3.22% in 2023, -1.4% in 2024, -4.25% in 2025 AND -10.11% in 2026 versus a one year FD return of 6.25% in SBI. The PAT of AMCs in FY26 meanwhile was Rs.18,000 crs and commissions paid to distributors upwards of Rs.20,000 crs. In the last two years Rs.4.8 trillion was withdrawn by FIIs and Rs.6.3 trillion came in through SIPs. More than 55% of this goes to small and Mid cap funds. PMS AUM has risen to Rs.44 trillion. Domestic investors are not buying what FIIs are selling, almost 80% of incremental investment of theirs is coming in small and Mid cap space - precisely the segment that is growing and precisely the segment not played by the institutional investors. Five years down the road, the persistency of Life Insurance Policies is 50% which means half the customers lose the premium paid and the cover by discontinuing policies taken and for this feat, they paid out a commission of Rs.65,000 crs in FY 26 while the Life Insurance companies themselves made a profit of Rs.65,000 crs in the same period with LIC accounting for 85% of it! The General Insurers make about Rs.10,000 crs of PAT after paying out about Rs.50,000 crs of commissions. Once upon a time a visitor to New York was admiring Yachts. That someone pointed out a few belonging to bankers, a few to brokers and he naively asks, "Where are the customer's Yachts? Now see the context in which IRDAI acted recently. Same think happened in China in 2023 - the immediate impact on insurance business was extremely negative but overtime it bounced back stronger with higher New business Value (NBV). The winners were the large insurance companies and the losers were the small ones that paid high to get access to bank assurance distribution). Niti Aayog has just released some data that I have been losing sleep over. There are about 370 million Indians in the age group of 15-29. Out of this 87 million have been classified as NEET. Not in education, employment or training. In other words, 1 in 4 Indians in this age group is doing nothing! In the prime of their life they are neither doing anything productive nor learning any skill that will make them productive going forward. This is a clear demographic volcano silently brewing. The recent outpouring of youth unrest shouldn’t be surprising after this. You can drown in average four feet of water, it is said. Rainfall is only 15% deficient is a calm way to look at it, another alarming slice of the same dataset is 40% of districts in the country have got deficient rains due to El Nino. A few years ago this would have been drought but thanks to irrigation we are unlikely to have runaway inflation in food prices this time. There are two clear areas of opportunity. After the US tariff shock, India has signed Free Trade Agreement with 38 countries and this will likely expand to 70 countries soon. This is massive. We are going to see exports boom in India aided by a falling currency. Manufacturing - high tech, deep tech, defence, forging, electronics, speciality chemicals, solar, chips, batteries, electric vehicles, drones. From where I sit, I see a lot of action. Pity, it is more in the small companies in small towns and MSME sector while most of our large companies have put their head in the sand and complaining about policy and growth rates. Numbers don’t lie but it is also said that if you beat up a number hard enough it will confess to anything so those whose interest do not ally with you, can throw different set of numbers to the above and spin it into a different yarn. It is a capital mistake to theorise before one has data. Insensibly, one begins to twist facts to suit theories, instead of theories to suit facts - Sherlock Holmes. Predicting the future is a fools game but we have to pick a side and place our bets for the future will reward or punish our actions and even non actions! I hope all of us Indians be a little more bold. Ignore the stock market, focus on the real economy. Manufacturing, Exports, Electronics, are going to be prime drivers of the economic engine also those that will create the much needed jobs. Nominal exports are already up 25% YOY and real exports up 12% YOY. As FTAs get activated there is going to be a major shift - Exports haven't been India's strong point but that will change. Just to get a sense the FTA with UK is now just 2 months old and already we are seeing month on month exports up 12%. Labour intensive goods like Textiles, Furniture, Footwear etc where in European Markets Indian goods had practically no entry versus Bangladesh, Pakistan, Indonesia that will change with the FTA. See I have managed to mess with your brain with numbers but hopefully there are some numbers with which you will connect in your own way and draw from. Caveat:: Data is from my memory (an eccentric, often unreliable chap!), so please validate and correct me where you need to. Do share your story through numbers as you see it.

text: #IndoAmines: Can It Become a True Specialty Chemical Company? Indo Amines (NSE: INDOAMIN) is a 34-year-old chemical manufacturer producing 550+ amine-based chemicals used in agrochemicals, pharma, personal care, textiles, roads and industrial applications. It operates across 70+ countries, with exports contributing nearly half of revenue. The interesting part is not just its growth. The real question is: Is Indo Amines becoming structurally better, or is it simply benefiting from the chemical cycle? The first structural tailwind is China+1. Global customers are increasingly diversifying their chemical supply chains instead of depending entirely on China. Indo Amines already has an export network across the US and Europe, so this shift can help it win additional volumes. FY26 exports were already growing faster than domestic revenue. The second tailwind is the lower US tariff burden on Indian goods, which improves the economics of exporting from India to the US. Combined with China+1, this creates a genuine export opportunity for Indo Amines. There is also a longer-term shift toward bio-based and biodegradable surfactants. Since fatty amines are derived from natural oils, Indo Amines is positioned in a market that could benefit from this transition. But this is a tailwind, not yet a major competitive advantage. Now comes the more interesting part. Indo Amines is trying to move up the chemical value chain. The company has already launched morpholine and its derivatives, while developing products such as di-n-propylamine, N-methyl benzylamine and methylene bis-morpholine. These products are smaller-volume, more specialised chemicals and some require customer approval. The idea is simple: Commodity chemicals → specialised derivatives → customer qualification → stickier business → better margins. Morpholine is particularly interesting because it is an import-substitution opportunity and was commercialised at the Dhule facility in 2025. But there is one big catch. The transformation is not proven yet. The company’s “Specialty Chemicals” revenue actually declined 7% in FY26 to about 8% of product sales. R&D spending was only about 0.1% of revenue, and the new products are currently too small to materially change group economics. That means investors should not confuse “new products” with “specialty transformation.” The real proof will come from the numbers: Does the specialty mix grow? Do new products scale? Do customer approvals increase? Does the margin floor move higher? Does higher profit finally convert into cash? Historically, EBITDA margins have remained cyclical, while the cash-conversion cycle has expanded sharply. So the next few years are about proving that Indo Amines can become more than a good chemical manufacturer riding the cycle. The story is interesting. The structural transformation is still a work in progress. That is exactly what I would watch.

text: Trump’s America is not India’s friend. A friend does not price your market access, your workers, and your wars as leverage. Washington is running a transaction. Trump rejected a trade deal, called India a “dead economy,” and treated a large US goods deficit — $58.4 billion in 2025, on $149.1 billion of trade — as a reason to squeeze the partner, not as proof the market works. 5. America First is not an alliance. The 10-year defence framework was renewed and India bought Javelins. Trump has also said that if India were attacked, the US would help.
