text: FAULTLINE | MORNING BRIEF 1 OCTOBER 2026 TODAY'S THOUGHT The biggest geopolitical shifts don't always happen when countries change sides, sometimes they happen when countries start building alternatives. IRAN-US | A QUICK UPDATE The Iran-US channel remains open through intermediaries, but no breakthrough has emerged. The more interesting development is that Gulf oil exports are recovering through alternative routes, with Saudi Arabia restarting shipments through Yanbu. Goldman Sachs estimates Gulf exports have returned to around 23.3 million barrels a day, while Brent has fallen below $97 as supply fears ease. The crisis is therefore beginning to demonstrate something important... chokepoints have power, but that power changes when the system around them learns to adapt. THE GULF | THE SECURITY MAP MAY BE CHANGING Something larger may be happening underneath the immediate Iran crisis. Gulf states are increasingly questioning whether the traditional US security umbrella is still sufficient. Qatar has proposed a regional security framework that would include Iran and the Arab Gulf states, while Saudi Arabia and the UAE have also begun repairing their relationship after months of tension. This is not yet a new regional security order. But it is a sign that countries which once relied heavily on an external guarantor are beginning to think about alternatives. THE G20 | THE NEXT BATTLE MAY BE OVER THE RULES OF TRADE While Washington and Beijing continue managing their own rivalry, a much larger argument is developing inside the G20. The US is pushing major economies to address China's industrial overcapacity and rethink parts of the global trading system, while European countries are discussing higher trade barriers against Chinese steel. Canada, meanwhile, is using the G20 to pursue greater trade diversification and deeper economic ties with India. The deeper story is not simply another US-China trade dispute. It is the possibility that the global trading system itself is becoming more fragmented, with countries protecting domestic industries, securing supply chains and searching for alternative markets at the same time. INDIA | A QUIET TEST OF STRATEGIC AUTONOMY India is sitting directly inside that adjustment. Narendra Modi spoke with Donald Trump as Trade Minister Piyush Goyal began discussions in Washington around an interim trade arrangement. The talks cover trade, defence, energy and critical technologies, while India continues trying to preserve room for manoeuvre on Russian oil and its wider strategic relationships. The interesting question is not simply whether India gets a trade agreement. It is how much strategic flexibility New Delhi can preserve while deepening its relationship with Washington. That is increasingly what middle-power geopolitics looks like: not choosing one relationship, but preventing any single relationship from becoming indispensable. SUDAN | THE DANGER OF A COUNTRY SPLITTING BEFORE THE WAR ENDS Sudan is quietly becoming important again. A US proposal for a 90-day ceasefire followed by political negotiations is facing resistance from Sudan's army-led authorities, while the RSF has been building a parallel authority in Darfur. The concern is that a poorly structured ceasefire could freeze competing centres of power rather than reunify the country. The question is therefore changing. It is no longer only whether Sudan can stop fighting. It is whether stopping the fighting without resolving the political geography could make partition more permanent. CHINA | THE HOLIDAY BOOM THAT ISN'T QUITE A CONSUMER BOOM China's Golden Week is producing strong travel activity, but underneath the crowds is a more complicated economic picture. People are travelling, yet household spending remains cautious. That matters because Beijing wants domestic consumption to become a stronger engine of growth at a time when external trade is becoming more politically difficult. The distinction between people moving and people spending tells us something important about the Chinese economy. A busy holiday does not automatically mean a confident consumer. MONEY | THE OLD SHOCK IS STILL THERE Oil is giving markets some relief, but the bond market remains the bigger warning signal. Brent gained around 14% in September even after today's decline, while US Treasury yields remain near their highest levels in years and the dollar strengthened around 2% during September. That creates an unusual starting point for October: energy pressure is easing at the margin, but financing costs remain high. The geopolitical shock may be fading in one market while remaining embedded in another. MORNING OBSERVATION The Iran war is still important, but it should no longer consume the entire brief. The more interesting story this morning is what is happening around it. Gulf states are reconsidering security arrangements. India is balancing Washington with other strategic interests. Canada is looking for markets beyond the US. The G20 is debating what global trade rules should look like. Sudan is confronting the possibility of fragmentation, while China is trying to turn travel activity into real consumption. These are not isolated developments, they are different versions of the same adjustment. Countries are not waiting for the next world order to arrive. They are quietly building room to operate inside it. FAULTLINE

text: Most people picture a data centre as a building. The building is the cheap part. Start with the number: roughly $60 billion of build cost per gigawatt. Strip out the chips and almost all of what remains is power, cooling and network. The shell — land, concrete, steel — is a rounding error next to it. Which is why the bottleneck has moved. It used to be who could put up the building. Now it is who can get power into the rack, heat out of the rack, and fibre between the racks. That shift is the whole opportunity, because it turns a construction story into a components story. Cooling and power. GPU racks draw far more power per square foot than anything before them, and air cooling runs out of road. You need liquid-cooling skids, immersion fluids, and power distribution units sitting at the rack. Aeroflex is expanding liquid-cooling skid capacity from about 2,000 to 15,000 units a year on an exclusive Vertiv relationship. Navin Fluorine supplies Chemours immersion fluid. Vivid Electromech makes the PDUs. Network. Every rack has to talk to every other rack, and that is fibre — a lot of it. HFCL is carrying a $1.1 billion hyperscaler contract with an order book around 5x revenue. Sterlite Tech's North America share has reached 54%. And a 35% US duty on Chinese fibre works as a policy wall, which is the cleanest kind of door for an Indian supplier: the buyer is not choosing you on price, the buyer cannot choose the incumbent at all. The useful reframe is this. "Data centre capex" is not one trade. It is three: The shell — cement, steel, construction. Lowest value, most competed. The rack layer — power, cooling, PDUs. Where the spend concentrated. The network layer — fibre and connectivity. Where duties have already reshuffled supply. If you are looking for exposure, the question is not whether India builds data centres. It is which of those three layers a company actually sells into, and whether it has a real relationship — an exclusive, a qualified contract, a tariff shelter — or is simply near the theme. text: I asked Grok what the Canadian government could do to turn Canada's economy around right now. This was #1👇 1. Settle the U.S. file — this dwarfs everything else! About three-quarters of goods exports still go south. Oxford Economics-type work puts a successful USMCA reset at on the order of +$250 billion of Canadian GDP over a decade versus the tariff status quo; a full breakdown is a similar-sized loss. That is larger than any housing bill or tax tweak. What the federal government can do this week: Treat a metals/autos deal as the economic priority, not a talking point. Accept a quota-for-lower-rate package if that is what Washington will sign (talks have already floated ~25% with a volume cap instead of 50%). Painful; still better than 50% into 2027. Stop matching “dollar for dollar” as a reflex. Retaliation on U.S. steel, appliances, ag equipment and electronics raises Canadian costs and inflation. Use it as leverage, then cash it in. Lock CUSMA review language so Section 232/338 cannot keep punching holes in the agreement. Fast-track rules of origin, customs staffing, and trusted-trader programs so compliant firms are not treated like smugglers. Diversification (EU, UK, CPTPP, India, ASEAN) is real but slow. Deloitte-style work says new markets recover only a fraction of what a U.S. rupture costs. Do both. Do not pretend Seoul replaces Detroit. Grok went on to say: 2. Stop pretending fiscal stimulus is the growth plan PBO and independent fiscal shops show large deficits, extra operating spend since Budget 2025, and an operating-balance target that slips. Debt service is rising. With slack modest and inflation not dead, another GST holiday or grocery rebate would juice Q2 consumption and then fade. That is not a turnaround. What Ottawa can do now: Make the operating budget actually balance on the announced timetable. Cut programs, consultants, and overlapping agencies — not just announce a “comprehensive expenditure review.” Shift remaining deficit dollars into capital that raises supply: ports, grid, nuclear, mines, pipelines, housing-enabling infrastructure. Stop booking operating programs as “investment.” Freeze new unfunded social expansions until potential GDP is growing again. Keep the GST/HST base broad. Temporary holidays are politically tasty and fiscally dumb. The Bank cannot cut if Ottawa keeps adding demand while tariffs add cost. Coordination is: tight-ish fiscal, patient monetary. 3. Attack the productivity slump — this is the decade problem Real GDP per capita has barely moved since 2019. Business investment per worker has been weak for years. Competition has thinned. That is why wages and housing feel broken even when headline GDP is not collapsing. Federal levers that actually exist: Internal free trade. Use the federal spending power and competition law to smash interprovincial barriers on trucking, alcohol, credentials, and procurement. A Canadian common market is still incomplete. This is the highest-ROI structural reform Ottawa can force. Execute the promised whole-of-government competition plan: telecom, airlines, groceries, banking, construction materials. Let foreign carriers and grocers in. Cap-and-trade of oligopoly rents is not industrial strategy. Tax the things you want less of. Cut the effective tax on new business investment (capital cost allowance, immediately expensing machinery, lower corporate rate on incremental capex). Stop piling boutique credits that consultants farm. Speed regulatory approvals for mines, LNG, nuclear, transmission, and data centres. The “15 nation-building projects” list only matters if shovels move this year, not after the next election. One federal assessment window. Hard clocks. Courts get standing rules that do not let a project die of delay. Procurement: Buy Canadian for steel and ships is fine as a bridge. Permanent protection of uncompetitive mills is how you get Stelco-style idling plus higher input costs for everyone else. 4. Housing: supply, not slogans PBO still has completions around ~220k versus ~290k net needed to close the gap by 2035. Starts for ground-oriented housing have been weak. CMHC tools already exist. What Ottawa can do immediately: Tie infrastructure and GST rebates to municipal zoning that actually allows multiplexes, mid-rise, and industrial-to-residential conversions. No density, no money. Pre-approve federal land dumps near transit. Sell or lease for housing on a 24-month clock. Standardize national building codes for modular and mass timber so factories can scale. Stop using immigration as a housing-demand shock without matching completions. Levels were cut; keep them tied to housing and health-care capacity, then raise them when supply catches up. Do not re-inflate demand with another first-time-buyer credit while inventories of tiny condos sit unsold. 5. Energy as a growth engine, not a branding exercise Higher oil has been one of the few offsets to tariffs. Alberta is outgrowing the manufacturing provinces. The federal government can: Approve and de-risk incremental pipeline and export capacity instead of another review of the review. Treat nuclear (including SMRs) and hydro interties as national projects with the same urgency as defence. Stop stacking carbon, clean-electricity, and project-review rules that make a Canadian mine or mill slower than a U.S. one. If the goal is emissions, use a simple price and let firms comply. Complexity is a tariff on Canadian capital. 6. Labour: skills and attachment, not headcount Population growth has slowed; in some quarters it fell. Youth unemployment is still ugly. Trade-exposed plants (steel, auto, aluminum) are cutting. Ottawa can: Make EI and training portable and fast for tariff-hit workers — wage insurance for 12–18 months beats a plant museum. Recognize foreign credentials in federally regulated trades and health professions in months, not years. Expand apprenticeship tax credits that pay employers who complete journeypersons, not just enroll them. Enforce the Temporary Foreign Worker program so it fills genuine shortages, not cheap labour that delays automation. 7. Use the tools already on the table — and stop not using them Steel firms just laid off hundreds without applying for Ontario tariff aid. Ottawa already has a Strategic Response Fund, BDC metal financing, TRQs on non-CUSMA steel, and Buy Canadian procurement. If the goal is keeping finishing lines alive, write cheques against production and reinvestment covenants, not press releases. If the goal is letting Nanticoke run hot-roll while Hamilton finishing dies, say that and recapitalize workers. Ambiguity is how you get 350 people laid off. 🔥8. What WILL NOT turn the economy around🔥 Another round of targeted rebates. Talking about EU accession as a substitute for a U.S. deal. Industrial strategy that picks losers and then is shocked when they idle lines. Blaming the Bank of Canada for not cutting into 3% energy inflation. “Nation-building” lists without permits, labour, and offtake. Sequence that actually matters: close a worse-but-real U.S. metals/autos/CUSMA deal; freeze operating spend; shove federal money into grid, housing-enabling infrastructure, and approvals; smash interprovincial barriers; tax new investment lightly; keep immigration matched to roofs and clinics. That does not deliver a boom by Christmas. It is the difference between 0.9% forever and getting back toward 2% with rising income per person. The federal government cannot rezone Toronto, drill a well, or staff a mill. It can stop adding cost, stop delaying projects, stop treating the U.S. market as optional, and stop running structural deficits that crowd out the capital stock Canada has underbuilt for a decade. Popularity and “failing the country” are not the same thing. A prime minister can be personally liked and still miss the job he defined. @MarkJCarney, you are missing the job you defined.

text: Dhaka pushes Yunnan trade deal and 1,200-km road to Kunming as it widens economic options beyond single-partner bargains DHAKA — Bangladesh has asked China for a direct road from Chattogram through Myanmar to Kunming and for faster access to Yunnan’s market, while separately arguing that new trade clubs such as RCEP should sit alongside — not replace — hard bilateral talks with Beijing, New Delhi and Washington. Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir put the corridor proposal to Yunnan Executive Vice Governor Zhao Junmin in Dhaka on 27 September. He said a working link of about 1,200 kilometres could move cargo between Chattogram and Kunming in roughly 24 hours, cutting time and freight costs and tying together supply chains among Bangladesh, Myanmar and southwest China. The same meeting covered a wider investment and market package. Dhaka wants bonded warehouses and exhibition space in Yunnan opened quickly so Bangladeshi goods can reach a provincial market of about 46.4 million people. Two-way trade between Bangladesh and Yunnan already passed 1.3 billion yuan in 2025. Zhao said Bangladesh is the first South Asian country under Yunnan’s special trade-facilitation policy, with bonded storage, showrooms and customs support still being rolled out. Both sides also discussed more direct cargo flights and two-way trade in jute, leather, frozen fish and fruit from Bangladesh, and flowers, fertiliser and animal feed from Yunnan. Prime Minister’s political adviser Zahir Uddin Swapon, speaking the same day, framed the pitch in blunt commercial terms: Bangladesh buys more than $22 billion a year from China and sells back less than $1 billion. He said Beijing’s near-100 percent duty-free access, plus a free display centre and storage in Kunming, and a new economic corridor from Kunming through Myanmar to Chattogram, were tools to shrink that gap. That bilateral push sits inside a larger argument now common in Dhaka: after the 2024 political change, Bangladesh faces strained ties with India, deeper economic and defence links with China, tougher U.S. trade talks, LDC graduation and the unresolved Rohingya file. Separate deals with each capital remain unavoidable, but they leave Dhaka exposed when one partner ties a port, loan or market opening to a concession elsewhere. A 27 September analysis in *The Daily Star* said the practical answer is extra institutional channels. RCEP ministers approved an ad hoc working group on 21 September to advance Bangladesh’s accession. China is inside RCEP; so are Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand and all 10 ASEAN members. India is outside. Accession would deepen trade with China inside a 15-member rulebook rather than as a one-to-one bargain — useful as tariff preferences fall away after LDC graduation, but only if Dhaka prepares industry for lower tariffs, rules of origin and customs reform. ASEAN Sectoral Dialogue Partner status and BIMSTEC chairmanship are being sold in the same spirit: more rooms in which to talk transport, disaster response and the blue economy instead of putting every file on an India or China table. None of those forums can substitute for the road itself. The Kunming–Myanmar–Chattogram idea revives the logic of a Bangladesh–China–Myanmar corridor floated during Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s June visit to Beijing. Officials have already noted the obvious limit: a land route only works if the Myanmar stretch — including Rakhine/Arakan — is stable enough to carry freight. That condition was not settled in the Yunnan talks. For now the government’s line is consistent across both stories: take the China market and the short road if they can be built; use RCEP, BIMSTEC and ASEAN so that one capital cannot close every other door; and judge each project by cheaper logistics, more buyers and less single-partner leverage — not by the number of communiqués. **References** 1. text: Pharma sector - key insights Pharma sector is shaping up as a two-engine growth story for FY27: strong domestic demand + export/CDMO recovery, but the key question is how much of the topline growth converts into earnings. Ind-Ra expects ~10% sector growth, while Crisil is somewhat more optimistic at 11–13%, driven by domestic demand and exports The domestic business of the 18 companies tracked by Ind-Ra grew 17% YoY in Q1FY27, while Pharmarack data showed the overall Indian pharma market growing 11.5%. August 2026 IPM growth subsequently accelerated to 12.96% YoY, with chronic therapies remaining a key driver. Diabetes, cardiovascular, respiratory and other chronic therapies provide recurring prescription demand, making the domestic portfolio less dependent on one-off acute launches. More than 30 companies launched generic versions of the anti-obesity drug in Q1FY27, across pens, vials and oral formats. This creates a new category opportunity, although competitive intensity will likely keep increasing. Generic Revlimid revenues have normalised sharply following patent expiry and increased competition. The US accounted for roughly 34% of revenue for the companies analysed by Ind-Ra over the past five years, so US pricing remains a major swing factor Upcoming patent expiries, complex generics, stable pricing and currency tailwinds could support recovery. Importantly, this will be company-specific—product pipeline, regulatory track record and exclusivity will matter more than simply having US exposure. CDMO + API is an increasingly important second growth engine. Global innovators are outsourcing more manufacturing, while India's API ecosystem is recovering. The government's pharma PLI has already attracted Rs. 46,744 CR of investment, with Rs. 4.03 lakh CR of cumulative sales, strengthening the domestic manufacturing ecosystem. Crisil expects operating margins to contract by around 150–200 bps to 21–21.5%, mainly because of higher raw-material, energy and freight costs. ⚠️Key risks => US generic pricing erosion => Higher USFDA scrutiny => Tariffs/geopolitical disruption => API/raw-material inflation => Freight costs => Increasing competition in products such as semaglutide => Regulatory/compliance issue The strongest structural combination is: Domestic chronic growth + complex US launches + CDMO outsourcing + API localisation. @vishan_29 @Dynamicinvstr @Anvith_

text: Quite the momentous article by Navtej Sarna, India's former ambassador to the US (until 2018): He says "it's time to call the bully's bluff" with respect to the US: start actively resisting them as opposed to giving "ego massages" to "Trump and his family" and "fawning over his proconsular envoys" that he says have gotten India nowhere. As he puts it, "the dignity of a nation is non-negotiable." He also says that India should stop hoping that better days will come: to him it's "self-deluding to put the blame solely on Donald Trump." He believes that the US's... and he doesn't mince his words... "economic nationalism, racial supremacism, moral poverty, naked aggression and wanton disregard for international law and norms" are all trends "which will outlast Trump." For proof, he points to the recent "Sanctioning Russia Act" which gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, including India. As he writes, "votes in favour of punishing India... cut across party lines, including in the Congressional India caucus." Which goes to show that when push comes to shove, India has no real friends in Washington. I don't know if India will follow Sarna's advice and indeed find the guts to stand up to the US, but what this illustrates - in many ways - is India's lack of strategic foresight. There's an old Chinese saying for this: 伴君如伴虎 (bàn jūn rú bàn hǔ), "keeping company with the sovereign is like keeping company with a tiger." India mistook a tiger that was being friendly for one that was tame. To his credit, Sarna admits to this: he writes that India must accept it "is not the strategic partner that we believed we were" and should cast overboard "comforting wishful thinking." But China, for one, never made this mistake: it could resist the US precisely because it used the years when the tiger was cuddly to grow claws of its own. And countries like India - or, to a far worse extent, the countries of Europe - that deluded themselves into believing the cuddles were genuine now face an impossible choice: get eaten, or fight a tiger with little claws of their own.

text: Background After WWI and the Great Depression, countries had fought "beggar-thy-neighbour" battles: competitive devaluations, tariffs, and currency blocs. The gold standard had collapsed. Allied planners wanted a stable postwar order before the war even ended. The conference •Held at Mount Washington Hotel, Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, USA, 1-22 July 1944 (formally the UN Monetary and Financial Conference). •44 Allied nations attended. The USSR attended but never ratified the agreements. •India took part as a British-ruled territory and became a founding member of the IMF and IBRD. The two architects •Harry Dexter White (USA): wanted a fund built on member quotas, with the dollar at the centre. This plan largely won, reflecting US financial power. •John Maynard Keynes (UK): proposed an International Clearing Union with a new world currency, the bancor, and symmetrical burdens on surplus and deficit countries. It was rejected. What was created •IMF: Oversees the exchange-rate system and gives short-term balance-of-payments support to members. Began operations in 1947, HQ Washington DC. •IBRD (World Bank): Initially financed postwar reconstruction of Europe, then shifted to long-term development lending. It is the core of today's World Bank Group. The system it set up •Adjustable peg: Currencies were pegged to the US dollar (allowed to move within about 1% of par), and the dollar was convertible to gold at $35 per ounce. •Devaluation was allowed only in "fundamental disequilibrium." •This is why it's called a gold-exchange standard, with the dollar as the anchor currency. Why it ended The Triffin dilemma: the world needed ever more dollars for liquidity, but supplying them through US deficits eroded confidence in the dollar's gold backing. US deficits (Vietnam War, domestic spending) led to Nixon closing the gold window in August 1971. The Smithsonian Agreement (1971) failed to rescue it, and floating rates became legitimate under the Jamaica Accords (1976). Exam pointers •Commonly asked: venue, year, number of countries, institutions created, the Keynes-White contrast, the bancor, and the dollar-gold peg. •GATT (1947) is often called the "third pillar" that was intended as the trade counterpart, since the proposed International Trade Organization never came into being.

text: Why Nifty is lagging global markets Oil shock hits India first India imports ~85% of its crude. Brent above $100 and Hormuz risk immediately mean a fatter import bill, inflation, a wider CAD, a weaker rupee and delayed rate cuts. A small disruption elsewhere is a growth tax here. Rupee eats the FII return Even a decent rupee return can turn flat or negative in dollars. FIIs price USD IRR, not Sensex headlines. Sustained INR weakness is a structural discount on Indian equities. US yields beat Nifty’s earnings yield With the US 10-year around 5%+, Treasuries compete directly with Indian stocks. When risk-free dollar paper pays more than Nifty’s implied yield, EM allocations shrink. Wrong index for the AI cycle Global money is crowding into AI hardware, foundries, memory and US mega-cap tech — Korea, Taiwan, USA, Japan. Nifty is financials, consumption, energy and IT services. India is not in the capex chain; parts of IT are seen as AI-disrupted, not AI-powered. EM money rotated to China / Korea / Taiwan After China stimulus and the semiconductor boom, “buy China, sell India” became a real flow. India’s weight in MSCI EM fell sharply, so passive money had to sell. Premium valuations, thinner earnings surprise GDP can look fine while listed EPS cools after the FY21–FY24 boom. Paying an EM-high multiple without a re-rating catalyst is a hard sell to global funds. Some large caps look like they are defending the old economy, not funding the next one. Tax and “social spending” optics Higher STT, STCG and LTCG raise the after-tax hurdle for FIIs and HNIs. That rarely starts a crash by itself, but it stacks on currency risk and already-rich multiples. Rule-tinkering premium Frequent CAS, ASM, surveillance and circuit changes add unpredictability. Markets hate moving goalposts more than a known high tax rate. Tariff mood swings Unclear, shifting US tariff threats on India keep export, supply-chain and earnings assumptions unstable. Policy uncertainty is priced as a discount. Primary supply soaks up cash Heavy IPOs and QIPs compete with secondary buying. SIPs can be strong and Nifty can still go nowhere if new paper absorbs the flow. FIIs sold the liquid stuff Outflows clustered in banks, IT and other high-ownership, high-liquidity names that make up the index. DIIs bought the dip; they did not fully offset dollar selling at the benchmark level. Oil + rupee + US yields set the macro tax; AI and China/Korea stole the theme; valuations and taxes made India easy to underweight; regulation and tariffs added noise; issuance and FII selling in index heavyweights did the rest.

text: MISSISSIPPI RIVER, Iowa – President Trump just announced that the largest steel plant in American history will be coming to Iowa, and it marks a return to the kind of large-scale American manufacturing that Trump promised to deliver. The project will be initiated by Mesabi Metallics, which has caused much controversy for being based in India, and not the United States. The Indian company that just opened the first new U.S. iron ore mine in 50 years in Minnesota, will now put a $15 billion mill in eastern Iowa near the Mississippi River. The official location will be named this afternoon. The Oval Office event is set for 2 PM on Monday with company executives, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Senator Joni Ernst. The first phase targets 7.5 million tons a year and can grow to about 10 million. The White House calls it the biggest steel plant ever built here, and the first mega-mill since the 1960s. The permanent jobs it will create will be close to 1,750, and will require around 5,000 to 6,000 construction workers. They aim to start opening the plant and steelmaking around 2030. The ore comes from Mesabi’s $2.5 billion Minnesota mine, so the whole chain stays on this side of the ocean. The White House says the first phase of the mine and mill together is nearly $18 billion in investment, and could generate about $95 billion in economic activity through construction and the first decade of operation. This is what tariffs, and a president who actually wants to bring back manufacturing, are supposed to produce. Trump’s 50% steel tariffs made a project this size pan out. A new plant being built that can put out 10% of last year’s entire U.S. steel output is the biggest win this country has seen in a long time. text: 🤔The Five-Power Convergence, Part Two: The Whole Board 2026. Eight months, 844 logged actions, 55 jurisdictions. The view from altitude. In February we drew five lines on one timeline. The United States, Russia, China, Saudi Arabia, India. Eight months later the lines are a map. And the map is bigger than five countries. Part One zoomed in on the purges. Part Two pulls back. Not country by country. The whole board what moved, where it spread, and what it looks like from high enough up that the individual headlines disappear and only the shape is left. I. The Purges Became Law In February, the five powers were running purges. By September, all five were writing statutes. Russia enacted a law to seize property from designated "foreign agents," effective September 1. Its Constitutional Court ruled that criminally acquired property can be taken no matter how long it was held or who it passed to including from heirs after an official's death. Crypto wallets were added to the forfeiture scope in February. A former First Deputy Defense Minister was arrested and charged with running a criminal organization. A deputy minister got 19 years. Aeroflot's CEO was arrested. Two agricultural-empire confiscations approached $7.6 billion. On September 22, the Prosecutor General reported 60,000 officials convicted and roughly $9.5 billion in property seized over five years. Saudi Arabia moved from arrests to legislation: a new anti-money-laundering statute and border authority to seize undeclared cash and metals. Its anti-corruption authority logged more than 32,000 raids and 4,800 investigations in 2025, then kept the monthly pace through 2026. Executives at a $63 billion sovereign-fund megaproject were detained. The sovereign wealth fund itself came into the frame. On September 21, 298 officials were detained in a single sweep including officers from the Defense and Interior ministries. The largest single action in our record. India's Enforcement Directorate attached a record $9.7 billion in assets in one fiscal year and doubled its raids. Real estate, police corruption, narcotics-hawala networks, betting syndicates, a former chief minister's residence. China's purge reached the people who run both the guns and the money. In January the Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission the second-ranked officer in the country and the Chief of the Joint Staff were placed under investigation together. The commission that runs the army went from seven members to two. Two former defense ministers were sentenced to death with reprieve. More than a hundred senior officers purged since 2022. Then finance: the head of the national banking regulator, a former chairman of the securities regulator, the president of a policy bank. A Politburo member expelled. A vice foreign minister removed days before a Washington visit. Ten institutional domains. The fiftieth ministerial-rank official of 2026 fell in September double the prior record pace. A party plenum is announced. The United States kept writing instruments as the money moved. Section 311 of the PATRIOT Act cut foreign banks off from the dollar. When money moved to crypto, Congress wrote Section 9714, and its first use hit a crypto exchange. When it moved to cartel-linked Mexican banks, Congress wrote Section 2313a. Three statutes, each written after the last one stopped reaching. Somebody was watching the money move and building ahead of it. And the targets climbed. In January a sitting head of state, indicted for narcoterrorism in 2020, was taken into U.S. custody. In April a sitting Mexican governor was indicted alongside a sitting senator, a deputy attorney general, police commanders, and a mayor. Both co-founders of the Sinaloa cartel are now serving life in U.S. custody at the same time a first. A purge ends. A statute stays. Every one of the five now publishes its numbers on a schedule. II. The Coalition Is Wider Than Five The workbook now logs enforcement touching 55 jurisdictions. The five powers are the loudest. They are not alone. A Swiss federal court criminally convicted Lombard Odier a Geneva private bank founded in 1796 and confiscated 400 million francs. Swiss banking used to settle. This one was convicted. Six Gulf states co-designated Hezbollah's financial network alongside the United States, including the NGO that operates as its bank. Seven sovereigns, one action. Spain, with Europol and INTERPOL, dismantled a crypto narco-bank that moved $2 billion. Twenty-one arrests in six countries. The case started with a cocaine ship seized in 2021 five years from the dock to the arrests. A Turkish bank inside a NATO country was cut off for moving Iranian oil money. The Treasury Secretary on what a designation means: "code for you are out of business." Australia shut down its largest Bitcoin ATM network. Canada revoked 23 money-service licenses in a single day. An Irish drugs unit in Galway froze crypto wallets alongside the amphetamines and cash. INTERPOL's Operation Synergia III took down 45,000 malicious IP addresses across 72 countries after six months of silence. From Washington to Galway. The capability that used to live in one Treasury building now lives at the beat-cop level in dozens of countries. III. The Dollar Changed Shape This is the movement that matters most, and it happened mostly out of sight. On July 14, while U.S. and Iranian forces were exchanging strikes, Treasury instructed a private company to freeze $131 million in stablecoins held in wallets tied to Iran's central bank. Tether froze them within hours. No court order. No correspondent bank. One instruction. Read that again from altitude. A sovereign central bank was holding reserves in a private, dollar-denominated token and the United States froze them faster than it could have frozen a bank account. Iran's total losses to these freezes and seizures ran near $1.5 billion by mid-year. Its four largest crypto exchanges were designated in a single action. The rails are being built in the open. Stablecoin law now requires issuers to hold reserves in short-dated U.S. government paper and to follow the same anti-money-laundering and freeze rules as banks. Every dollar token issued is a new buyer of Treasury bills and a new wallet that can be frozen on instruction. In September a new institutional blockchain went live with BlackRock, DTCC which clears virtually all U.S. securities and Visa among its validators. Not proposed. Running. And the government stopped selling what it seized. The U.S. used to routinely auction confiscated Bitcoin. After 2018 the routine stopped and the holding began. The formal "do not sell" order came in March 2025. The behavior came first seven years first. Who made that call, and when, has never been made public. Not proven. But the reserve now sits at the end of a pipeline that took two decades to build: investigation, seizure, forfeiture, custody, reserve. The $15 billion Prince Group forfeiture the largest in DOJ history feeds straight into it. Crypto was supposed to be the exit from the dollar system. In 2026 it became the dollar system's fastest freeze button. IV. The Exits Keep Closing After the Huione payment network was cut off from the dollar, the business moved to successor networks. The enforcement followed. In September, one of those successors a Telegram-based marketplace that processed an estimated $24 billion since 2022 was designated a transnational criminal organization. Treasury has proposed letting a dollar cutoff follow "any successor entity," so a rebrand no longer protects anyone. Cut. Move. Cut again. Rewrite the rule so the cut follows the function instead of the name. That is the real shape of enforcement now. Not one knockout. A campaign with the rulebook updating between rounds and every round the rulebook gets longer. V. Pressure and Deals, Same Week Russia shows the tool at its most precise. On September 18, a veto-proof Russia and Iran sanctions law was signed mandatory triggers, secondary sanctions on buyers of Russian energy. On September 19, the U.S. extended the license keeping Lukoil's wind-down running. Earlier that month the acting head of the office that signs U.S. sanctions sat in the delegation at the Kremlin. Maximum pressure on the network. A narrow door left open for the deal. Both at once, both on the record. Why that combination, and who decided it not proven. What is proven is that it keeps repeating, license after license, and the pressure side never comes off. VI. The Other Side Is Building Too This isn't one system absorbing the world. It's a contest, and both sides are pouring concrete. Russia seized sixteen Western businesses by presidential decree in September. China runs its own cross-border payment system and a live digital currency. BRICS met in New Delhi and instructed its payments task force to keep building. Saudi Arabia's exit from mBridge the China-anchored central bank currency platform surfaced in September. The Saudi central bank says its participation ended in May 2025 and the exit was planned. It left quietly and said nothing for sixteen months. And the gold is moving. The Dutch central bank moved 86 tonnes out of New York to London between March and August. France moved 129 tonnes out of the New York Fed the year before. Two NATO central banks, 215 tonnes, fourteen months. Not home to the most liquid trading hub on earth, where the Dutch say it can be deployed fastest in a crisis. Why now: a guess, not proven. But it's on the board. VII. Firsts The clearest signal isn't volume. It's instruments crossing lines they had never crossed before. A 1930 tariff authority used for the first time in 96 years. Both co-founders of the Sinaloa cartel serving life in U.S. custody simultaneously. A sovereign central bank's reserves frozen through a private token issuer. The first criminal conviction of a Swiss private bank in our record. Five Latin American criminal organizations designated as foreign terrorist organizations in a single quarter. A dollar-cutoff rule proposed to follow "any successor entity." Russia and China's military commands both hollowed out in the same year. One first is a headline. Seven in the same window is a pattern. VIII. What It Is From 40,000 feet, the read is this: coordinated capacity across the whole board. Rival states running the same kind of machine at the same time. Allies sharing tools and data. Adversaries building their own versions. Every one of them reaching the same conclusion that financial opacity inside their own institutions is a threat and moving on it through whatever system they have. The laws came first. Then the data. Then the tracing. Then the seizures. Then the statutes to make it permanent. Then the vault. Whether one hand sits above all of it is not proven. It's the guess this entire project exists to test. What's documented is enough to take the guess seriously: a machine built over twenty-five years, now running in 55 jurisdictions, freezing in hours, reaching sitting governors and military commissions, and writing itself into law in five systems that agree on almost nothing else. Part One asked whether it was always the plan. From high enough up, the board answers part of it. The purges became statutes. The statutes became standing machines. The machines spread to 55 jurisdictions. The dollar learned to freeze in hours. And the other side started building its own. The board is set. Nobody's flipping it over. I am the guy on the couch, and you have been debriefed.

text: "Apple in China" A few takeaways and my thoughts on supply chains, India opportunities and risks after reading the book. In the last few months, a number of CEOs and Promoters of auto component companies encouraged me to read the book "Apple in China" by Patrick Mcgee to understand Apple’s overdependence on China, supply chain nuances, China+1 opportunities, risks of operating in China, opportunities for Indian companies, the entrepreneurial zeal of Steve Jobs and more. I'm glad I did!! Below are a few key takeaways from the book, along with my own thoughts on certain topics. A) STEVE JOBS' ENTREPRENEURIAL ZEAL A founder who refused to accept what manufacturing could do today (it resonated with what I had read in Elon Musk’s biography too). Jobs demanded designs that were, at the time, close to unbuildable: the original iPhone's switch from plastic to glass weeks before launch is a well-known example, and Apple's early Foxconn work involved tooling timelines far shorter than the industry norm (about 25 days against the usual 12 weeks). The friction between Apple's design team and its engineers, who had to prove something truly could not be done before saying no, kept pushing suppliers up the capability curve. My thought: the brashness was the mechanism. But it worked because Apple also had the balance sheet, razor sharp focus, ability to change tack and stick to it when needed, the customer leverage and a supplier base willing to absorb the pressure. Intensity alone is necessary, not sufficient. B) APPLE'S RISE IN CHINA, THE DEPENDENCE AND THE SQUEEZE Apple's model was never plain outsourcing. As per the author, it owned about 7.3bn USD of machinery inside supplier plants by 2012, embedded engineers in over 1,600 factories, and often negotiated raw materials on the supplier's behalf. Suppliers earned low-single-digit assembly margins (2-3% for Foxconn-type work). Apple’s suppliers in China were ready to work for these thin margins and hence while Apple has ~20% of global smartphone shipments share by industry estimates, it has a staggering around 80% of industry profit share. In one of the instances, one Apple employee himself agreed that – “which supplier would sign such a one-sided contract”. But suppliers actually did just to gain Apple’s business and then they would use that knowledge and gain margins from other customers.* My thought: I think the Indian suppliers who have won orders from Apple, could be on somewhat similar competitive and low margins. It’s how the capability of the supplier is built over the years, which will be crucial for Indian suppliers to gain margins from other customers. C) HOW CHINA’S GOVERNMENT TIGHTENED ITS GRIP Many such instances are given in book when Apple from a position of dominance became increasingly ceding to a lot of Xi Jinping’s demands, as by then it had grown extremely dependent on China’s supply chain. The book's conclusion lists five risks for Apple's China relationship this decade: (1) Huawei's return with HarmonyOS and improved features and tech capability likely to put pressure on Apple in China; (2) backlash from Beijing and Chinese consumers as assembly shifts to India; (3) the services business being lucrative for Apple and Govt could tweak regulations to make it unfavourable; (4) the AI push, constrained by China as local competitors have access to better data; and (5) tariffs and trade wars under Trump. D) THE OPPORTUNITY: APPLE DIVERSIFYING TO INDIA – HOWEVER DEPTH OF LOCALISATION IS NECESSARY India has gone from under 1% of iPhone assembly in 2017 to roughly one in four iPhones now. The supplier base has grown from 8 companies in 2018 to about 40. Apple runs several contract manufacturers here at once (Foxconn, Pegatron, Tata Electronics and a few others who are not yet in public domain). But the book's caution is depth. India's iPhone output went from zero to about 15mn units in 2016-23, versus China's zero to 153mn in 2006-13, about a tenth of the pace. Most work is final assembly with components flown in from China (known as FATP – final assembly test and pack out) E) APPLE AND TESLA: THE SAME PLAYBOOK IN ELECTRONICS AND AUTOS Both companies, in different industries, educated China's ecosystem, and that ecosystem then produced global competitors. Apple's suppliers helped Huawei, Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo. Tesla's wholly owned Shanghai plant (the first of its kind in China, outside the JV rule) lifted local supply-chain content. A number of Chinese companies benefited from this know-how and eventually now Chinese brands now hold ~70% of China's car market, up from ~35% in 2020, while foreign brands fell from 65% to ~30%. The result threatens the very companies that helped build the ecosystem, as well as legacy global OEMs such as VW and GM. This was highlighted in detail showing graphs etc in our Thematic note “China Energising Seismic Shifts”. My thought: Learn from Apple as suppliers, but use that knowledge to diversify rapidly. Full ownership of innovative global corporations in China taught the China ecosystem more than joint ventures did. The classic China auto JV kept product definition and core technology with the foreign partner, and transferred the least. Apple and Tesla, operating without JV partners, invested in educating suppliers themselves, and local entrepreneurs (BYD, Huawei, Xiaomi) became globally competitive. One instance in the book mentioned of Apple’s senior engineers sleeping in factories in China to fastrack production inturn helping the local supplier base and human talent. India could therefore consider conditioned access for Chinese OEMs, with local-content thresholds, local cell manufacturing and data safeguards, instead of viewing them only as competition. The state matters as much as the founder. Apple can neither leave China quickly nor stay comfortably, and that in-between period is India's opening.

text: Anandrathi Conference KTA's Sector Overview 1. Aerospace : Strong order backlogs underpin a robust demand outlook , with focus shifting to execution and NPDled growth. Margins remain stable despite elevated capex for expansion, while WC is likely to remain elevated as imports remain the key source of raw materials. 2. Auto: Demand remains strong across segments, with monsoon deficiency yet to impact demand. Factors such as the 8th Pay Commission could further boost demand. High-to-double-digit growth is expected to continue through the festive season/Q3 despite a high base . Commodity cost pressures will persist, partly offset by price hikes, mix and scale. 3. Auto Ancs: Growth outlook remains robust, driven by the strong auto upcycle , higher content from premiumisation, regulation and powertrain shift s (e.g., EVs), diversification into non-auto segments such as aerospace, semiconductors, consumer electronics and defence, product diversification through JVs/M&A, and exports. Margin impact remains limited due to better scale, mix and pass-through. 4. Banks/NBFCs: Most banks/NBFCs expect stable or improving loan growth , with deposit growth also improving . NIMs could face some pressure in 2Q due to high-cost FCNR deposits, but the outlook is positive for 2HFY27. Asset quality remains broadly stable, with no visible signs of stress. Investments in technology are expected to drive cost efficiencies going forward. 5. Cement : Demand (7–8% y/y) remained firm in Q2. Cement price hikes implemented in March/April weresustained until 8 August, after which prices declined due to heavy rainfall. In September, prices increased by ₹25–30/bag in the South and ₹10–12/bag across other regions. Cost pressures persist on gypsum sourced from the Middle East. Petcoke prices have again risen above US$170/tonne, while heavy rains have increased domestic coal prices as coal evacuation declined. 6. Chemicals : Demand is improving but remains uneven. Energy, polymers, oil & gas, F&F, and Indian pharma and FMCG are firm/improving; Agro is recovering only in select products, while textiles and CPVC remain soft near term, and dyes and pigments continue to weaken. The West Asia conflict has pushed freight costs higher. Capex is giving way to asset sweating, with capex cycles ending over FY27–28, while 2–2.5-year ramp-ups push much of the earnings uplift into FY29–30. Chinese pricing appears to have stabilised, with growth plans shifting towards import substitution. Overseas localisation is also increasing, de-risking freight and tariff risks. 7. Consumer Durables: Q2 remains seasonally weak , with recovery expected from H2. The FY27 outlook remains constructive, aided by a low base and El Niño tailwinds . However, margins remain under pressure from elevated commodity costs and intense price competition. 8. FMCG/Consumer: Demand trends remain steady across most FMCG/Alcobev/QSR companies, with recent price hikes supporting revenue growth. Premiumisation continues to aid growth, with most players launching or planning premium brands to ride the premium/D2C wave. E-commerce/digital remains a major growth driver for most FMCG/QSR players. A sharp rise in crude, crude-linked derivatives and certain commodities has pressured margins. 9. Infra: Disciplined bidding and improving execution remain key, while BOT/HAM/PPP, asset-light and international opportunities are emerging as incremental growth levers. 10. IT Services : Near-term, IT services will remain weighed down by AI-led revenue deflation , compounded by weak discretionary demand and Middle East geopolitics. Most companies are embedding AI into workflows to drive growth, albeit off a low base. 11. Real Estate: Redevelopment and geographic expansion are widening growth pipelines, while better project mix, pricing power and cash generation are supporting a shift towards profit-led growth.

text: A former Ambassador to Washington has now put in print what official briefings still prefer to describe as a “phase.” Navtej Sarna’s column in The Week is not an Opposition pamphlet. It is a diplomat’s stark assessment of a relationship under strain. His central message is difficult to ignore: in Washington, India may no longer occupy the strategic position New Delhi assumed it did. The Russia sanctions law makes that shift harder to dismiss. The legislation gives the US President sweeping powers to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian energy, including India. Its passage also demonstrated significant bipartisan support. (The Week) The implications go beyond Donald Trump. • Do not personalise a structural shift. Economic nationalism, tariff politics and greater pressure on partners who refuse to fall in line may outlast one administration. A different president may be more diplomatic without being more accommodating. • Do not confuse access with alignment. Summit photographs, personal chemistry and investment announcements are instruments of diplomacy, not a strategy in themselves. Strategic relationships must be judged by outcomes, not optics. • Do not treat “America remains our best choice” as the end of the argument. A relationship can remain important while demanding a reassessment of its costs, risks and limits. • Do not outsource national dignity to diplomatic mood. Self-respect in foreign policy means having the capacity to absorb costs when core interests are involved. India’s strategic autonomy has historically been strongest when it created choices rather than dependencies. The missing part of the debate is domestic. For years, India was encouraged to believe that personal chemistry had created a privileged space for it in American strategic thinking. The Quad was presented as architecture, energy deals as statecraft, and criticism of over-personalised diplomacy as needless pessimism. Recent developments should compel a more sober assessment. Strategic autonomy cannot be a slogan invoked only when Washington applies pressure. It means diversified energy sources, multiple export markets, resilient defence supply chains, a neighbourhood policy based on Indian interests, and a Russia relationship managed pragmatically rather than sentimentally. Calling Washington’s bluff is the easy part. The harder work begins afterwards: Tell the country clearly what the sanctions law could mean for oil, shipping, banking and defence supplies. Put credible alternatives and their costs on the table, without turning foreign policy into defiance theatre. Stop measuring diplomacy by the warmth of bilateral meetings. Measure it by the options India retains after those meetings end. Keep the United States as an important partner where interests converge, while refusing a subordinate role where they do not. India does not need a new enemy in Washington. It needs a foreign policy grounded in interests rather than the mythology of a “special relationship.” America remains an important partner. But a country that cannot say “not at this price” will eventually find itself paying every price. That is not anti-Americanism. It is strategic autonomy with self-respect.

text: António Guterres, the UN secretary general said the following: "We continue to reward polluters to wreck our planet. The fossil fuel industry continues to pocket massive profits and subsidies while everyday people bear the costs of climate catastrophe from rising insurance premiums and lost livelihoods. I call on G20 countries to shift money from fossil fuel subsidies and investments to a just energy transition. To put an effective price on carbon. And to implement new and innovative sources of financing including solidarity levies on fossil fuel extraction through legally binding transparent mechanisms. All by next year". To me, this reeks of "wealth transfer" instead of "solutions to global warming". So I had a chat with Grok... "Does the UN leader talk about anything other than 'To put an effective price on carbon. And to implement new and innovative sources of financing including solidarity levies on fossil fuel extraction through legally binding transparent mechanisms' as a solution to global warming?" Thought for 17s Yes. António Guterres talks about many other climate measures besides carbon pricing and fossil-fuel extraction levies.Carbon pricing and “innovative” finance (including levies on extraction or high-emitting sectors) appear in his speeches as one piece of a larger package. He repeatedly frames the core solutions as a fast, just shift off fossil fuels plus large-scale finance and adaptation. Typical elements include: Immediate peaking of emissions, steep cuts this decade, and global net zero by 2050, with developed countries moving faster. Phase-out of coal (2030 for OECD countries, 2040 for others), no new coal plants, and an accelerated transition away from oil and gas. Tripling renewable capacity and doubling energy efficiency by 2030, plus massive investment in grids and storage. Aggressive methane cuts (he has launched a Global Call to Action on Methane), noting they can deliver near-term temperature relief. Ending fossil-fuel subsidies and redirecting that money. Windfall or profits taxes on fossil-fuel companies, with proceeds going to adaptation, loss-and-damage, and the energy transition. $1.3 trillion a year in climate finance for developing countries by 2035, more grant-based and adaptation-focused finance, multilateral development bank reform, blended finance, and debt-for-climate swaps. Halting deforestation and protecting forests as carbon sinks. National climate plans (NDCs) that cover the whole economy and align with 1.5 °C. Just-transition policies so workers and communities are not left behind. Transparency and renewable-power requirements for AI data centers. Heat-action plans, early-warning systems, and sustainable cooling. He has used language close to the quoted passage—calling for “an effective price on carbon,” taxing fossil-fuel profits, and exploring solidarity levies—but those are presented as financing and incentive tools inside a much broader program centered on ending fossil-fuel dependence and scaling clean energy and adaptation. "This clearly does not provide enough energy, though? Where's the "tesla style industrialism and the mass produced new nuclear?" The “Tesla-style industrialism” he does invoke is the one that already happened to photovoltaics and lithium batteries: costs collapsed because factories scaled. He wants more of that for solar, wind, storage, and grids—not a matching factory revolution for reactors. So your objection is fair on his own terms. If the constraint is always-on, high-density, dispatchable, low-land power at civilizational scale (industry, desalination, AI, winter heating, poor countries industrializing), his package is renewables-plus-storage-plus-efficiency plus finance. He does not argue that package is insufficient and therefore nuclear must be mass-manufactured. Other UN-system voices (notably the IAEA) say decarbonizing by 2050 is extremely hard without a large nuclear contribution. Guterres’s own climate messaging does not lead with that. You’re pointing at a real gap between Guterres’s speeches and an energy-abundance program.He does not treat mass-produced nuclear (factory SMRs, high-volume reactor lines, “Tesla for fission”) as a central solution. His public case is almost entirely:solar and wind as the cheap, fast, scalable sources batteries and grids efficiency and electrification methane cuts, forests, subsidy reform, climate finance Nuclear shows up only as a brief aside. In his “clean energy age” speech he said energy history runs from fire to steam to “splitting the atom,” then immediately argued the next era is renewables. He added that nuclear “will be part of the global energy mix” but “can never fill the access gaps”—meaning it is too slow, centralized, and capital-heavy to connect the hundreds of millions still without power the way cheap solar can.indonesia.un.orgThat is the opposite of an industrial nuclear build-out pitch. That is the whole point of the new world order Carney describes: middle powers banding together to form a buffer against hegemons that treat the rules as optional whenever it suits them. And it is not just theory. It is what Canada is doing in practice. Deeper ties with the European Union. Free trade talks with India, the one partner approaching great-power status. Beyond that, a growing network of middle powers: more than 20 trade and security deals across 5 continents in the past year, by Carney’s count. He now calls Canada the most connected economy in the world. That is the point. Canada is connecting with many partners so that it is never a subsidiary of any single hegemon, whether that is Washington or Beijing. The logic is simple: middle powers are stronger together. Acting as a group still preserves more sovereignty than facing a superpower one-on-one. She has Carney’s strategy completely wrong. Carney’s point is that the rupture in the old order has already happened: Canada can no longer assume that overwhelming dependence on one market is risk-free when the U.S. is willing to use tariffs, coercive trade policy, and increasingly transactional politics against allies. Reducing that vulnerability is not anti-American. It is basic Canadian risk management. The China EV deal is also being inflated beyond recognition. The 49,000-vehicle quota is less than 3% of Canada’s new-vehicle market and is essentially a return to pre-trade-friction import levels at the normal 6.1% MFN tariff, not a surrender of Canada’s auto market or evidence that Canada is entering China’s orbit. Canada remains economically, geographically, industrially, and militarily tied to the United States in ways no China agreement could remotely replace. The issue is not choosing Beijing over Washington. It is refusing to be dangerously dependent on either. And Carney’s “extreme tail risk” comment was not a claim that an American attack is imminent. He explicitly said it was not his base case; he was explaining why governments assess even remote catastrophic risks. Frankly, disclosing it was also shrewd. Canada cannot outmatch the United States economically or militarily, but Carney holds the political advantage. Revealing the plan hands Trump’s critics ammunition well past the midterms, at a time when he is already weakened and needs a win. Deal or no deal, a diminished Trump can do less damage. Meanwhile, Canada keeps diversifying its trade, and if that means waiting roughly 2 years for a more reasonable president, so be it. Tucker’s theory about American decline and Chinese ascendance may be a debate worth having. But it does not prove that Carney is facilitating China’s rise. A Canadian government engaging China selectively for trade while diversifying away from excessive U.S. exposure is not building a Chinese-led world order. It is trying to preserve Canadian room to manoeuvre in a world where neither great power should be allowed to dictate Canada’s choices.

text: I think something very important changed in global markets this week, and surprisingly the clearest signal may be coming from Bitcoin. Look at the environment Bitcoin is operating in. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.23%, its highest level since 2007. The 30-year yield reached 5.53%, the highest since 2004. Bond-market volatility jumped roughly 30% in a single week. The Fed has already raised rates and markets are now pricing the possibility of additional hikes because the American economy is simply refusing to slow down: the latest U.S. composite PMI jumped to 58.4, the strongest reading since 2021. Normally, this combination of rising real yields, a strong dollar and tighter monetary policy should be extremely difficult for Bitcoin and absolutely brutal for altcoins. But instead of institutional investors running away from crypto, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs just absorbed $2.4 BILLION in one week—the largest weekly inflow in almost a year. Bitcoin ETFs have now gone from almost $5.8 billion of net outflows for 2026 in July to positive net flows for the year. Ethereum ETFs attracted another $690 million this week, and Solana ETFs took in $188 million, including a record $86.7 million on Friday alone. Bitcoin itself is around $84,000, the total crypto market is approaching $3 trillion, Bitcoin dominance is still around 56%-57%, and stablecoins are worth more than $300 billion. That is not broad altseason yet, but it is a very significant return of institutional capital. Now zoom out from crypto and look at where money is moving globally. Just one week after investors pulled heavily from equities, global equity funds attracted $44.1 billion this week—the largest inflow since early July. U.S. equity funds alone took in $37.6 billion, while European and Asian equity funds also returned to positive flows. Technology funds attracted $5.3 billion as the AI trade regained momentum. At the same time investors put almost $9.7 billion into global bond funds, but government-bond funds actually suffered outflows because sovereign yields are becoming increasingly uncomfortable. In other words, investors are not simply going “risk-on.” They are becoming very selective: AI, technology, selected equities and now Bitcoin are attracting capital while long-duration sovereign debt is struggling. That may be one of the most important macro developments of this entire cycle. For decades, government bonds were where capital went when investors wanted safety. But when governments are running enormous deficits, defense spending is rising, energy remains expensive and inflation refuses to disappear, investors demand a much higher yield to hold long-duration sovereign debt. That is exactly what a 5%+ U.S. 10-year and 5.5% 30-year Treasury are telling us. If that continues, the question becomes increasingly interesting: where does global capital look for protection and long-term returns if government bonds themselves are losing purchasing-power credibility? Gold has already been one answer. It remains above roughly $4,280 despite a difficult week, although it fell around 2% as Treasury yields surged. Silver remains around $64. Gold's inability to keep rising while yields explode reminds us that even hard assets are not immune to the cost of money. But the larger trend remains extraordinary: capital has spent years increasing its allocation toward scarce assets while sovereign debt and currencies face increasingly complicated fiscal pressures. Then there is oil, which may currently be the single most important macro variable in the world. Oil fell around 3% on Friday on hopes that negotiations could eventually reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that immediately helped stabilize bonds and equities. But the geopolitical situation remains extremely fragile. President Trump rejected an Iranian proposal on Saturday that Tehran said could have reopened Hormuz and ended hostilities within seven days, while Saudi Arabia says its coalition intercepted Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Saudi territory. Shipping through Hormuz has been dramatically disrupted during the conflict. If oil falls sustainably, inflation and bond yields could eventually ease. If the war escalates again and oil spikes, central banks may have to remain tighter for longer. Crypto liquidity is therefore being influenced right now by events thousands of kilometres away from any blockchain. Europe has another geopolitical problem developing underneath the markets. European officials say Russia is intensifying cyberattacks, sabotage, drone incursions and other hybrid activity across Europe. Denmark's intelligence service now expects more frequent hybrid attacks and describes a “low but growing” risk of a limited Russian military attack against one or more NATO-border countries. At the same time, other European officials told Reuters they do not believe Russia currently has the capacity for a conventional large-scale assault on NATO while its forces remain heavily committed in Ukraine. That distinction matters: Europe is preparing more seriously for security risks, but the evidence does not justify treating a direct NATO-Russia war as inevitable. Economically, however, the consequence is already visible—higher defense spending, larger government borrowing and a longer-term reallocation of European capital toward defense, cybersecurity, energy security and strategic infrastructure. Then look at America and China. The Trump-Xi summit produced no huge breakthrough, but the two sides extended their trade truce by another two months and are expected to release additional details on Monday. The dispute now goes far beyond tariffs. AI, advanced semiconductors, Taiwan and critical minerals are at the centre of the relationship. China's control over rare earths remains one reason Washington has limited room to completely decouple, while America continues protecting its most advanced semiconductor technology. The world is gradually moving from pure globalization toward strategic supply chains, domestic manufacturing and competition over resources. That means more capital expenditure, more government subsidies and potentially more fiscal spending for years. Japan is another piece people should not ignore. Japanese 10-year government-bond yields touched 3.12%, levels not seen since 1996, while the yen remains weak enough that currency intervention is again becoming a serious discussion. President Trump even raised yen weakness with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi during their summit this week. Japan matters enormously because decades of extremely cheap Japanese money helped finance carry trades throughout global markets. When Japanese yields rise sharply, it changes the relative attractiveness of holding U.S. bonds, foreign equities and leveraged risk positions around the world. India is experiencing the same global pressures from another direction. The Nifty just completed its seventh consecutive losing week, its longest such run since 2020. India remains one of the stronger structural growth economies, but Brent crude around $105 is particularly painful for a major energy importer. Higher oil means pressure on inflation, the rupee, bond yields and corporate margins, while the RBI has simultaneously been managing excess banking liquidity and defending the currency. India is a perfect example of why one country's geopolitical conflict can rapidly become another country's monetary-policy problem. China has the opposite problem. Its property sector remains weak and private credit demand remains soft, which means Beijing still needs domestic support even while Western central banks worry about excessive inflation. Korea, meanwhile, remains deeply exposed to the AI semiconductor boom: record chip demand continues attracting capital, and SK Hynix's Solidigm is even considering an IPO that could value the business at as much as $150 billion. So again, there is no single global economic cycle. America has unusually strong activity and rising yields, China has weak property and credit demand, India is fighting imported energy inflation, Japan is normalizing rates after decades of cheap money, while Korea is riding one of the largest semiconductor investment cycles ever. And then we come back to crypto, because this is where the contrast becomes fascinating. This week also gave us a reminder that crypto still has serious weaknesses. Bitget confirmed unauthorized transfers worth roughly $387 million from some exchange wallets and temporarily suspended withdrawals. The exchange says customer funds are covered by its protection fund; the exact attack mechanism remains under investigation. That is a major reminder that infrastructure and cybersecurity remain real risks regardless of how bullish the macro thesis becomes. But regulatory infrastructure is simultaneously becoming clearer. Just yesterday the SEC staff published new guidance on how certain crypto assets and activities may be treated under securities law, including staking-receipt tokens and token buybacks. Importantly, the SEC says the document is staff guidance rather than binding law, but it nevertheless provides significantly more detail than the industry had in previous cycles. So put the whole world together. America's economy is running hot enough to push Treasury yields to levels last seen before the financial crisis. Europe is rearming and dealing with increasingly serious hybrid-security threats. The Middle East war continues threatening one of the most important energy corridors on earth. America and China are competing over AI, semiconductors and critical minerals. Japan is moving away from decades of ultra-cheap money. India is absorbing the consequences of $100+ oil. China still has to repair a huge property and credit problem. Gold remains extremely elevated. AI investment continues attracting enormous capital. Global equity inflows have suddenly returned. And right in the middle of all of this, institutions just put $2.4 billion into Bitcoin ETFs in one week. That is the signal I find difficult to ignore. If this were simply another speculative crypto mania, I would expect Bitcoin to need falling rates, collapsing yields, a weak dollar and easy liquidity before institutional demand returned. Instead, institutional capital is returning while the U.S. 10-year is above 5%, the Fed is talking about further tightening, oil is above $100 and geopolitical risk is extraordinarily high. That does not mean Bitcoin cannot correct. It absolutely can. And with Bitcoin dominance still around 56%-57%, I still do not see evidence of the kind of broad excess liquidity required for a true everything-pumps altseason. But I think something deeper may be changing. Bitcoin is increasingly competing not merely with other cryptocurrencies, but with gold, sovereign bonds, cash and other global stores of capital. At the same time Ethereum, Solana and other networks are increasingly competing to become infrastructure for stablecoins, tokenized assets, payments, DeFi and 24/7 financial markets. If oil eventually falls, inflation pressure cools, long-term yields peak and global monetary conditions become less restrictive, the institutional infrastructure will already be sitting there. Bitcoin ETFs will already exist. Ethereum ETFs will already exist. Solana ETFs will already exist. Stablecoin supply will already be above $300 billion. Regulatory frameworks will be clearer. Tokenized financial markets will already be developing. That is why I am watching the sequence carefully. First institutional capital is returning to Bitcoin even under difficult liquidity conditions. Now Ethereum and Solana are beginning to receive meaningful ETF flows as well. If the macro environment eventually turns from a headwind into even a neutral environment, and Bitcoin dominance then begins declining, that could be the signal that liquidity is finally spreading much deeper into crypto. The biggest story this week was not that Bitcoin reached $84,000. It was that Bitcoin attracted its strongest institutional inflows in almost a year at exactly the same time that the supposedly safest and deepest bond market in the world was experiencing one of its most violent yield shocks in decades. That tells me Bitcoin's place inside the global capital system may be changing faster than the price chart alone suggests.

text: TL;DR Silver Ramblings (you have been warned!) .@Sorenthek quotes Goldman Sachs:"The risk of tariffs may nevertheless be advancing the domestic security objective by pulling metal into the US." Some thoughts/observations: 👉We actually have UK silver export data for July indicating ~59.6 metric tons of silver exported to the USA. That while the average EFP spread during my daily morning snapshot readings was +$0.08 across the month (ie. it was relatively expensive to buy in London and ship to USA versus buying from the COMEX front month contract). There is a bit of fuzziness(1) to import/export data, but the latest such data that we have would indicate some support for GS statement. 👉When the initial silver tariff risk mitigation began circa December 2025 and through February 2026, the silver front month EFP spread averaged about +0.50% (h/t @BankerWeimar ) as bullion banks were shipping silver from London (LBMA) to NYC (COMEX). I can't speak to copper, platinum or palladium, but the silver front month EFP spread (COMEX futures - LBMA spot) has, with the exception of August 6th, remained near zero and negative for the most part (which means that buying silver in London to ship to the USA has been more expensive than buying from the COMEX(2)) since the end of July. If the bullion banks have been "pulling silver into the US" from London (LBMA) since the end of July, they have been paying a premium to do so. Banks don't like to lose money, so if they are actually doing it, it's serious business. 👉Per my calculations(3), LBMA liquid silver free float vault stock ranged from 6,988​ metric tons (using LBMA report) to just 6,132 metric tons (adjusting for import data discrepancies since February(4)). In October 2025, the LBMA silver market seized up when they had roughly 3,421 metric tons of supposed free float per public data at that time. Therefore, we can estimated that the LBMA's effective (liquid) silver free float as of the end of August was in the range of ~3,567 to ~2,711 metric tons. India started importing silver again in August though we don't know how much yet. ~3,000 metric tons of liquid free float vault stock sounds like a lot, but India alone imported over 1,000 metric tons of silver from the LBMA across just a few months at the end of 2025. Silver ETFs/ETPs (like SLV et al) are also increasing vault stock lately(5) which directly eats away at the LBMA's liquid free float vault stock. If both India and bullion banks are also draining LBMA vault stock, I would expect we should see some stress in the silver lease rates before too long. SLV is the 800lb gorilla in the silver ETF/ETP space (representing ~61% of total London vaulted ETF/ETP vault stock). The 1 month silver lease rate has shown high correlation(6) with movements in SLV vault stock when the LBMA's free float gets constrained. Lately, the correlation has been tightening up. We saw it recently as 1 month lease rates fell (more negative) while SLV shed vault stock and the COMEX reported heavy withdrawals(7) in the 3rd week of September. Then when SLV added a massive 6.5M ozt in one day on Sep 21, the 1 month silver lease rate moved from negative to positive that same day. In the big picture, it looks to me like the LBMA really doesn't have that much left in the tank to give if the bullion banks are indeed draining LBMA silver for US vaults (outside of the COMEX system). The 1 month lease rate isn't really confirming or denying anything yet IMO. 👉@Sorenthek et al have opined that the US is (has been) shoring up domestic (non-COMEX) silver stock using LATAM mining proceeds. The latest news I've seen is that silver mining production from Mexico and Peru is down ~15% in the first half of this year(8). Seems like if the US is indeed trying to shore up private vault stock, they might need to supplement waning LATAM mining proceeds. ~~~ Seems to be a lot of intrigue happening below the surface of price action. It reminds me that I don't own enough popcorn.
