text: The headline taking up most, if not all, of the attention from Mark Carney’s interview with the New York Times isn’t the most important point the PM made. Media outlet after media outlet focused on Carney saying that he examined the “extreme tail risk” of an American invasion of Canada. “That’s just risk management,” Carney told the Times. “It would be irresponsible not to (prepare).” That’s nice click fodder and the type of thing that gets Canadians agitated, but the most important thing Carney told the Times had to do with currency and its implications could be explosive. The real story they missed According to the Times, Carney spent more than an hour at their offices in midtown Manhattan for a wide-ranging interview. Toward the end of their report on the interview, the Times dropped the nugget that would concern Washington the most: Carney wants an end to the U.S. dollar as the global reserve currency. “Mr. Carney on Wednesday also reiterated his long-held view that a global financial system wholly dependent on the U.S. dollar was unsustainable. A move to a multipolar system in which there are several reserve currencies would ‘provide more flexibility,’ he said,” the Times reported. He also admitted that there would need to be changes and a liberalization of China’s currency and financial markets for this to happen. It’s not the first time Carney has advocated moving away from the U.S. dollar as the global reserve currency, a system set up at Bretton Woods in the post-Second World War order. While governor of the Bank of England, he gave a speech in Jackson Hole, Wyo., that was hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City and argued for China’s currency to take on a greater role as a reserve currency. While governor of the Bank of England, Carney expanded the trade of Chinese currency in London, one of the world’s great financial centres. He clearly has a different view of the role of the yuan, or renminbi, than the Americans do and Carney’s view is closer to that of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, the BRICS countries that want to break American dominance. A message Washington will notice If we were a smaller country, such a position would be inconsequential. But more than 70% of Canada’s exports still go to the U.S., even in the middle of a trade war. That’s how reliant we are on the American market. “That’s a declaration of war,” a friend said to me after I read the passages about the currency issue from the New York Times report. And that’s where this becomes dangerous. Will the Trump administration see Canada calling for the end of the U.S. dollar as a global reserve currency as a hostile act? There is an argument to be made that any administration, regardless of party, would see Carney’s comments to the Times, coming from a supposed ally, as an attack. Picking a fight we don’t need Carney likes to use the language of trade war. So do many Canadians. Winning a war means knowing when to escalate, when to retreat and when to make peace. With Carney making his comments about the U.S. dollar no longer being the reserve currency, he is escalating the battle at a time when he doesn’t need to. Exacerbating this fight does nothing to lower tariffs, secure Canadian jobs or grow our economy. What it does is further alienate the other side, make a deal more difficult to achieve and put more jobs in jeopardy. As with all things Carney, it is all about good politics and bad economics

text: Finally I am back after break. Will start posting more analysis soon....... Black Box: The Picks-and-Shovels Company Wiring Together the Gigawatt Data Centers Behind Every AI Model Every AI model needs a physical home a data center wired precisely enough to handle unimaginable amounts of power and heat. Someone has to actually build that wiring, that cabling, that networking. Black Box is an India-origin company doing exactly that, at a scale most competitors globally simply can't match. Let me walk you through it. First what does Black Box actually do? Black Box Limited, formerly known as AGC Networks, is a global digital infrastructure integrator operating across six continents. They provide end-to-end IT infrastructure services spanning Data Center Build-outs, Enterprise Networking, Connected Buildings, Cybersecurity, and Managed Services. The scale here is genuinely global over 4,000 employees, including a 630+ employee global capability center in India, serving 1,000+ global customers, including 120+ Fortune 500 clients. Two businesses one is the growth engine, the other supports it 1. Global Solutions Integration 84% of FY26 revenue -->Data Center Infrastructure & Cabling the physical wiring, structured cabling, and network architecture inside hyperscale AI campuses and colocation centers. -->Enterprise Networking LAN, WAN, and Private LTE network builds. -->Cybersecurity Managed Extended Detection and Response (XDR) and Identity Access Management. -->Managed Professional Services. 2. Technology Product Solutions 14% of FY26 revenue -->High-Performance IP KVM Switching (letting operators control multiple computers remotely). -->Video Wall Control & Digital Signage. -->IoT Monitoring, Sensors & Gateways. -->Audio-Visual Switching & Extension. The five "horizontals" that make up the full digital infrastructure stack 1. Data Centers (~30% of FY27 expected revenue) physical connectivity, structured cabling, and network architecture for massive hyperscale AI campuses and colocation centers. 2. Connectivity Infrastructure :- large-scale fiber cabling, IoT sensors, physical security cameras, and distributed antenna systems across corporate campuses and airports. 3. Enterprise Networking :- LAN, WAN, wireless, and private 5G/LTE networks for hospitals, manufacturing plants, and financial institutions. 4. Modern Workplace :- unified communications, audio-visual collaboration spaces, and contact center solutions. 5. Cybersecurity :- protecting network perimeters via managed threat detection and identity access controls. Where their revenue and clients actually sit -->Geographic mix (Q1 FY27): North America 69%, Europe 9%, APAC 8%, Latin America 6%, India 6% genuinely a US-anchored business. -->Client mix: Technology 27%, Financial Services 26%, Commercial/Industrial 15%, Healthcare 10%. -->Blue-chip footprint: 4 of the 5 largest US banks (Bank of America, Citi, Wells Fargo, JPMorgan), 3 of the top 5 tech firms (Meta, Google, Microsoft), and 5 of the top 10 US hospitals. The megatrend behind all of this and the numbers are genuinely staggering Management describes this as one of the largest digital infrastructure investment cycles in history, driven by AI's physical compute needs. Global data center IT load capacity is projected to surge from 87 GW in 2025 to 233 GW by 2030 nearly a 3x jump in five years. AI workloads specifically are expected to consume ~50% of that total capacity (117 GW), fundamentally changing the power density, cooling needs, and cabling complexity required inside every data center. There's also a genuinely smart secondary thesis here management expects an "enterprise lag effect." As hyperscale data centers upgrade to handle AI compute, hospitals, banks, and airports will eventually be forced to overhaul their own local network infrastructure just to consume that higher-bandwidth data flowing to them. That's a second, delayed wave of demand riding on top of the initial hyperscale buildout. The moat and gigawatt-scale execution is genuinely a rare capability -->Execution at hyperscale :- as data centers move from 10-megawatt builds to full gigawatt-scale campuses, hyperscalers stop caring about the lowest-cost bidder. They need integrators who can mobilize thousands of specialized technicians globally without delaying mission-critical launch timelines. Black Box's track record executing nearly a gigawatt of capacity restricts real competition to a small handful of global players. -->Global reach with offshore leverage :- ~4,000 professionals across 35 countries, backed by their India capability center. Offshoring currently sits at ~20%, letting them optimize project margins by using Indian engineering talent for global network design and monitoring. -->Unionized deployment expertise a genuinely unique operational moat in the US specifically: the ability to execute complex IT infrastructure installations across 800+ US zip codes, in both unionized and non-unionized labor environments, without triggering labor disputes. That's a niche skill most competitors can't replicate quickly. Now the numbers Q1 FY27, and the operating leverage story is real Q1 FY26 versus Q4 FY26 versus Q1 FY27: -->Revenue: ₹1,387 Cr → ₹1,691 Cr → ₹1,719 Cr, up 24.0% YoY — their highest-ever quarterly revenue. -->Operating EBITDA: ₹116 Cr → ₹164 Cr → ₹160 Cr, up a strong 38.0% YoY. EBITDA Margin: 8.4% → 9.7% → 9.3%, up 90 bps YoY. -->PAT: ₹47 Cr → ₹65 Cr → ₹56 Cr, up 18.0% YoY. Worth being precise here: Q1 FY27 revenue includes two months of consolidation from a recently acquired Brazilian entity, 2S Inovações Tecnológicas, contributing approximately ₹60 Cr. Strip that out, and the remaining 20% YoY growth was entirely organic a genuinely strong underlying number even before counting the acquisition. The order book is arguably the most important number in this entire story -->New order bookings in Q1 FY27: $339 million (₹3,208 Cr). -->Total order backlog: a record $949 million (₹8,986 Cr), up 83% YoY. -->The single biggest driver: a massive $131 million (₹1,240 Cr) contract secured with a US-based global hyperscaler during Q1, cementing Black Box's position as the only India-origin digital infrastructure company executing gigawatt-scale data center programs. An 83% YoY jump in the order backlog is a genuinely strong forward indicator this isn't just current-quarter strength, it's visibility stacking up for multiple future quarters. The balance sheet — genuinely de-risked over the past year -->Net debt-to-equity improved sharply from roughly 0.83x in FY25 to just 0.17x in FY26, following a ₹386 Cr preferential equity issue. -->The average tenure of the order backlog expanded from 12-15 months in FY26 to ~18 months currently, heavily weighted toward long-cycle data center projects (24-36 months) extending revenue visibility all the way through FY28. -->They're also benefiting from a tax shield historical carryforward operating losses across various geographies keep the effective tax rate low (10-15%) through FY27 and FY28, before normalizing to ~20%. Where management is guiding this next and the ambition here is genuinely bold -->FY27 revenue guidance: ₹7,800-8,000 Cr (23-27% YoY growth), with EBITDA expanding to ₹725-750 Cr at a 9.3-9.4% margin. -->The FY30 vision: tripling revenue to hit $2 Billion (₹18,000 Cr). Of that, ~₹12,000 Cr ($1.3B) is targeted from purely organic execution (a ~17% CAGR over FY26), and ~₹6,000 Cr ($0.7B) is targeted through strategic, margin-accretive acquisitions. -->Margin expansion target: pushing toward a sustainable 10%+ EBITDA margin at scale, driven by scaling offshore delivery leverage in India, AI-led internal productivity gains, and deliberately shedding low-margin, long-tail clients that don't fit the higher-value hyperscale strategy. The risks worth understanding clearly -->Hyperscaler concentration risk a huge portion of future growth depends on the capex budgets of a handful of global hyperscalers like Microsoft, Google, and Meta. Any unexpected slowdown or delay in AI data center buildouts could stall revenue conversion meaningfully. -->Geopolitical supply chain shocks building data centers requires massive quantities of optical fiber, copper cabling, and networking switchgear. Supply shortages or tariffs on raw materials from China could delay project execution and compress margins. -->M&A integration risk hitting that ₹6,000 Cr inorganic FY30 target requires executing several large acquisitions successfully. Failing to properly integrate targets, or overpaying, could destroy shareholder value and stress the balance sheet they've only recently cleaned up. Why I'm sharing this I'm not calling this risk-free a large chunk of near-term and long-term growth depends on continued hyperscaler capex spending that's entirely outside Black Box's control, and the FY30 target leans meaningfully on M&A execution that hasn't happened yet. I'm sharing it because a genuinely rare gigawatt-scale execution track record most global competitors can't match, an order backlog up 83% YoY with visibility stretching through FY28, and a balance sheet that de-risked from 0.83x to 0.17x net debt-to-equity in a single year, are exactly the traits worth tracking as this AI infrastructure buildout continues.

(Very good explainer on the impact of Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, 2026,on Indian Economy.For India, the most crucial aspect of the Act is what it says about countries that import Russian oil. Thirty days after its enactment, the Act. allows the U.S. to impose a 100% tariff on goods.According to the latest data, Russia accounted for more than 51% of Indian crude oil imports in July 2026. Scaling this back drastically within 30 days, at a time when passage through the Strait of Hormuz is still constrained, will likely be impossible for India.Historical data, however, show that India as chosen to comply with U.S. pressure to reduce oil imports from countries such as Venezuel, Iran, and Russia.If India again cuts down on Russian oil imports, this could have serious ramifications for the supply and price of fuel within India ) Why did the US. introduce the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, 2026? What does this new law say about tariffs? What particular condition impacts India's imports of Russian oil? How could this impact India's economy? Is there any provision for a waiver of tariffs? US. President Donald Trump has signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, 2026, which could see tariffs of up to 100% being levied on imports from India if it continues to import oil from Russia. This Act, therefore, has significant implications for India with regard to its export ambitions and energy security. The Indian government's concerns over the tariffs have so far gone unheeded. Why did the U.S. introduce this law? The initial purpose of the Act proposed by the late Senator Lindsey O. Graham and named after him was to cut off financing for Russia so as to choke its funding of its war with Ukraine. To this end, the Act provides for sanctions to be levied on Russia's top leadership and its biggest energy customers. Recently, the 'and Iran' part of the title was added to the Act to convey that such measures are also aimed at Iran. The text was amended to say that sanctions on Iran would be levied for another five years until 2031. What does the Act say about tariffs? For India, the most crucial aspect of the Act is what it says about countries that import Russian oil. Thirty days after its enactment, the Act. allows the U.S. to impose a 100% tariff on goods originating in a country that meets one of two broad criteria. The first is a country that was among the five largest importers, by total volume, of crude oil or natural gas from Russia during the 12 months preceding the Act's enactment, and that continues to import oil or gas from Russia after the 30-day period. If India again cuts down on Russian oil imports, this could have serious ramifications for the supply and price of fuel within India. This is the criterion that will likely impact India. China and India are the top two importers of Russian crude oil. Russian crude oil has accounted for a rising share of India's oil imports since February 2026, when the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Mr. Trump's tariff regime, including the 25% punitive tariff he had imposed on India for its Russian oil imports. According to the latest data, Russia accounted for more than 51% of Indian crude oil imports in July 2026. Scaling this back drastically within 30 days, at a time when passage through the Strait of Hormuz is still constrained, will likely be impossible for India. The second criterion for imposition of tariffs is if a country was among the top five nations "facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion during the 12 months preceding the date of the enactment of the Act". India runs a much lower risk of qualifying for tariffs under this criterion as Indian oil marketing companies have repeatedly said that all their purchases have been made without violating sanctions. Will these be the total tariffs on imports from India? No. The law clearly states that an import tariff imposed under this Act "shall be in addition to any other duty" levied on any good. This includes tariffs imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the United States Trade Representative to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that harm American commerce, and Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which authorises the U.S. President to restrict imports or impose tariffs if an investigation finds that foreign goods threaten national security. These two other Acts are important because India is among the countries that already face tariffs under them. That is, the U.S. Trade Representative used Section 301 to investigate American trade partners to determine whether they had done enough to stop the import of goods made using forced labour. Based on its findings, it imposed a tariff of 10% on imports from India. In addition, Mr. Trump had widened existing tariffs under Section 232 to include steel, aluminium, copper, and related derivative products, and hiked the rate to 50%. Since this applied to all countries equally, it placed India on a level playing-field with its competitors. A potential 100% tariff on top of that will severely dent India's competitiveness in these sectors. Will these tariffs come into force immediately? No. A period of 30 days has to elapse before the U.S. can determine whether countries are still importing oil and gas from Russia. It is only after this period that the U.S. can levy the tariffs under the law. Further, the text of the Act says that the U.S. Trade Representative, in consultation with the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Energy would, within 180 days after the initial imposition of tariffs, again review the countries that are the five largest importers of crude oil and natural gas from Russia based on the most recent 12-month period. What is the potential impact on India's economy? The impact on India's economy has to be looked at in terms of two eventualities. The first is if India continues to buy large quantities of Russian oil and bears the tariffs. The second is if India cuts back on Russian oil imports and manages to have the potential tariffs removed. In the event that India continues to buy Russian oil and bears the tariffs, we can look at what happened during the period when the 50% tariffs were in force, between August 2025 and February 2026, to gauge the likely impact. The April to August 2025 period saw merchandise exports to the U.S. grow nearly 18% compared with the same period the previous year. While some of this was due to front-loaded exports in anticipation of future tariffs, it nevertheless highlighted the strong momentum of exports from India to the U.S. However, over the longer April 2025 to February 2026 period, exports to the U.S. grew at a much slower 3.8%, showing a substantial slowdown in exports after August, when the tariffs came into effect. Conversations with exporters at the time showed that many of them were sharing the cost of the higher tariffs with their U.S. customers in order to retain them. At the rate of 50%, thi was already a body blow to most of them. These exporters will not be in a position to share a 100% tariff. Historical data, however, show that India as chosen to comply with U.S. pressure to reduce oil imports from countries such as Venezuel, Iran, and Russia. If India again cuts down of Russian oil imports, this could have serious ramifications for the supply and price of fuel within India. At a time when the Strait of Hormuz is constrained, and oil prices are again comfortably above $100 a barrel, India will likely find it very expensive to look for newer sources of oil. For Indian citizens, this could translate into more fuel price hikes. For the government, such hikes would be politically unpalatable since there are several key State elections next year. Is there a third way out? The Act includes a provision for a waiver of tariffs. The U.S. President can waive the tariffs once he has submitted to Congress a certification in writing that the waiver "is in the national interests of the U.S." and a report explaining the basis for the certification. The other way out is if Russia signs "a peace agreement that is accepted by the free and independent Government of Ukraine" and ceases "all military hostilities against and any activities to overthrow, dismantle, and subvert the Government of Ukraine".

On September 23, 2026, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Washington and Beijing had extended their Busan Agreement until January 10, 2027. During President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington, the two sides agreed to avoid new tariffs and trade restrictions on each other. The timing matters. Just five days earlier, on September 18, President Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. It allows tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy. China is among the largest buyers, yet the US–China understanding gives Beijing protection while India remains exposed. We saw this pattern in July 2025, when Washington spared China but imposed an additional 25% tariff on India for buying Russian crude. If Russian oil purchases are the issue, why does India face the tariff while China gets an exemption? The tariff threat appears aimed at forcing India to cut Russian oil purchases and sign a deeply unequal bilateral trade agreement. Washington could offer a lower rate in return for concessions, but that would give India no lasting certainty. India should not trade its energy security for temporary tariff relief or let US tariff threats dictate its national energy policy.

text: Morning Market Report 🌞 Friday, September 25, 2026 Focus: U.S.-China Bilateral Relations & The Extension of the Xi Trade Truce Executive Overview: A Temporary Respite in Washington U.S. equities and global markets are trading with a mild upward bias this morning following high-stakes meetings in Washington between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed that Washington and Beijing have agreed to extend the trade war truce—originally negotiated under the Busan Agreement—by two months, moving the expiration date from November 10 to January 10, 2027. The extension maintains lower tariff rates and holds off on new trade restrictions while keeping China’s commitment to purchase 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans intact and pausing Beijing’s export controls on critical rare earth minerals. While the reprieve provides short-term visibility for supply chain planners and agricultural markets, Wall Street remains acutely aware that fundamental structural divides over artificial intelligence, state subsidies, and geopolitical dominance remain largely unaddressed. Anatomy of the Truce: Terms and Immediate Market Impact Under the extended agreement announced by Treasury Secretary Bessent, both nations agreed to freeze current tariff frameworks and suspend additional retaliatory measures: Agricultural Obligations: China continues to fulfill its commitment to import 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans over a three-year period, alongside discussions regarding an additional $17 billion in broader U.S. farm purchases. Supply Chain Protections: Beijing has paused implementation of export restrictions on critical rare earth minerals, easing immediate cost pressures for U.S. defense contractors and advanced technology manufacturers. Regulatory Suspensions: Washington will maintain reduced tariffs tied to illicit supply chains and continue its suspension of the Section 301 investigation into China’s maritime and logistics industries. Technology & AI Bilateral Channels: Leaders established a preliminary dialogue mechanism to discuss artificial intelligence risk prevention, with follow-up technical sessions slated for Shenzhen later this quarter. Despite the tactical calm, institutional investors view the extension as a pause rather than a pivot. The underlying tensions stem from two decades of bilateral economic friction that fundamentally transformed American industrial capacity. Historical Context: The Legacy of PNTR and the "China Shock" To understand why current trade negotiations remain fraught, market participants must look back to the structural turning point of 2000–2001. The decision to grant China Permanent Normal Trade Relations (PNTR) in 2000 and support its entry into the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2001 removed annual congressional renewal risks, triggering an unprecedented surge in offshore corporate investment and low-cost imports. U.S. Manufacturing Job Losses (2000–2014) During the initial economic shift between 2000 and 2003, the U.S. manufacturing sector suffered a sharp drop with the loss of 935,000 jobs. This contraction deepened during the Great Recession from 2007 to 2009, which eliminated another 2 million positions. In total, across the entire 2000 to 2014 deindustrialization era, the United States lost 5 million manufacturing jobs and saw approximately 70,000 factories close permanently. The Deindustrialization Timeline The Initial Cliff (2000–2003): Following China's WTO accession, a rapid expansion of the trade deficit accounted for roughly 935,000 U.S. manufacturing jobs lost in just three years. Direct competition with Chinese imports directly accounted for 1.5 to 2 million U.S. manufacturing job losses between 2000 and 2007. Total Manufacturing Contraction (2000–2014): Between January 2000 and 2014, the U.S. lost 5 million manufacturing jobs and nearly 70,000 factories due to global trade shifts, currency imbalances, and accelerated automation. The Great Recession Blow (2007–2009): The financial crisis delivered a second severe shock, wiping out 2 million manufacturing jobs—representing nearly 15% of the sector's total workforce—and contracting total U.S. industrial output by 20%. Unfulfilled Promises and Localized Blight When Washington originally pushed for WTO entry, political consensus held that market integration would force Beijing to liberalize its economy, respect intellectual property, and adopt free-market norms. Instead, Beijing deployed state subsidies, currency management, and mandatory technology transfer rules to construct a state-directed manufacturing powerhouse. The benefits of trade (cheaper consumer goods, tech sector expansion, corporate efficiency) proved broad, while the losses were sharply concentrated: Urban Base Collapse: When anchor plants shut down in industrial hubs like Muncie, Indiana, or Flint, Michigan, regional supply chains dissolved instantly. This destroyed generationally held residential equity and cratered municipal tax bases, leaving local governments unable to maintain basic infrastructure or public services. Persistent Regional Scarring: Worker retraining initiatives across the Rust Belt historically yielded success rates below 25%. High-margin service and technology jobs concentrated heavily in coastal metropolitan areas, leaving former factory towns in prolonged cycles of wage stagnation and economic dislocation. Investor Implications & Long-Term Outlook The permanent scarring from the China Shock built the modern bipartisan political consensus around economic nationalism, persistent tariffs, and targeted industrial policy (such as state-backed subsidies for domestic semiconductor fabrication and green energy supply chains). For corporate boards and asset managers, the January 10 truce extension changes little regarding long-term capital allocation: Near-Shoring Acceleration: Multinationals continue to diversify assembly lines into Vietnam, Mexico, and India to insulate operations against sudden tariff shifts after the January deadline. Capital Goods Re-Rating: Industrial automation, domestic construction equipment, and U.S. semiconductor infrastructure stocks retain structural tailwinds as reshoring incentives remain a pillar of federal economic strategy. Agricultural Volatility: U.S. agricultural exporters face ongoing exposure; while short-term soybean commitments offer relief, analysts caution that structural trade shifts continue to prompt major buyers to diversify purchasing toward South American markets. The two-month extension buys precious time for corporate earnings planning through year-end, but institutional strategy continues to price in a permanently fragmented global trading architecture. Fool me once, shame on you. Allow temporary trade truces to mask structural non-compliance twenty-five times over twenty-five years, and it is no longer a diplomatic miscalculation—it is a permanent market regime.

text: MARKET UPDATE — FRIDAY, 25 SEPTEMBER 2026 All week, one chain has driven markets: oil up → bond yields up → stocks down. On Thursday it tightened further. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.23%, its highest in 19 years, and Brent reached as much as $108 after Houthi missiles targeted Saudi Arabia's Red Sea oil coast. This morning the chain is running in reverse. Iran has offered a "7-day" plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Oil is slipping, yields are easing and stock futures are up. The question for traders is whether this is a turning point or just a pause. 🟢 BONDS: A 19-YEAR HIGH, THEN A BREATHER Quick basics: a bond yield is the interest a government pays to borrow. When investors sell bonds, yields rise. The 10-year Treasury yield is the anchor for mortgages, company loans and share valuations worldwide. Thursday was another bruising day: 🔸 The 10-year hit 5.2251% during the day, its highest since 2007. 🔸 It rose 20 basis points (0.20 percentage points) in two days, the biggest two-day jump since the April 2025 "Liberation Day" tariff shock (Reuters). 🔸 The 30-year touched 5.50%, its highest since 2004. The seven-year reached its highest since 2009. 🔸 The Treasury's buyback of long-term bonds was smaller than expected, the second time this week that a plan to calm markets has fallen short. 🔸 The MOVE index, the bond market's "fear gauge", jumped to levels last seen in the early days of the Iran war. Choppy bond markets can raise borrowing costs for companies too. This morning: 10-year 5.167% · two-year 4.901% · 30-year 5.462% · one-year 4.492%. It's global. Japan's 10-year yield hit 3.115%, its highest since 1996. Australia's rose to 5.408% (Reuters). "Once risk-free rates sit above 5% in the world's largest economy, every asset on the planet has to justify its price against that" — Nigel Green, deVere Group. 💡 In plain English: if the US government pays you more than 5% a year, almost risk-free, then a share, a house or a Bitcoin has to promise a lot more to be worth the risk. That's why rising yields put pressure on everything else. Keep this morning's move in proportion: a drop of about 0.04 points after a 0.20-point surge is a breather, not a reversal. 🟢 IS THE BOND MARKET PAYING TOO MUCH ATTENTION TO OIL? WSJ columnist James Mackintosh raises the most useful question of the week. This month, the daily link between oil prices and the 10-year yield has been the tightest on record. Oddly, it is tighter for long-dated bonds than short-dated ones. Part of that link makes sense. Costlier oil lifts inflation. The Fed, under Chair Kevin Warsh, has already started raising rates. Futures now price a better-than-even chance of four more hikes by the end of 2027. That rightly pushes up two-year yields, which mainly track the Fed's next few moves. 💠 The puzzle is the 10- and 30-year bonds. 🔸 An oil shock lifts inflation once. Suppose oil jumps from $70 to $100 and then stays there. Prices are painfully higher, but they are no longer rising because of oil. 🔸 The exception is if it spreads: oil → diesel → freight → food → wages. That second round is what the Fed is watching for. 🔸 A higher price level is not the same as a permanently higher inflation rate. So why should today's oil price decide what investors want for lending until the 2050s? "It makes no sense that what happens to oil today should affect the 10-year" — Vítor Constâncio, former ECB vice-president. 💠 The case that the link is rational: 🔸 Debt: expensive energy pushes governments into subsidies and tax cuts, which means more borrowing when investors are already worried about deficits. 🔸 A common cause: the AI investment boom is keeping the economy hot. A strong economy pushes up both oil demand and yields. Wednesday was a good example: blockbuster business data sent both higher. They may be moving together without one causing the other. 🔸 No one knows how permanent a rate rise will be. So markets assume part of it will last (Sushil Wadhwani, former Bank of England policymaker). 💠 There are two ways to read a 10-year above 5%. (1) A structural reset: AI's appetite for capital, heavy government borrowing and sticky inflation mean money should simply cost more now. (2) An overshoot: the market has projected a temporary oil shock decades into the future. If Hormuz reopens and long yields fall with oil, the 5%+ yields could look like a bargain in hindsight. Mackintosh himself likes Treasuries (and UK gilts even more) as a hedge in case the AI trade goes wrong for stocks. 🟢 THE FED AND THE WORLD'S CENTRAL BANKS: THE HIKING CYCLE SPREADS US rates are at 3.75%–4.00% after last week's hike, the first in three years. 🔸 Chance of another hike at the 27–28 October meeting: about 64% on Thursday morning (CME) → 71% by this morning (Reuters). Markets expect more than 0.90 points of further tightening this cycle, close to four quarter-point hikes. 🔸 Why: the jobs market is solid (next section), and Citi's Andrew Hollenhorst says Fed officials can now focus "entirely toward inflation". 💠 Other central banks are following: 🔸 Norway's Norges Bank raised rates on Thursday. Sweden's Riksbank signalled a likely hike by year-end. 🔸 Mexico's Banxico held rates but dropped its promise of a long pause. 🔸 Bank of America now expects the ECB to hike in December (markets price ~93%) and the Bank of England in November and February 2027. The dollar is set for a 1% weekly gain (Reuters). The DXY, which measures it against six major currencies, is at 101.14 this morning (−0.11%). Higher US rates draw money into dollars. 💡 Why it matters: when central banks raise rates together, borrowing gets dearer everywhere at once. That is the backdrop that has pushed Japan's and Australia's yields to multi-decade highs. 🟢 THE ECONOMY: HOT JOBS, COLD HOUSING 💠 Jobs: layoffs are near historic lows. 🔸 Weekly jobless claims fell to 197,000 (forecast: 201,000), near levels last seen in 1969. The four-week average is 202,250. 🔸 Continuing claims are 1.719m, near a three-year low. September unemployment looks steady at 4.1%. 🔸 Caveat: Labor Day distorts the seasonal figures. Companies are holding on to staff but are wary of hiring, and an immigration crackdown has shrunk the labour supply. "In mid-September the economy seems to be firing on all cylinders in part due to the extraordinary capex expenditures on AI" — Christopher Rupkey, FWDBONDS. 💠 Housing is the part of the economy feeling the squeeze. 🔸 The 30-year mortgage averaged 7.03% (Freddie Mac), the highest since January 2025, and up more than a full point since the Iran war began in February. 🔸 New home sales jumped 6.4% to 684,000 (forecast 615,000), the best since December 2025. But that was bought with discounts: the median new-home price fell 5.8% from a year ago to $393,700. 🔸 8.5 months of unsold supply. Builders are cutting prices to clear stock, not because demand is booming. 💡 In plain English: the Fed wants to cool the economy. Housing is cooling. Jobs and AI spending aren't. That's why the Fed may need to hike further, and why bonds keep feeling the pressure. 🟢 OIL AND THE MIDDLE EAST: A HORMUZ OFFER, A RED SEA THREAT 💠 First, the threat that sent oil to $108. 🔸 Saudi Arabia intercepted six ballistic missiles it says were fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis. Alerts went out for Mecca, Jeddah, Taif, Tabuk and Yanbu. 🔸 Yanbu is Saudi Arabia's main Red Sea oil port. A Greek-operated Patriot system shot down a missile and a drone near the area. It was the fifth time that system has been used in combat since February. 🔸 The Houthis have seized Yemen's entire Red Sea coast this month and are pushing towards Aden. 🔸 Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are calling an urgent military meeting under their joint defence pact. Tehran is trying to distance itself from the Houthis' advance (Reuters). A senior Iranian military official also warned the war could spread to the Indian Ocean (The Economist). 💡 Why Yanbu matters so much: with Hormuz shut, Saudi Arabia exports much of its oil through a pipeline across the kingdom to the Red Sea, ending at Yanbu. That is the main route that bypasses Hormuz. If Houthi missiles threaten it, the world's backup supply route is at risk too (Barron's: "the Red Sea alternate route… may also face disruption"). 💠 Then, the offer that is pulling oil back down. 🔸 Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi says mediators have given the White House a plan: if "certain conditions" are met, "the strait will be open in seven days", and broader talks would restart (FT). He added: "We don't care about the timing." 🔸 Behind the scenes (Reuters): Iran reopens Hormuz → the US lifts its economic blockade → Iran may regain frozen assets. Iran would move its demand for transit fees into a side agreement, but it won't give up "administrative control" of the strait. Gulf states reject both. 🔸 The White House says the talks are "positive and constructive" but "we are not in a rush". It claims "nearly 22 million barrels of oil left the Strait last night" (unverified). It won't return to June's collapsed agreement, which President Pezeshkian wants restored before the 3 November midterms. 🔸 The odds: former US negotiator Dennis Ross puts a deal before the midterms at 30%. Neither side wants to give up its leverage first: the US has the blockade, Iran has the strait. Meanwhile, the US keeps tightening the squeeze. The UAE, the region's biggest air hub, has suspended all Iranian airline flights under new US "secondary sanctions", which penalise foreign firms that do business with Iran. Oman, Iraq (Baghdad), Georgia and Azerbaijan have done the same. Oil this morning: Brent about $105 (front-month, −0.8% to −1.4%), WTI about $92.50–93.50. The next Brent contract trades nearer $99. That discount is a sign the market expects today's shortage to ease with time. 💡 Why it matters for everything above: a credible Hormuz deal is the fastest route to lower oil. Lower oil should mean lower yields, cheaper mortgages and relief for stocks. "Any easing of geopolitical tensions… could go a long way toward stabilizing the bond market" — Angelo Kourkafas, Edward Jones. 🟢 TRUMP–XI: WARM WORDS, FEW DEALS Xi Jinping's first White House visit in over a decade was high on ceremony and low on breakthroughs (Reuters). 🔸 Xi's message: the US and China should "coexist in peace", with "healthy" competition, "not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses". He said China "keeps its doors wide open" to US firms and asked for fair treatment of Chinese companies in the US. 🔸 Trade: the tariff truce now runs to 10 January. The US refused a longer extension, saying China hasn't kept to the deal. 🔸 AI: the leaders will create an "AI Dialogue" on security risks. Their tone differed. Trump wants to "leave it exactly where it is". Xi wants AI "always under human control". 🔸 Taiwan: Xi pressed Trump to actively "oppose" Taiwan independence. That would go further than the current US line of "not supporting" it. The White House hasn't released its account of the talks. 🔸 Iran: Xi backed a return to June's US–Iran agreement, which Washington has rejected. 🔸 Next: Trump is expected at APEC in Shenzhen in November and Xi at the G20 in Miami in December. At the state dinner: Apple's Tim Cook, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon and Citi's Jane Fraser. No Chinese chief executives were invited. 💡 For markets, no bad news is the good news. The truce holds until January and the two sides are still talking. The risk to watch is Taiwan wording. Any shift would matter most for chipmakers. 🟢 STOCKS: HOLDING THEIR NERVE Thursday: the S&P 500 fell 0.02%, the Nasdaq rose 0.01% and the Dow fell 0.3% (−161 points). Stocks opened lower, jumped on Reuters' report of a "phased" Hormuz deal, then gave the gains back as yields rose. Most stocks fell even though the index was flat. This morning (futures): S&P 500 7,776 (+0.12%) · Nasdaq 100 30,870 (+0.34%) · Dow 51,773 (+0.11%). The S&P 500 and Nasdaq are only about 1% below their records. VIX: 15.57 (Thursday's close). Asia: Japan's Nikkei +1%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng −1%, Australia −0.6%. China, Taiwan and South Korea were closed for a holiday. What strategists say: 🔸 Citi: stay invested in US stocks, but wait for a pullback before buying more. Pullbacks tend to come after a first Fed hike, and markets tend to dip into the midterms before the usual year-end rally. 🔸 Edward Jones: growth and profits are solid, but fast-rising yields and choppy bond markets are "a more meaningful headwind" for shares. 💡 In plain English: stocks are close to their highs because company profits and AI spending are strong. But every rise in yields makes shares look more expensive relative to safe bonds. For now that tension is the main thing holding stocks back. 🟢 CRYPTO: STEADY, BUT STILL UNDER WATER Bitcoin is at $84,004 (−0.45%) and Ether at $2,671 (−0.59%). 🔸 Bitcoin has held above the $82,000–83,000 support zone (the May high) after dipping to about $83,500 yesterday. 🔸 It is still below about $85,600, the average price paid by US spot Bitcoin ETF investors (Glassnode). Many recent buyers are sitting on small losses. 🔸 The main pressures are a firm dollar and 5%+ yields. Crypto trades like tech stocks: it needs yields to cool before it can rally properly. 🗓️ CALENDAR Today (ET): 🔸 8:30am US durable goods orders, August (usual release time) 🔸 10:00am University of Michigan consumer sentiment, final September, including inflation expectations (usual release time) 🔸 Fed speakers: New York Fed's John Williams and Cleveland Fed's Beth Hammack (times not confirmed) 🔸 Trump–Xi talks continue, and US–Iran contacts continue at the UN Key dates ahead: 🔸 27–28 October: Fed meeting (~71% chance of a hike) 🔸 3 November: US midterm elections 🔸 November: possible BoE hike (BofA) · APEC summit, Shenzhen 🔸 December: ECB meeting (~93% hike priced) · G20, Miami 🔸 10 January: US–China trade truce expires 🟢 WHAT IT ALL MEANS 1️⃣ Watch oil to predict bonds. Oil and 10-year yields have never moved so closely day to day. If Iran's seven-day plan gains traction, lower oil should bring yields down, and stocks, housing and crypto should benefit. 2️⃣ Watch the long end for the truth. If oil falls but 10- and 30-year yields don't, the market is telling you 5% is the new normal. That would point to AI demand for capital, government debt and sticky inflation, not oil. Valuations would have to adjust. 3️⃣ The world is tightening. The Fed, Norway, soon Sweden, the ECB and the BoE are all raising rates or leaning that way. That keeps the dollar firm and pressure on assets priced in dollars, including emerging markets, gold and crypto. 4️⃣ Yanbu is the new flashpoint. Hormuz explains the oil price. The Red Sea explains the risk of another spike. A successful Houthi strike on Saudi export infrastructure would be the market's worst case. 5️⃣ Keep a balanced portfolio. Citi's advice is to stay invested but wait for dips. Mackintosh holds bonds as a hedge in case AI stocks stumble. Both are sensible in a market where one headline can reverse a day's move. 🔸 What would prove this reading wrong: Hormuz reopening with long yields still stuck above 5.2% (a structural reset: bad for valuations). Or a Red Sea attack pushing Brent well above $110 (inflation and hike fears return). 💭 THOUGHT FOR THE DAY "The two most powerful warriors are patience and time."— Leo Tolstoy, War and Peace This week the market was pushed around by missiles, auctions and headlines, often within the same hour. Yet the S&P 500 still sits within about 1% of its record, and bonds now pay savers more than they have in almost two decades. Wars end. Oil shocks fade. Rate cycles turn. The investors who come out ahead are rarely the fastest to react. They are the ones who keep their plan and let time work for them. Have a great weekend. 📌 Sources: TradingView, The Wall Street Journal (James Mackintosh), Financial Times, Barron's, Reuters, MarketWatch, The Economist, Al Jazeera English, Freddie Mac, US Labor Department, US Census Bureau, CME FedWatch, LSEG, Glassnode, Citi, Edward Jones, Bank of America Global Research, deVere Group. 💬 How can I make these updates better? text: Anand Rathi G200 Summit: Chemicals - Demand is improving but uneven; cost pass-through and ramp-ups decide delivery We hosted ten chemical companies at our G200 Summit: Aarti Industries, Epigral, Fine Organic Industries, Fineotex Chemical, Galaxy Surfactants, IG Petro, Navin Fluorine Intl, Privi Specialty, Rossari Biotech and Vishnu Chemicals. The tone was constructive; the following themes stood out: ■ Demand is improving but uneven. Energy, polymers, oil & gas, F&F and Indian pharma and FMCG are firm / improving; Agro is recovering only in select products, textiles and CPVC are soft near-term, and dyes and pigments are still weakening. Part of the strength is conflict-driven, notably Aarti's energy business, which depends on elevated cracks, and some full plants reflect tight supply as much as strong demand. Galaxy posted its first double-digit India volume growth in two years, Fine Organic sold out, Privi at about 90%. ■Freight and inputs are the swing factor. The West Asia conflict has pushed freight higher; Lifted Aarti's raw material costs to roughly twice February levels ,13-14% of export value for Vishnu (from 3–4%), Fine Organic flagged sharply higher freight to the US and South America. EO, aniline and methanol remain tight. Who keeps margins depends on pricing structure: Protected: Aarti's quarterly formula resets, Privi's price resets on freight or FX moves above 5%, and Fineotex's cost-plus model. Exposed: Fine Organic's CIF/DDP contracts and Vishnu's chrome exports, where competitors aren't facing the same freight burden. Currency: Largely treated as a pass-through item in contracts rather than a source of gains. Side-effect: Higher prices inflate revenue and working capital; Aarti's debt is up Rs7-9bn since January. ■ Capex is giving way to asset-sweating . Capex cycles end over FY27-28 (Aarti, Rossari, Epigral, Fineotex), but 2–2.5-year ramp-ups push much of the earnings uplift into FY29–30. Execution is the risk - the Zone 4 delay puts Aarti's FY28 full year EBITDA guidance of Rs18-22bn at risk (~1-2 quarters). ■ China has bottomed, and companies are going local. Chinese pricing appears to have stabilized, and growth plans are tilting towards import substitution (Epigral's epoxy, Vishnu's DMSO, Privi's maltol). Overseas localization is also growing (Fine Organic's US plant, Galaxy's Mexico and Egypt routes, Fineotex's US CCT), also de-risks freight and tariff risk.

text: PARADISE FOR SOME, HELL FOR OTHERS. Globalization — Socio-Economic Consequences - sequel to the book- Chapter 8. Destroyed Small Business and the Local Economy“ When Walmart comes to town, mom and pop close up. This isn’t a market. It’s a natural disaster.” — owner of a closed hardware store in Iowa, 2019 8.1. Paradise for the Buyer, Death for the Seller Imagine a small town in Ohio (USA), or in Yorkshire in Britain, or in Brittany in France, or in Tottori Prefecture in Japan. Population: 20,000. The main street is High Street, Main Street, Rue de la République. There you find: a butcher shop, a bakery, a hardware store, a bookstore, a shoe shop, a pharmacy, a café, a barbershop where everyone knows everyone else.This is the Main Street economy — the millennia-old foundation of local communities. Family businesses passed from father to son. Prices are not the lowest, but there is trust, quality, service, and “until payday” credit for people you know. And there is a “middle class” that rests on these small enterprises — the owners, their employees, their suppliers.Then Walmart arrives (or Carrefour, or Tesco, or Amazon) — and everything disappears.What happens in the five years after a Walmart opens in a town (Institute for Local Self-Reliance study, 2024): 25–40% of small retail stores within a 10-mile radius close. 20–30% of small cafés and restaurants close (because Walmart opens its own prepared-foods section and a coffee shop at the entrance). 50% of local hardware and housewares stores close (price competition kills them). Retail employment in the town falls 15–20% (because Walmart hires 200 people, but before Walmart arrived the town had 400 owners/workers in small stores — a net loss of 200 jobs). The paradox: Walmart brings cheap goods. Consumers save 15–25% on purchases. It is paradise for the wallet. But those same consumers can no longer buy fresh meat at the butcher shop (it closed) and are forced to buy meat at Walmart — cheap, but raised on a farm 2,000 km away, frozen, pumped full of antibiotics. They cannot buy a book at the bookstore — they buy the book (or a Kindle) on Amazon. They cannot get a bicycle repaired — because the local workshop closed, and Walmart only sells bicycles, it does not repair them.The local economy dies. Instead of 30 small businesses — one hypermarket, two chain coffee shops (Starbucks, Costa), three fast-food outlets (McDonald’s, KFC, Subway) and an empty main street with “For Lease” signs in the windows. The town ceases to be a town. It becomes a “consumption node” without a soul, without community, without economic resilience. 8.2. The Killing Mechanism: How Global Chains WinHow do Walmart, Amazon and other “killers of small business” do it? They have three systemic advantages that small players cannot match. 8.2.1. Economies of Scale Walmart buys goods in lots of a million units directly from a factory in China or Bangladesh. The unit price is pennies. A small store buys the same goods from a local distributor (who bought from an importer, who bought from China). Each link adds a 10–20% markup. As a result Walmart can sell 30–50% cheaper. The consumer wins on price — but loses on choice and quality, because Walmart decides what it is profitable to sell. 8.2.2. Bargaining Power with Suppliers P&G, Coca-Cola, Unilever, Nestlé — these are giants. But Walmart is their No. 1 sales channel worldwide. If Walmart says “Cut the price 10% or we take your product off the shelves,” the supplier cuts the price. A small store never has that power. Walmart also charges “slotting fees” (payment for shelf space) that the supplier pays to Walmart. The supplier does not pay a small store — on the contrary, the distributor dictates terms to it. 8.2.3. Tax Optimization Walmart, Amazon and Carrefour have armies of lawyers and tax consultants who build schemes for paying taxes through Luxembourg, Ireland, Delaware, “shifting” profits to low-tax EU Tax Observatory study (2024) showed: large retail chains pay an effective corporate tax rate of 9–12% in Europe (nominal rate 20–25%). Small business cannot do this — it pays the full rate. Unfair tax competition.Result: small business closes, the global chain expands, the town loses local jobs, and the taxes collected do not offset the losses, because the chain pays taxes where its headquarters is, not where its store is. 8.3. The Amazon Effect: How Online Finished Off Offline Walmart is the twentieth century. Amazon is the twenty-first. And it is even more destructive for small business, because Amazon is “the store inside your phone,” open 24/7, with delivery in 24 hours and prices that cannot be beaten.Figures (2025, USA): Amazon controls 43% of the e-commerce market. 75 million households have an Amazon Prime subscription (they pay $139 a year for free delivery). Amazon sells more than $600 billion of goods a year — more than Switzerland’s GDP. What this means for Main Street:Case: bookstores. Before Amazon there were 12,000 independent bookstores in the United States. In 2025 — 3,500. The rest closed or survive thanks to niche formats (children’s books, poetry, mystery) and local-community activity. Barnes & Noble (the large chain) shrank from 700 stores to 250.The book business became a market in which Amazon sells 70% of all physical books. Publishers depend on Amazon. Authors depend on Amazon (Kindle Direct Publishing). Readers save money — books became cheaper. But mid-list writers earn $5,000 a year (instead of $30,000 in the 1990s), because Amazon dictates low hardware, electronics, toys, clothing. The same story. A small electronics store in town closes because “on AliExpress it’s all the same for half the price, shipping free (even if you wait three weeks).” But Amazon (and AliExpress, and Temu) are not free: they win because they do not bear the costs of a physical store — rent, staff, heating, lighting, cash registers, theft. They shift part of the costs onto the postal service (which is subsidized by the state) and onto the environment (packaging waste, the carbon footprint of delivery).Small business cannot compete with this. Even if it opens an online shop, it cannot compete with Amazon on SEO, advertising, logistics and price. Either it sells through Amazon as a “third party,” paying Amazon a 15–30% commission and handing over its customer data. Or it dies. 8.4. Walmart in Mexico and Tesco in Thailand: Colonization 2.0 Global chains do not kill small business only in the United States and Europe. In developing countries their expansion is even more ruthless — because local small business was already on the edge of survival.Mexico and Walmart: Walmart entered Mexico in 1991. By 2025 Walmart de México y Centroamérica is the country’s largest employer (230,000 employees) and controls 25% of all retail sales.Meanwhile: Over 30 years, 670,000 “tianguis” (tiny stalls, family grocery shops) closed. That is 1.2 million jobs lost. Local producers (cheese, bread, salsa, tortillas) cannot get onto Walmart shelves — certificates, packaging, volumes and deadlines are required. Prices of basic foods in regions without Walmart are higher than in those with Walmart, because Walmart dumps prices at the start to kill competitors and then raises them. Mexico’s Federal Competition Commission fined Walmart in 2020 for dumping. The fine was 0.1% of its annual profit. Insignificant.Thailand and Tesco Lotus (now Lotus’s): British Tesco entered Thailand in 1998, built hypermarkets, and in 2021 sold the business to a Thai conglomerate for $10 billion. By then: 2,500 stores across Thailand, 50,000 employees.The Thai Small Business Association stated that Tesco destroyed 300,000 family shops (previously 80% of the country’s retail trade went through them).The government tried to regulate — requiring hypermarkets to close one day a week, setting product quotas, banning new openings within 5 km of markets.Tesco lobbied against the rules, sometimes successfully.Outcome for developing countries: the import of modern capitalism destroys the traditional economy faster than it can create new jobs in the modern sector. People from the closed shops go to work as sales clerks at Walmart or Tesco for one-third the one got paradise except Walmart’s shareholders. 8.5. “Local Currencies” and “Slow Cities”: Resistance to Hell Globalization did not destroy small business completely. Resistance movements arose. The most interesting:Local currencies: In some regions they issue money that cannot be used at Walmart or Amazon. Example: the Bristol Pound (2012–2021, later moved to the digital platform Bristol Pay) — 1 British pound = 1 Bristol Pound. The difference: a Bristol Pound cannot be spent at Tesco — only at independent shops, cafés and markets in Bristol. More than 1,000 businesses accepted it; 2 million Bristol Pounds were in circulation. Analogues: Ithaca Hours (New York), the BerkShare (a Swiss regional franc), the Chiemgauer (Germany).Effect: a 5–10% shift in consumption toward local business — enough for it to survive.Slow Cities (Cittàslow): A movement that began in Italy as a response to fast chains. Principles: protection of small shops, ban on chain hypermarkets in historic centers, support for local farmers and artisans. By 2025, 280 towns in 30 countries (most in Italy, Germany, Japan, Korea). Residents pay 10–15% more for food but get quality, community, preserved jobs and tourism (people travel to “slow cities” for the weekend).“Keep it Local” platforms: United Kingdom — Totally Locally; United States — Independent We Stand; Germany — Wir kaufen lokal. Campaigns argue: “If you don’t want your main street to die, spend 10% of your budget in small shops. Even 10% will save 50% of them.”Limitations: all of this works at the micro level. Against Amazon’s $600 billion and Walmart’s $650 billion, 2 million Bristol Pounds are a drop in the ocean. But there is a psychological effect: people realize that cheap goods have a social price, and sometimes they are willing to pay more so as not to live in a ghost town. 8.6. The Argument in Defense of Global Chains (and Why It Is Weak) Supporters of globalization say: “The market works. Small business is inefficient. Walmart and Amazon give people cheap goods, which is especially important for the poor. The money saved can be spent on education, health, entertainment — that raises quality of life. The closing of small shops is Schumpeterian creative destruction, inevitable under capitalism.”There is truth in this logic: for a poor family, saving $50 a month on groceries at Walmart is the chance to buy a child medicine or textbooks. And no one has the right to forbid the poor from saving.The problem is two things: The saving is one-time, the loss of jobs is permanent. When Main Street dies, small business will never be reborn there (banks will not lend to a “dying format,” buildings decay). Creative destruction creates nothing new — it simply kills. Monopsony. Walmart and Amazon become the only buyers for local suppliers. If you produce cheese in Wisconsin, you either sell to Walmart at the price it sets, or you sell to no one. Classical market equilibrium is broken: one side (the buyer) holds dictatorial power. In antitrust law this is called “abuse of a dominant position,” but antitrust suits against Walmart almost always lose (lobbying, difficulty of proof). Schumpeter called “creative destruction” the engine of progress. But he meant that steam locomotives give way to diesel locomotives, not that entire classes of small entrepreneurs disappear and their place is taken by one giant monopolist.This is not creation. It is hierarchical centralization of capital. 8.7. Gastronomic Imperialism: How Global Corporations Destroy Local Cuisine “Control the food and you control the people. Control the seed and you control the future.” — Vandana Shiva, Indian philosopher, ecologist and activist If Walmart destroyed the shops on Main Street and Amazon turned independent sellers into digital proletarians, global food corporations attack something far more intimate — our stomachs. Food is not merely fuel for the body. It is ancestral memory, social ritual, cultural identity, economic independence. That is why it became the main battlefield between transnational capital and local communities. When a corporation takes from a people the right to decide what, how and from where they eat — it takes something larger than an economic resource. It takes this section we examine the mechanisms of “gastronomic imperialism” — the systematic invasion of local food systems by global corporations. We will see how Nestlé turns African mothers’ breast milk into a commercial scarcity, how NAFTA turns Mexican corn farmers into landless migrants, how McDonald’s replaces millennia-old culinary traditions with a standardized hamburger. And how all of this is not merely a cultural tragedy but also the prologue to the ecological catastrophe we will discuss in the next chapter. Gastronomic imperialism is the bridge between the economic destruction of small business and the ecological destruction of the planet. It shows how the destruction of the local economy is inseparably linked to the destruction of ecosystems .8.7.1. Food as a Weapon: Three Corporations That Changed the World In 1974 the British magazine New Internationalist published an investigation titled “The Baby Killer.” The article, prepared with the support of War on Want, described how the Swiss corporation Nestlé promoted infant formula in countries of Africa, Asia and Latin America. Nurses in white coats — actually saleswomen in uniform — handed out free samples in maternity wards. By the time the free supplies ran out, the mother’s breast milk had already disappeared — physiology works so that regular bottle-feeding suppresses prolactin production and lactation. The mother was trapped: either buy formula or watch the child die. But water in these regions was often contaminated with bacteria, and the instructions on the package — in a language local women could not read — required boiling that was unavailable. According to World Health Organization estimates, improper formula feeding led to hundreds of thousands of cases of diarrhea and tens of thousands of infant deaths every year.Nestlé held roughly 40% of the world infant-formula market and regarded countries of the Global South as a key market for expanding sales as European markets shrank. In its 1961 annual report the company boasted: “Growing awareness among African peoples of the need to improve the nutrition of young children contributed to increased sales of Lactogen.” The 1962 report contained an even more cynical formulation: “The local population is more aware than ever of the practical advantages and nutritional value of milk specialties for children, which made it possible to set new sales records.” Infant mortality as a marketing opportunity. Breastfeeding in Chile after the introduction of formula collapsed from 90% in 1960 to 10% by 1968. The corporation turned the most natural act of motherhood into commercial dependence.The scandal led to an international boycott of Nestlé in 1977 — one of the largest in history. The boycott covered trade unions, churches, universities and hospitals around the world. In 1981 the World Health Assembly adopted the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes — the first document in history to recognize that the marketing of food products can kill. But the corporation did not stop. In the 2010s whistleblowers reported that in Pakistan Nestlé “medical delegates” still bribed nurses to enter postnatal wards, and in Nigeria a Nestlé Pure Life plant dumped untreated wastewater, poisoning local communities’ drinking-water sources. In 2018 Pakistan’s Supreme Court found that Nestlé extracted billions of liters of water without paying the state, while ~43% of the water was lost in the filtration process. The corporation turned a public water resource into a privatized commodity and then sold it back to those from whom it had stolen it.If Nestlé used the absence of food as a weapon, Coca-Cola used water scarcity. In San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chiapas, Mexico, a Coca-Cola FEMSA plant consumes more than 750,000 liters of water daily — in a region where local communities suffer chronic water shortage. Village residents are forced to drink contaminated well water while the corporation bottles the local resource in plastic and sells it back at a price the poorest cannot afford. According to human-rights organizations, consumption of soft drinks in the region reached critical levels: one can of Coca-Cola contains 39 grams of sugar, and diabetes became one of the leading causes of death among the indigenous Tzotzil and Tzeltal communities. Food is replaced by a liquid that causes disease, and water becomes a commodity unavailable to those without money.And McDonald’s? McDonald’s is an industrial complex. The chain includes more than 44,000 restaurants in more than 100 countries. The corporation sells 75 hamburgers every second. But its product is not food. Its product is standardization. A hamburger in Tokyo is identical to a hamburger in Cape Town and Munich. The golden arches became a symbol not merely of American culture but of global homogeneity — a cultural tin can in which millennia-old flavor landscapes disappear. Every McDonald’s restaurant is a small outpost where local culinary memory is erased for the sake of a single global format. French sociologist Georges Perec wrote that McDonald’s creates a “space of nowhere” — a place stripped of geography, history, identity. And there are more and more such places on the planet. 8.7.2. Loss of Food Sovereignty: When the Land Stops Feeding Food sovereignty is the right of peoples to determine their own food and agricultural systems. This right is systematically destroyed by global trade agreements, transgenic seeds and agrochemical giants. When a farmer cannot choose what to plant because all seeds are patented, when a country cannot feed itself because cheap imports destroyed local production — food sovereignty turns into food dependence.Mexico: corn under NAFTA control. Before 1994 Mexico grew enough corn for domestic consumption, importing it only in years of poor harvest. Corn — maíz — was sacred: the Aztecs worshipped the maize god Centeotl, and even today remote communities in Oaxaca hold sowing and harvest rituals. But NAFTA abolished tariffs on agricultural imports while preserving U.S. subsidies to American farmers — $106 billion from 1995 to 2016. Cheap American corn, sold below the cost of production (dumping), flooded the Mexican market. In the first decade of the agreement, U.S. corn exports to Mexico quadrupled while the price of Mexican corn collapsed 66%. According to Public Citizen, about 2 million Mexicans employed in agriculture lost their livelihoods. 1.4 million people dependent on the agrarian sector were thrown to the margins of the economy. The average monthly income of self-employed farmers plunged from 1,959 pesos a month in 1991 to 228 pesos in 2003. Agricultural workers were forced to migrate to cities and then across the border to the United States, where the number of undocumented migrants rose 75% in the five years after NAFTA took effect. Free trade turned the peasant into an illegal. But the most cynical part — the price of the tortilla, the staple food of the poorest, rose 279% in the first ten years of NAFTA. Why? Because trade killed small farmers but created an oligopoly of large traders, mills and retail chains that could dictate any prices. Today Mexico — a country where corn was a sacred crop 5,000 years before Europeans arrived — imports corn from the United States. We are not observing trade — we are observing a cultural paradox in which the free market takes from a people the right to eat the fruits of their own land.India: seeds of death. The Green Revolution of the 1960s promised to free India from hunger. Instead it turned Indian farmers into hostages of transnational corporations. When in 2002 Monsanto brought transgenic Bt Cotton onto the Indian market, the company acquired control of local seed suppliers and raised their price 8,000%. Traditional seeds that farmers had saved and exchanged for centuries were displaced by hybrids that could not be reused. Monsanto contracts forbade farmers from saving seed from their harvest — new seed had to be bought every year. A patent on a seed is not merely a legal construct. It is a weapon that turns self-reproducing wealth into an annual tax. In regions where Monsanto dominated, farmers sank into a debt trap. Crop failures, falling world cotton prices and astronomical outlays on seed and agrochemicals produced a wave of suicides. According to India’s National Crime Records Bureau, between 1995 and 2015 more than 300,000 farmers took their own lives — many by drinking the pesticides they had bought on credit. The product that was supposed to protect the harvest became an instrument of death. As Indian activist Vandana Shiva notes, in Gujarat, the largest cotton-producing state, where a local (non-transgenic) variety predominates, the problem of farmer suicides is virtually absent. But in every region where Monsanto established itself, debts and deaths follow one after another. Every year India loses 10,000+ farmer suicides.Indonesia: palm oil and the price of biodiversity. Palm oil is the cheapest vegetable fat in the world, used in half the packaged products on supermarket shelves: from chocolate bars to cosmetics and biodiesel. Its production brings Indonesia and Malaysia billions of dollars in export revenue. The price? Between 2018 and 2022 an average of 32,406 hectares of forest were cleared annually for palm plantations. Over the last twenty years the Bornean orangutan population fell from 200,000 to 104,700 individuals. We pay 50 cents for a chocolate bar; Indonesian orangutans pay with their species. Indigenous Dayak communities lose territories that supplied them with water, food and livelihoods for millennia. And palm oil certified as “harmless to forests” enters global supply chains through loopholes in the control system — palm fruit is sold to mills hundreds of kilometers away, masking its origin. 8.7.3. Fast Food as Cultural Colonization: Standardization of Taste The world fast-food market is valued at $863–939 billion (2025) and grows 4–7% a year. By 2032–2035 it will exceed $1.2 trillion. But this is not merely economics — it is cultural homogenization through the stomach. When a global chain replaces a family noodle shop or a street vendor, it destroys not just a competitor — it erases an entire way of life, a system of knowledge, a social infrastructure. A street vendor in Mumbai is not merely a seller of food. He is part of the social fabric of the neighborhood; his smells and sounds shape the space; his recipes are passed from generation to generation.China: KFC as empire. Yum China, operator of KFC, Pizza Hut and Lavazza in China, runs 16,395 restaurants (2024), of which 11,648 are KFC. In 2024 the chain opened a record 1,352 new KFC restaurants — an average of 3.7 outlets every day. KFC revenue in China reached $8.5 billion. China’s food-delivery market is valued at $450+ billion. Traditional noodle shops, family restaurants and street vendors prove unable to compete with the logistical apparatus of a global corporation. KFC in China adapts the menu — it offers coffee with pear, a traditional northern Chinese snack, and noodles in the morning. But this is not “cultural exchange” — it is a tactic of absorption. Local dishes are integrated into a standardized format in order to lower cultural resistance. In the end, every new KFC restaurant is not merely a point of sale for food; it is a vector of cultural normalization in which “normal” food is the kind wrapped in paper, served in 90 seconds and identical in Shanghai and New York. India: McAloo Tikki as Trojan horse. McDonald’s in India is a lesson in cultural adaptation. There is no Big Mac here: instead there is McAloo Tikki (a potato patty), McSpicy Paneer and vegetarian options. The corporation displays flexibility — but the goal remains the same. India’s fast-food market grows 10%+ a year, and McDonald’s, KFC, Domino’s and Subway capture share from traditional dhabas (roadside cafés) and street vendors. The McDonald’s chain in India numbers more than 500 restaurants. It sounds modest compared with China — but each of them displaces dozens of family enterprises that fed local residents for generations.

text: ⚠️ The Iran war is becoming an inflation trade, not just a geopolitical headline. The US Israel conflict with Iran is still unresolved. The US naval blockade remains around the Strait of Hormuz, which handles roughly 20% of global oil supply. On Sept 24, Indian cargo ship MV Cape Dao was attacked near Hormuz, killing one sailor and forcing the crew to evacuate. WTI is around $91 to $92. Brent is around $102 to $103 after jumping almost 4% on Sept 23. That move is already showing up in rates. The Fed raised 25 bps on Sept 16 to 3.75% to 4%, and the September US composite PMI rose to 58.4, its highest since July 2021. The 10 year yield hit about 5.11%, the highest since 2007. text: HOW INDIA CAN COUNTER THE GRAHAM ACT Introduction The article examines India’s economic exposure to the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 and discusses how India can reduce vulnerability to possible U.S. tariff pressure. The Act was signed into law on September 18, 2026 and authorises tariffs of up to 100% on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas; importantly, it does not automatically impose a 100% tariff on India. Main Facts India remains heavily dependent on imported crude and has recently sourced a substantial share from Russia. The article highlights the two-sided exposure: India depends on Russian oil for energy security. Indian exporters depend significantly on the U.S. market. The Act therefore creates a potential energy–trade policy dilemma. India’s large forex reserves provide a partial buffer, but reserves cannot indefinitely compensate for a major export shock. The law contains scope for exemptions/waivers and gives the U.S. President considerable discretion. At the same time, abrupt disengagement from Russian energy could create its own economic costs. Hence, de-risking rather than sudden decoupling is the relevant policy challenge. Way Forward 1. Strengthen strategic petroleum reserves. 5. Increase domestic renewable and alternative-energy capacity. 6. Build a larger foreign-exchange and trade resilience buffer. 7. Use diplomatic engagement to seek exemptions where appropriate.
