text: MARKET UPDATE — WEDNESDAY, 23 SEPTEMBER 2026 Oil is on course for its longest losing streak in over a year, and the AI trade is using the gap. The Nasdaq closed at a second straight record, memory-chip stocks led and Asia rose for a sixth day. But the energy crisis hasn't ended. It has moved from the barrel to the pump. US diesel hit another record, and Washington is now openly discussing keeping it at home. The question is no longer just what energy costs. It is who gets it. 🟢 OIL: ABOUT A WEEK OF FALLS, FOR TWO REASONS Brent is at about $99 this morning and WTI at about $90. Brent is down more than 5% this week and well off the $109.97 peak it hit after Saudi Arabia's main bypass pipeline was attacked on 11 September (FT). On Tuesday it briefly fell towards $97, its lowest since 8 September (Reuters). 💠 Reason 1: Saudi Arabia's detour is back, slowly. 🔸 The East-West pipeline has restarted, three sources told Reuters. It carries Saudi oil 1,200km to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, avoiding the Strait of Hormuz. The first cargo, bound for China, was due to load on Tuesday. 🔸 Before the attack it carried about 4m barrels a day, roughly 4% of world supply. It is restarting at a low rate. Reaching 40% of capacity takes "a couple of days"; a full recovery takes six to eight weeks, as three pumping stations were damaged (Reuters). 🔸 The detail that matters: if only a quarter of the flow returns, Saudi refineries on the Red Sea coast use all of it and no extra oil reaches the world market. At 40%, about 1m extra barrels a day reach buyers. European refiners have already been told they won't get their October Yanbu cargoes. 💠 Reason 2: talks in New York. 🔸 US envoy Steve Witkoff and Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi held talks on Tuesday, at least partly through mediators. Trump called it a "very good" three-hour meeting, with another "in the very near future". 🔸 Iran's offer: a senior official told Reuters that Iran can reopen Hormuz within seven days if the US eases military pressure and lifts its blockade of Iranian ports. Why it matters: analysts estimate up to half of America's inflation overshoot comes from energy and commodity prices (Reuters). A lasting fall in oil would weaken the case for more rate rises. But oil is still up about 50% on a year ago. 💠 The risks haven't gone away: 🔸 Bank of America warns that a prolonged disruption could push Brent above $150 (Cointelegraph). 🔸 Goldman Sachs says the main upside risk is not Chinese demand, since China is mainly drawing on its reserves rather than buying more. It is further strikes on Gulf oil facilities. 🔸 India is buying less Russian oil (down 16.5% in August) for fear of a US tariff of up to 100% on buyers of Russian crude. That pushes India towards the same Middle Eastern barrels everyone else wants. 💡 In plain English: oil is falling because traders expect more supply soon. Most of that supply hasn't arrived yet. The pipeline needs weeks, and Hormuz needs a deal. 🟢 DIESEL: FROM A PRICE PROBLEM TO A SUPPLY FIGHT Cheaper crude still isn't reaching the pump. The average US diesel price hit a record $6.53 a gallon on Tuesday, up 83% this year (CNN, AAA). Adjusted for inflation, it is pennies away from its highest since 2008. Diesel is short worldwide because the Iran war has cut Middle Eastern exports, Ukrainian drones have hit Russian refineries, and Russia and China have restricted their own exports. 💠 Now Washington may keep its diesel at home. 🔸 Trump on Tuesday: "I've said let's not send out the diesel… I've called for it within my people." 🔸 Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the administration is "examining" whether a full or partial export ban would work (FT). A White House official had told CNN on Monday that no ban was under consideration. 🔸 The pressure is political. Senator Chuck Grassley says high diesel prices are "killing farmers' income". Louisiana's governor, whose state is a refining hub, wants a 90-day ban. The midterms are on 3 November. 💠 Why most experts think it would backfire: 🔸 Prices would fall on the Gulf Coast and in the Midwest, where the fuel is made and would be trapped. But the East and West Coasts rely on imports. "If he bans exports, the coasts are screwed" (Bob McNally, Rapidan Energy). 🔸 Refiners would process less crude, so petrol and jet fuel could rise too (Lipow Oil Associates). "Some refiners may not survive." 🔸 The US is the world's biggest diesel exporter. A ban would push up global prices, and allies could retaliate. McNally calls it potentially "the king of the APEs" ("authentic policy errors"). Europe would feel it first. It relies heavily on US diesel, and a ban would be bad news for European inflation, which already faces a natural gas shortage heading into winter (Reuters). 🔸 France is spending another €450m on fuel relief (€1.4bn in total). Aid for low-income commuters doubles and extends to 5.5m people, after fishermen blocked ports last week. The cost is pushing France's deficit target out of reach, another reason French borrowing costs are elevated. 🔸 Britain: Ineos is suspending three chemical plants in Hull. UK gas costs about $23.51 per unit against $2.84 in the US, roughly eight times as much (Reuters data; Ratcliffe says 12 times). "We just cannot compete." 💡 The US is thinking about keeping diesel in. Europe is shutting factories because energy costs too much. These are two symptoms of the same shortage. When governments begin deciding who gets scarce fuel, an energy shock becomes a trade problem as well. As Eurasia Group's Gregory Brew puts it, "Unless they are prepared to make a deal with Iran, they don't have good options for lowering prices." 🟢 WALL STREET: NASDAQ RECORD, WITH A "MUSE-SHAPED" HOLE 💠 Tuesday's closes: Nasdaq 27,244.28 (+0.45%), a second straight record close · S&P 500 7,764.64 (flat) · Dow 51,863.69 (−0.36%) . The Nasdaq 100 (+0.8%) also hit a record (FT) . The S&P is less than 0.5% below its 13 August record of 7,798.99. 💠 The winners: Memory chips. SanDisk +7%, Micron +5%, Seagate +4.8%, Western Digital +3.7%. Chip stocks rose for a sixth straight day. The bet is that AI agents need far more computing power and data storage than chatbots. Barclays' Emmanuel Cau: "AI Fomo is back in force." He adds that investors hold fewer tech stocks after June's sell-off, so there is room to buy. 💠 The losers: Businesses an AI agent could bypass. Meta's Muse assistant, which books, shops and sends emails for its users, has topped US app-download charts for two weeks. Investors are now asking who loses. 🔸 Charles Schwab −6.1% (online brokerage), GoDaddy −6%, Airbnb −3%, Uber and Lyft each −1%+. 🔸 "People fear that Muse will be used to manage your insurance relationships, book your travel and search for stuff to buy." — Jed Ellerbroek, Argent Capital 🔸 Amazon has now blocked Muse from shopping on its platform, a step up from Monday's request to be removed. 🔸 Meta itself fell 0.6% after Monday's 11.4% jump. Google Labs has a similar product called "CC", and analysts want to see how it performs. Financials were the worst sector (−1.7%). JPMorgan and Wells Fargo each fell more than 3%. Materials rose about 2%. 💠 Beneath the surface, weakness persists: Nasdaq stocks hitting one-year lows (110) outnumbered those hitting one-year highs (48). As we noted yesterday, the records are being carried by a narrow group. 💠 This morning (futures): · S&P 500 7,839.75 (+0.10%) · Nasdaq 100 31,037 (+0.03%) · Dow 52,346 (+0.13%) · Euro Stoxx 50 6,360.85 (+0.08%) · VIX 14.18, a calm reading. 💡 Why it matters: AI is starting to create losers as well as winners. The chipmakers that supply AI rise. Companies whose business depends on customers visiting their site or app can fall. For investors, "AI exposure" now cuts both ways. 🟢 THE FED: OIL IS FALLING, BUT THE FED ISN'T BACKING DOWN 💠 Rates are 3.75%–4.00% after last week's rise. Markets see a 53–54% chance of another rise in October and about a third of a percentage point of tightening by year-end (CME FedWatch, Reuters). 🔸 Boston Fed's Susan Collins and Richmond Fed's Tom Barkin both backed last week's rise. Barkin says the economy may be firming and that inflation isn't limited to energy and tariffs. That is his answer to the argument that falling oil will solve the problem. 🔸 Chicago Fed's Austan Goolsbee says that if inflation proves more lasting than an oil shock, the Fed would need to respond in an "aggressive" and "frontloaded" way. 🔸 Governor Michael Barr speaks today. 💠 Bonds: The two-year yield, which follows expected Fed rates most closely, is at 4.769%, near its highest since mid-2024. The 10-year is at 4.959%, still just below the 5% level that has become a pain point, and the 30-year at 5.294%. Tuesday's two-year auction met soft demand. Today the Treasury sells $70bn of five-year notes. 💠 A question worth asking (ARK Invest): What if yields are high not only because of inflation, but because AI is raising expected growth and returns on capital? ARK forecasts growth above 7% and short-term rates of 6–8% even as inflation falls. Those forecasts are extremely aggressive. Official US productivity growth was 2.2% a year in the second quarter: strong, but far from that. 💡 Why the distinction matters: if yields are high because inflation is getting out of control, that is bad for shares. If they are high because the economy is genuinely more productive, strong companies can cope. But companies with heavy floating-rate debt can't, either way. A tech boom and a credit squeeze can happen at the same time. 🟢 DOLLAR, YEN AND ASIA 🔸 The dollar is at a seven-week high (DXY 100.78, +0.24%) because markets expect more US rate rises. The euro is at $1.1440, near a two-month low. 🔸 Yen: about ¥157.60 per dollar. Traders are wary of pushing it past ¥160, the level where Japan may step in to support its currency. 🔸 Asia is up for a sixth day (MSCI Asia ex-Japan +0.7%). South Korea +1.2% (Samsung and SK Hynix both +2%+), Taiwan +0.9%, near a record. The Korean won had its best day in a month (+1.3%) after a Bank of Korea board member discussed rate rises. Japan is closed today; Nikkei futures are about 2,000 points above Friday's close, pointing to a strong reopening on Thursday. 🔸 Gold eased 0.3% to $4,341. Copper is near a record, up 18% this year. 🟢 TRUMP–XI: WHERE TRADE AND AI MEET Xi Jinping arrives in Washington today for a three-day visit. The main meeting is on Thursday. Analysts expect the uneasy trade truce (due to expire on 10 November) to hold, but expect no big breakthroughs (FT). 🔸 AI is now on the agenda. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has led preparatory AI talks with China, proposing a formal dialogue and a system to notify each other of AI incidents that affect national security. He is reportedly under consideration as Trump's new AI czar, though no decision has been made. 🔸 At the UN, Secretary-General António Guterres called on the countries leading the AI race to share safety risks and work towards common safeguards. "The danger is not technology, the danger is technology without accountability." 🔸 The broader worry (Reuters' Jamie McGeever): cheaper Chinese AI could make America's expensive AI model look uneconomical. "Investors should avoid blindly chasing highs… waiting for clearer policy signals" — Kenny Ng, Everbright Securities 💡 Why it matters: the chips rally rests on AI spending continuing and exports to China not being cut off. Thursday's summit could strengthen both of those assumptions, or challenge them. 🟢 CRYPTO: HOLDING THE BREAKOUT Bitcoin is at $86,118 (−0.10%) and Ether at $2,741.86 (−0.42%), a quiet pause after Monday's surge above $87,000. 🔸 Bitcoin is sitting just above about $85,600, the average price US spot Bitcoin ETF buyers paid (Glassnode). Holding above that level keeps ETF investors in profit and less likely to sell. 🔸 The key support remains the May high of about $82,000–83,000. Holding above it would confirm the first "higher high" since the October 2025 peak. 🔸 The headwind: a stronger dollar and rising rate-rise odds. Both make riskier assets less attractive. 🟢 GEOPOLITICS: TALKS AND THREATS AT THE SAME TIME 🔸 Trump at the UN: he faces a "big decision" and could "annihilate the Islamic Republic" if there's no deal. He expects a deal "right after the election" and called for the "complete economic isolation of Iran". He also threatened possible military action against Mexico, Cuba and others in the western hemisphere, and Cuba's delegation walked out. 🔸 Iran's President Pezeshkian addresses the UN today. An Iranian official says he won't meet Trump. 🔸 Iran is tightening its grip on Hormuz. Legislation would fine ships that break its blockade 20% of their cargo's value and hold them until they pay (parliamentary spokesperson to Fars; not clear whether the law has passed). In other words, Iran is offering to reopen the strait and writing rules to charge for passage at the same time. 🔸 France is drafting a UN Security Council resolution with the US for an international mission to restore shipping through Hormuz. It would not take an offensive stance against Iran. China and Russia have blocked previous attempts. Concern that the Houthis could threaten the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the Red Sea's southern entrance, is adding urgency. 🔸 Qatar's Emir told the UN that the Gulf is in "one of its most dangerous phases" and urged diplomacy. 💡 Markets are pricing the talks, not the threats. Both are real. Trump's own timeline ("after the election") suggests any deal is at least six weeks away, while the pipeline needs six to eight weeks to recover fully. That is a long time for oil traders to stay optimistic. 🗓️ CALENDAR 💠 Today (ET): 🔸 7:00am MBA mortgage applications 🔸 9:45am US flash PMIs for September (manufacturing and services) 🔸 10:30am EIA weekly oil inventories, including diesel stocks 🔸 1:00pm Result of $70bn five-year Treasury auction 🔸 Also: Fed Governor Michael Barr speaks · Pezeshkian addresses the UN · Xi arrives in Washington · Meta Connect begins · US sanctions on Iranian airlines take effect 🔸 Thursday: Trump–Xi summit · Japan reopens 🔸 October: Fed meeting (~54% chance of a rise) 🔸 3 November: US midterm elections 🔸 10 November: US–China trade truce expires 🟢 WHAT IT ALL MEANS 1️⃣ Oil is falling on expected supply, not delivered supply. The pipeline needs weeks, Hormuz needs a deal, and Trump points to "after the election". Wait for tanker loadings to confirm the price moves. 2️⃣ The energy shock has moved to diesel, and to politics. An export ban would be the most important policy change to watch for refiners (Valero, Marathon, Phillips 66), European inflation and US petrol prices. Today's EIA data on diesel stocks is the next clue. 3️⃣ AI is now dividing the market. Memory-chip makers win; businesses that depend on customers coming to them are at risk from agents like Muse. Selectivity matters more than simply "owning AI". 4️⃣ The Fed isn't relying on oil to do its job. Two-year yields near highs and a firm dollar show markets believe it. Today's PMIs and the five-year auction test that view. 5️⃣ Thursday matters. An extended truce and an AI dialogue support chipmakers. A breakdown would hit them hardest. 🔸 What would prove this reading wrong: Brent back above $105 on new attacks or a diesel export ban (bearish); or a confirmed US–Iran framework and faster pipeline recovery (bullish for everything except energy). 💭 THOUGHT FOR THE DAY "The years teach much which the days never know."— Ralph Waldo Emerson Look at this week's news. Oil has fallen for about a week, diesel has hit a record, and one speech threatened annihilation while another promised a deal. Each day brings a new headline, and every headline seems urgent. The years tell a calmer story. Supply shocks end. Pipelines get repaired. New technology finds its customers. Patient investors are usually rewarded. Let the days inform you, but let the years guide you. Your long-term plan is your advantage. 💬 How can I make these updates better? text: Aarti Pharmalabs may be entering the phase where the capex undertaken over the last few years finally begins contributing meaningfully to earnings. Q1 FY27 provided the first evidence: • Revenue: ₹535 Cr, up 42% • EBITDA: ₹133 Cr, up 40% • PAT: ₹71 Cr, up 49% • EBITDA margin: 24.8% However, Q1 should not simply be annualised. Xanthine realisations benefited from raw-material pass-through and favourable supply conditions. Management itself acknowledged: “This quarter was exceptional.” The more durable opportunity lies in capacity utilisation and a richer CDMO-led business mix. Xanthine capacity has almost doubled Aarti has expanded Xanthine capacity from 5,000 TPA to 9,600 TPA, with the new capacity commercialised in Q1 FY27. The company is one of the few large, fully backward-integrated caffeine manufacturers outside China. This becomes relevant as customers seek supply-chain diversification. Management is targeting: • FY27 Xanthine revenue of ₹900–1,100 Cr • Over 80% capacity utilisation by FY28 • Around 30–35% volume growth by FY28 China’s withdrawal of export incentives and the tariff advantage available to Indian caffeine in the US could support a structurally better pricing floor. But quarterly revenue may moderate as temporary raw-material-linked pricing normalises. Atali is the key CDMO growth platform Atali Block 1, with 440 kL of multipurpose capacity, is now fully operational. This capacity can support commercial and late-stage CDMO projects while also shifting intermediate production away from existing plants—freeing older assets for additional API volumes. The CDMO business has already grown from ₹32 Cr in FY22 to ₹276 Cr in FY26. Aarti currently works with: • 22 CDMO customers • 57 projects • 37 commercialised projects Management expects CDMO revenue to grow 40–50% in FY27, implying approximately ₹386–414 Cr. Revenue is expected to remain H2-heavy, making execution during Q3 and Q4 particularly important. The longer-term ambition is to build a ₹1,000 Cr CDMO business. The next dedicated block can improve the earnings mix The board has approved a ₹149 Cr dedicated CDMO block at Atali, with approximately 405 kL of capacity. The facility is expected to be commissioned in H2 FY28 and will initially cater to three or four projects. This is strategically important because dedicated blocks involve fewer product changeovers, cleaning validations and downtime. They can therefore deliver better utilisation and asset turns than multipurpose facilities. CDMO is also the most margin-accretive part of the portfolio. The research note estimates CDMO gross margins at around 60–65%, compared with approximately 45–50% for generic APIs. Therefore, the value of the CDMO ramp lies not just in revenue growth—it can improve the consolidated margin mix and lift returns on the recently created asset base. APIs could recover from a weak base Q1 API revenue was affected by a planned six-week steroid facility shutdown. The debottlenecking has now increased steroid capacity by around 33%. Other triggers include: • Oncology block debottlenecking • API process-cost reduction • New oncology and lifestyle-drug launches • Management’s ₹170–190 Cr quarterly API revenue guidance • Potential to cross ₹1,000 Cr API revenue without major additional capex Aarti now has 61 commercialised APIs, 60 US DMFs and 44 European CEPs. More importantly, approximately 12 US DMFs were filed in the last 15 months. Several relate to complex oncology, chiral and heterocyclic chemistries—indicating that the development pipeline is moving towards more technically demanding products. What needs to be monitored A softer Q2 is possible as Xanthine pricing normalises while CDMO deliveries remain weighted towards H2. The critical checkpoints are: • FY27 CDMO revenue of at least ₹385–400 Cr • API recovery towards ₹170–190 Cr per quarter • Atali Block 1 utilisation • Timely construction of Block 2 • Xanthine volume growth despite lower realisations • Improvement in ROCE from the FY26 level of 9.8% CDMO concentration also remains a risk, with around 80% of segment revenue coming from seven or eight projects. The central thesis is therefore not that Q1 earnings will repeat every quarter. It is that roughly ₹1,000 Cr of cumulative investment is moving from being a depreciation and interest burden to becoming a productive asset base—and that CDMO can gradually replace Xanthine pricing as the company’s principal earnings driver. Aarti Pharmalabs is moving from a Xanthine and generic-API company towards a broader, higher-value chemistry platform. Way Forward Strengthen Atmanirbharta in critical sectors. Diversify defence and energy suppliers. Build resilient semiconductor and technology ecosystems. text: THE RUSSIAN OIL TRAP: IS INDIA’S STRATEGIC AUTONOMY UNDER PRESSURE? A new geopolitical fault line is emerging around India’s purchase of Russian oil. The video examines the reported US legislative framework that could enable tariffs of up to 100% on imports from countries buying Russian oil, while stressing an important distinction: the legislation does not itself impose a 100% tariff on India; rather, it creates a mechanism through which such tariffs could potentially be imposed. The video also highlights a 180-day review mechanism as a crucial element of the framework. The larger question is therefore not simply about Russia or oil. It is about how much strategic autonomy India can retain when economic pressure becomes an instrument of foreign policy. The video points to India’s increased Russian crude imports since the Ukraine war and argues that this dependence has become part of the wider India-US negotiating equation. It also raises questions about Nayara Energy, Rosneft’s stake in the refinery, and the movement of refined petroleum products between India and Russia. But there is another side that deserves equal attention. The video itself notes the US argument that Indian Russian-oil imports declined in August. It then presents an alternative explanation based on reported supply constraints in Russia following attacks on Russian refineries—not necessarily a voluntary Indian policy shift. That distinction matters. Foreign policy should not be reduced to America versus Russia, nor to slogans about nationalism. The real issue is whether India can build an economy strong and diversified enough that no external power can easily turn trade, energy or tariffs into a lever over Indian decision-making. Strategic autonomy is not merely the ability to say no. It is the economic capacity to remain independent when saying no becomes expensive. The coming months—and especially the proposed 180-day review mechanism and the India-US trade negotiations—will therefore deserve close public scrutiny. Will strategic autonomy remain a principle written in diplomatic documents—or become an economic capability strong enough to withstand pressure from any foreign capital? text: “When future historians look back at U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term, the Iran debacle will probably feature as a decisive turning point in his presidency. The conflict exposed the limits of American power. It isolated the United States internationally, added inflationary pressures to the world economy, and drove the president’s domestic approval ratings to unprecedented lows just ahead of midterm elections. But historians may ultimately deem a different development to be far more consequential: the failure of Trump’s China policy. Beijing seeks, in other words, to accelerate the historical trend President Xi Jinping has described as the rise of the East and the decline of the West. In less than two years, the Trump administration has done much to bring that outcome closer. China has weathered the trade war, narrowed the technology gap, tightened its leverage over critical supply chains, increased pressure on Taiwan, and deepened ties with Russia and much of the global south. It is better positioned relative to the United States than it was when Trump returned to office. Some failures of the White House’s economic policies toward China are already apparent: The administration has not reduced the trade deficit, it has not significantly lowered U.S. economic vulnerabilities, and it has not prevented Beijing from narrowing the gap in AI competition Despite long being Trump’s bête noire, the balance of payment has hardly improved. The administration may well claim that “America First Trade Policy is working” and that “China is no longer the trading partner with which the United States has its largest trade deficit. Second, and more critically, the Trump administration failed to meaningfully reduce the U.S. economy’s supply-chain dependencies on China. This is for rare earths and magnets, the so-called chokepoints that the administration inexplicably failed to anticipate Beijing would use as leverage against Washington’s punitive tariffs Much as Iran discovered by blocking the Strait of Hormuz that its leverage over the United States was stronger than it could have imagined before the war, China has shown that it can withstand, find workarounds, and retaliate against even Washington’s most aggressive trade-war measures. The October 2025 Busan agreement when Trump and Xi met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting made the point plain: Trump abandoned his threat of an additional 100 percent tariff on Chinese imports in exchange for a fragile truce on rare earths, soybeans, fentanyl, and export controls. The rest of the world duly took note of the limits of American economic leverage with China. U.S. still leads, but China has gained ground in both innovation and adoption. Its large language models now rival, and in some functions exceed, U.S. models at a fraction of the cost. The popularity of China’s open-weight models, combined with its manufacturing strength and lead in industrial robot deployment, gives it significant strengths in spreading AI at home and abroad. It’s also making steady progress to overcome its key weakness: limited computing power. Trump keeps claiming that the United States is “leading China by a lot” in AI. But that lead is narrowing, and not simply because of Chinese policy and ingenuity. The administration ignored the requirements of its own strategy and was incoherent in applying the tools it inherited China is consolidating its worldwide dominance in batteries, solar, and EVs. And while Washington alienates trading partners with tariffs, threats, and the disruption of long-standing trade arrangements. Washington has also needlessly strained its relationship with India, patiently cultivated over several administrations as a key regional counterweight to China. Beijing and New Delhi remain distrustful of each other but are pragmatically converging through BRICS around alternative trade and financial systems insulated from U.S. interference.”

text: Adroit: High margins, harder cash Adroit Industries prints unusual margins for a mid-size driveline exporter. That is not the same as a business that will travel at twice the capacity, with a 237-day cycle, an unhedged US book and no volume contracts. 1. Sticky customers — but no contracted volumes About 90% of FY26 product sales came from repeat customers (₹115 Cr). Qualification is slow (12–18 months at OEM / Tier-1 level), and specs such as G6.3 balancing plus tooling raise switching costs. There are no long-term agreements. Sales run on purchase orders. Repeat history is not booked volume. Monitor: PO coverage, new wins after qualification, and whether any key account actually thins out. 2. High margins — the next phase has to keep them FY26 EBITDA/PAT was 27.7%/18.7%, above Hindustan Hardy (11.1%/7.7%), GNA Axles (16.1%/7.9%) and Talbros Engineering (11.3%/5.4%). PAT moved ₹14.5 Cr → ₹18.1 Cr → ₹26.2 Cr. RoNW 22.5%, RoCE 19.0%. In the IPO webinar, management said usage of FORGE and SOLIDWORKS softwares helped them cut raw-steel use by about 9–10%. The test is whether those margins hold while ₹19.9 Cr of forging kit is added at Dewas and ₹44.0 Cr of CNC / cells / testing at Pithampur. Monitor: commissioning, utilisation, incremental EBITDA, and margin on the new asset base. 3. Profits on paper — cash is slower FY26 net working capital is 237 days, with 135 inventory days, 111 debtor days and 42 creditor days. Export receivables are uninsured. A long cycle plus uninsured overseas debtors is why reported PAT and free cash can diverge. Monitor: inventory and debtor days, cash conversion — not just EBITDA. 4. Export engine — concentrated and unhedged Exports are ~95% of product sales. The US is ~51% of that book. The RHP states US driveline exports face an extra 25% Section 232 duty. There is no FX hedge policy. Net FX was a ₹5.4 Cr loss in FY24, ₹3.8 Cr in FY25, and a ₹0.5 Cr gain in FY26. Unhedged cuts both ways. Monitor: US mix, tariff pass-through vs volume, and FX P&L. 5. Non-auto is real — still the minority FY26 product sales were 74.5% automotive / 25.5% non-auto (defence, mining, construction, industrial). That mix is the only real EV / CV hedge. China+1, Make in India, defence spend and NATRAX are industry backdrop, not an Adroit order log. Monitor: non-auto share of sales and whether those logos turn into repeat volume. 6. Cleaner balance sheet — returns still sit in execution Debt/equity is 0.41x. ₹24.1 Cr of IPO proceeds go to repay or prepay subsidiary borrowings. Capacity can rise on paper. Returns depend on the new lines qualifying and running. Monitor: debt, utilisation on new capex, and cash return on the incremental spend. 7. The shop floor has to keep up Permanent-employee attrition was 24% in FY26 and 29% in FY25, against a typical auto-component band of about 12–15%. Contract strength was 208 at FY26-end. In the IPO interview, management said the high rate is in lower-level / contract roles, critical jobs stay on payroll, and mid-to-senior retention is strong. Monitor: attrition by layer, contract vs permanent mix, and whether output quality holds as headcount and automation rise. Bottom line The manufacturing capability is not the debate. The debate is whether 28% EBITDA survives utilisation, tariffs, FX and a working-capital cycle that already absorbs most of the earnings story. Until cash, US mix and the new lines move the right way, treat the print as rear-view, not a run-rate. Track utilisation, incremental margins, cash conversion, US/tariff economics, non-auto mix and workforce stability. DYOR. text: Geopolitical risk is putting a premium on reliable resource supply. I think the market is still treating the current energy shock as an oil price story. I see it differently. The more important change is that energy is becoming harder to move across borders safely, predictably and without political consequences. This is a dislocation call for as long as shipping risk and sanctions exposure stay elevated, not a structural re-rating of coal's role in the energy transition. In a normal oil cycle, price does most of the work. A higher price encourages producers to sell more, gives traders an incentive to move barrels and eventually brings additional supply into the market. That mechanism becomes much less reliable when geopolitics gets involved. Oil can trade at $30 or $200, but neither price guarantees that a barrel will reach the buyer. If the seller faces sanctions, the shipper faces security risks, the insurer refuses the cargo or the refinery does not want the compliance exposure, the physical market can remain constrained regardless of the headline price. Russia is the clearest example. Trump has now signed legislation giving the US administration the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. The measure is not an automatic 100% tariff on every country buying Russian oil, but it materially raises the risk attached to those transactions. Europe has already taken a similar direction. Russian oil accounted for less than 3% of EU oil imports in 2025, down from 27% in 2021, while Russian coal imports have effectively been eliminated. Europe has therefore already done much of the obvious substitution. The remaining problem is that replacing a source of energy does not create new supply. The alternative barrels still have to come from somewhere. Saudi Arabia illustrates the problem from another angle. Following attacks on the kingdom's East-West pipeline, Saudi Aramco halted some October crude deliveries to European refiners and began rerouting supply through alternative channels. Saudi Arabia has not run out of oil. The disruption is about getting the oil from the producer to the customer. None of this stays contained in Europe. Sanctioned and tariff-exposed Russian oil and gas doesn't disappear, it gets redirected east, often at a discount, and that reshuffling changes the energy mix in China and India at the margin. At the same time, if Europe is willing to outbid Asia for LNG cargoes to plug its own gas security gap, Asian utilities that would have burned that gas burn more coal instead. Tankers aren't fungible the way price is. So the same forces making European buyers nervous about deliverability, shipping risk, insurance, sanctions exposure, apply just as directly to any buyer sourcing energy from contested routes. Europe needs energy, and its options are narrower than they appear. It can buy oil from another producer, but competing for replacement barrels raises prices and puts pressure on other buyers. It can buy more LNG, but LNG itself is exposed to the same shipping and geopolitical problems. Or it can use generation capacity that is already connected to its power system. And here where coal gets interesting. Europe does not want coal. Its long-term policy is still to reduce coal consumption, and I don't think the current situation changes that direction. What changes is the short-term value of coal when gas becomes expensive or uncertain. Existing coal plants can produce electricity without waiting for a new energy infrastructure to be built, and utilities respond to economics before they respond to political preference. The IEA is already seeing this. It has revised its 2026 outlook and now expects global coal demand to increase by 1.2%, with higher gas prices driving additional coal generation in Europe and other markets. European coal consumption is still declining structurally, but the decline is proving less severe as gas becomes more expensive. And here is the Indonesian coal story for me. Not because Europe is suddenly going back to coal. It isn't. The interesting part is that the world is beginning to put a higher value on energy that can actually be secured and delivered. Indonesia happens to control a large amount of exactly that kind of resource. Indonesia remains a major thermal coal exporter, while also holding substantial nickel and copper resources. That said, this external tailwind doesn't transmit cleanly to Indonesian producers or the state's fiscal position without running through domestic policy. RKAB approval delays constrain how much production can actually respond to a demand pull. DMO obligations cap how much of a global security premium producers get to keep versus subsidizing domestic power pricing. There is a cost to this for Indonesia too. We import oil, so a prolonged period of expensive crude would pressure the trade balance, inflation and the fiscal position. That is real and cannot be ignored.But the same geopolitical environment that makes imported energy more expensive can increase the value of what Indonesia exports. If oil rises simply because global demand is strong, Indonesian resource equities are still largely a conventional commodity trade. But if energy prices rise because supply is becoming politically and physically difficult to secure, the economics change. Buyers become less sensitive to the last dollar of commodity price and more concerned with whether the cargo will actually arrive. That creates a different environment for Indonesian coal producers. The value is no longer just in the coal sitting in the ground. It is in the combination of reserves, production capacity and access to the seaborne market. A buyer facing uncertainty over Russian energy, Middle Eastern supply or LNG availability has fewer alternatives when the physical market tightens. This is also why I don't think the right way to frame the trade is simply "oil up, coal up." Indonesia is unusually exposed to both sides of that shift. We are vulnerable because we import oil, but we also own and export resources that other economies need when their preferred sources of energy become less dependable. That makes Indonesian resource companies more interesting to me than a simple commodity-price thesis would suggest. I would focus on producers with competitive costs, established export infrastructure and the ability to deliver into the seaborne market. Those characteristics matter more when the constraint moves from demand to physical availability. The market is still focused on where Brent goes next. I am more interested in where the next reliable barrel, cargo of LNG or shipment of coal is going to come from. Because when supply becomes the scarce part of the equation, the owner of the resource gains bargaining power.

text: Why do Russians dislike the Lindsey Graham Act? Because it is not just another sanctions package. Above all, it represents a major restructuring of the sanctions architecture toward Russia. The law simultaneously codifies some of the sanctions already in place against Russia, creates new mandatory mechanisms for the U.S. administration, and expands the range of Russian and foreign companies, banks, vessels, and individuals that may be subject to blocking sanctions. Part of the sanctions policy is being moved from presidential executive orders into federal law. This means that a future president will have a harder time quickly dismantling a significant portion of the sanctions regime through a single executive order. The second major change is that the administration will now be required to regularly determine exactly who falls under the sanctions criteria. For a number of provisions, the first review must take place within 30 days of the law being signed - that is, by October 18 - and then every 180 days thereafter. In many cases, once an individual or company is determined to meet the relevant criteria, the law requires sanctions to be imposed. One of the broadest sections concerns Russian state-owned enterprises. The law covers entities in which the Russian government holds a controlling or majority stake, as well as those that are “otherwise affiliated with the Government of the Russian Federation.” Such companies are subject to full blocking sanctions. Potentially, this provision could apply to Gazprom, Transneft, Russian Railways, Rostelecom, Rosatom, and other major state-owned entities. However, the practical scope of the sanctions will depend on how broadly the Treasury Department interprets the term “affiliated.” That is why the focus should be not only on formal waivers, but primarily on the methodology and the first lists. Another major section targets the financial system and international networks used to circumvent sanctions. The law codifies sanctions on Sberbank, VTB, Gazprombank, and other Russian financial institutions with state participation, while allowing action against foreign banks that conduct significant transactions with them. It also allows sanctions to be imposed on financial messaging services and specific payment infrastructure knowingly used to evade sanctions. At the same time, the law covers foreign suppliers to Russia’s defense industry - companies supplying CNC machines, nitrocellulose, military-grade fiber optics, advanced sensors, and other critical components. This creates direct risks for companies in China, Turkey, the UAE, Central Asia, the Caucasus, and other jurisdictions if they meet the criteria established by the law. The “shadow fleet” is addressed separately. Sanctions may target not only tankers transporting Russian energy products in circumvention of sanctions or the price cap, but also their owners, operators, managers, insurers, related parties, and foreign ports that service already-sanctioned vessels. The entire infrastructure supporting Russia’s maritime exports therefore comes under pressure. At the same time, sanctions imposed by the EU, the UK, G7, or Five Eyes may be used by the U.S. administration as prima facie evidence. The energy section of the law prohibits new U.S. investments in Russia’s energy sector and allows sanctions against foreign persons providing goods, technology, services, or other support for the production of oil, gas, LNG, uranium, petroleum products, and coal for already-sanctioned Russian entities. Yamal LNG, Arctic LNG 1, 2, and 3, as well as future Arctic LNG projects, are specifically named. Sanctions could apply to their executives, board members, and controlling or majority shareholders. This is particularly important for Europe, since Russian LNG from Yamal still reaches France, Belgium, and Spain ahead of the EU’s full ban taking effect. Rosatom is also addressed separately, although the specific provision concerning its leadership and controlling shareholders is tied to the U.S. exemption regime for imports of Russian low-enriched uranium. Individual Rosatom entities could nevertheless be covered earlier under other provisions, including the state-owned enterprise provision. Tariffs remain the most visible part of the law, but their practical impact has yet to be determined. For goods imported directly from Russia, the law provides for an additional tariff of up to 500%. For third countries, tariffs of up to 100% could be imposed on all of their exports to the United States if they are among the five largest purchasers of Russian oil or gas and continue making new purchases after the law takes effect, or if they are among the five countries providing the greatest assistance in circumventing oil sanctions. The law does not establish a minimum tariff rate. For gas purchasers, there is an exception: the tariff may not apply if a country purchases less than 15% of Russia’s total gas exports and takes “significant steps” to reduce those purchases. The term “significant steps” itself is not defined. Among the obvious potential targets of the tariff mechanism are China, India, and Turkey as major purchasers of Russian oil. China is also a major purchaser of Russian gas. For Japan and European countries, the outcome will depend on how the administration applies the gas exception. Another unresolved question is whether Washington will count the EU as a single entity or treat each member state separately. If they are counted separately, Hungary and Slovakia would be among the countries most exposed on oil, while Hungary would be exposed on gas. If the EU is counted as a bloc, it could itself fall within the group of major purchasers of Russian energy. An even more open question concerns the five countries providing the greatest assistance in circumventing oil sanctions. The law allows the administration to consider financing of purchases, transportation, shadow-fleet operations, and other services, but it does not establish a clear formula for determining the top five. The UAE is an obvious candidate, but the rest of the list will depend on the administration’s methodology. The law simultaneously strengthens Ukraine’s and Congress’s positions while creating new tools for the U.S. administration. For Ukraine, it provides additional mechanisms for pressuring Russian state revenues, the financial system, the defense industry, the energy sector, and international sanctions-evasion networks. In addition, the termination of key sanctions is tied to a peace agreement adopted by a free and independent government of Ukraine, the cessation of hostilities, and Russia’s renunciation of activities aimed at undermining the Ukrainian government. Congress gains greater control through the codification of sanctions, regular reviews, reporting requirements, and a 30-day review period before the termination of the sanctions regime. The administration, meanwhile, receives stronger tools for influencing third countries - including secondary sanctions against banks and companies and the ability to impose tariffs on a country’s entire exports to the United States. The key date now is October 18. The first things to watch are the initial designations and the methodology: which Russian state-owned companies the administration determines are covered by Section 104; how far it goes against the shadow fleet; whether it imposes sanctions on foreign defense-industry suppliers and banks; what it does with Yamal LNG and other Arctic projects; which countries it places on the lists of Russian energy purchasers and sanctions-evasion facilitators; what tariff rates it sets; and which exemptions it uses. These decisions will show how broadly the Trump administration intends to use the powers granted to it by the law.

The main constraints are not tax. They are land aggregation, permitting, grid access, electricity economics, water, cooling, and climate resilience. If those bottlenecks are addressed credibly, India can become a major global node for generative AI deployment and cloud export. If they are not, the proposal will still support local inference and enterprise AI growth, but the largest frontier-scale AI clusters will continue to concentrate where power, land, and cooling are structurally easier to secure.

text: There is a litany of uncomfortable facts about the country’s economy and, disturbingly, Canadians are content to trudge on in a constant, delusional state of “vranyo” about Canada and its economic prospects. Yet, this is a fool’s game and cannot end well, just as Ayn Rand noted, “We can evade reality, but we cannot evade the consequences of evading reality.” One uncomfortable fact for the Liberal government that was revealed by Bloomberg News this summer is that Mark Carney has had the worst first year of growth for a prime minister since 1963. With Carney in charge for a year, the Canadian economy has actually shrank. The global-banker-turned-prime minister is the first to achieve this dubious feat. In Justin Trudeau’s first year the economy grew 1.7 per cent real GDP, and in Stephen Harper’s first year it grew 1.4 per cent. It is evident now that changing leaders did not produce a change of fortune for the Liberals and their hapless, at times inept, management of the economy. There are many signs that the Canadian economy is in trouble. Tom Czitron, investment strategist and global macro analyst wrote recently in the Epoch Times that key indicators of ordinary Canadian economic life are moving in the wrong direction and jeopardizing the standard of living. Here are three indicators Czitron highlighted: The house price-to-income ratio has skyrocketed: in the 1983–1989 era, a median Canadian home cost roughly three times the median household income and today it costs eight times that much. Canada grew at roughly 2.8 per cent GDP per capita in the 1980s recovery. That figure has declined in every subsequent era, reaching an almost negligible 0.3 per cent growth in 2020–2025. Canadians are working approximately 27 per cent more hours to cover median rent and 23 per cent more hours to cover food costs than they were just five years ago. Trevor Tombe, economist at the University of Calgary, cites OECD data in a revealing piece he wrote in early August in The Hub that demonstrates just how badly Canada’s economy is falling behind its competitors. It is this international comparison that should alarm Canadians. Since the first quarter of 2025 (when Carney took office), as mentioned above, Canada’s real GDP shrunk by 0.1 per cent. It is the only industrialized country where the economy shrank – and there is no excuse blaming Canada’s ill fortunes with the Trump administration: Mexico’s economy grew 0.4 per cent. The OECD countries grew on average 1.7 per cent, and the G-7 nations grew on average 1.7 per cent. Australia grew 2.5 per cent. The American economy grew 2.7 per cent. In another Epoch Times finance column, wealth advisor Bryan Brulotte focused on the signs of an ailing business environment in the country. He too cited OECD statistics, “Canadian workers produced approximately US$75 of economic output per hour worked in 2023, compared with US$97 in the United States. In other words, American workers generated almost 30 per cent more output for every hour worked.” Brulotte also pointed out that business investment per worker in Canada has fallen to only 85 per cent of its 2014 level. Over that same period, investment per worker increased on average in OECD countries by two per cent, but more striking is that it rose by 21 per cent in the U.S. and 13 per cent in Europe. When the business climate is stormy and dark, businesses do not have the confidence to re-invest. More troubling is that loss of confidence becomes a defeatist attitude – and this is seen in a Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB) report published earlier this year. CFIB reports that more than half of small business owners surveyed (55 per cent) would recommend against starting a business in Canada right now. How far has the Canadian economy fallen? The International Institute for Management Development measured the economies of countries and produced a comprehensive report, World Competitiveness Ranking, that puts Canada at 16th in size in the world and the greatest challenge it faces is the uncertainty caused by the trade dispute with the U.S. And in a recent EnergyNow editorial column, it is reported that Canada’s annual $2.5 trillion economy trails the economies of U.S., China, Germany, Japan, the U.K., India, France, Italy, Russia and Brazil. The editorial explores the reputational impact of the weakened Canadian economy and questions, “If the G-7 were created today, would Canada make the cut?” Perhaps there is no greater sign of a failing economy than plant closures and the exodus of companies to a friendly business environment in the U.S.; it is unsettling. Last week, 425 workers in Temiscaming, Quebec learned that the Rayonier Advanced Materials (RYAM) complex will be closing immediately. The week before, Heico announced 140 workers laid off at its steel operations in Quebec. Interfor Corporation, one of the largest lumber companies in Canada, plans to shift most of its executive power from Burnaby, B.C. to Atlanta, Georgia. In April, Interfor paused production at two Northern Ontario sawmills, which employed 200 forestry jobs. Canfor closed its Fox Creek, Alberta sawmill and announced it will be closing its Northwood pulp mill in Prince George, B.C. before Christmas. There has been a rash of closures in Quebec: Acier Orford in Sherbrooke, South Shore Furniture of Sainte-Croix, and Bestar in Lac-Megantic. Ontario lost the Crown Royal bottling plant and 200 jobs in Amherstburg to Montgomery, Alabama. Taking a page from Brookfield Corp’s playbook to take advantage of better U.S. tax rules is Algonquin Power & Utilities Corp of Oakville, Ontario, which announced its plan to establish its headquarters in Chicago. Earlier this year, GFL Environmental Inc., Canada’s largest waste management company, moved its headquarters from Sault Ste Marie to Miami Beach, Florida. There has also been ugly news in the Canadian auto sector, and the loss of tens of billions of dollars of economic activity is sending shockwaves through Ontario’s manufacturing heartland. Honda’s $15 billion EV complex in Alliston is indefinitely suspended. GM’s CAMI assembly plant in Ingersoll had its $2 billion refit for the BrightDrop electric van production shut down – with 1,000 jobs lost. The GM Oshawa plant lost a shift (1,200 jobs) to Fort Wayne, Indiana. Stellantis dumped its stake making EV batteries in Windsor. Hyundai just announced they are dropping $3.4 billion of investment into Canada, including plans for an Ontario truck factory. Ford’s Oakville facility scrapped its $1.8 billion EV plan and the union rumour is Ford is also considering moving tens of thousands of jobs south of the border. More recently, Stellantis put 2,200 workers out with its planned sale of its Brampton plant and move of Jeep production to Illinois. Umicore Loyalist’s $2.7 billion battery plant has been paused for two years now – and there was also the cancellation of the $7 billion mega battery facility planned in Northvolt in McMasterville and Saint-Basile-le-Grand, Quebec when the Swedish parent company went bankrupt. Remarkably, all of this economic mayhem can get far more serious for Canadian businesses. Today, the most concerning economic danger for Canadians (though many seem oblivious to the pain it will inflict) is the Carney government’s withdrawal from trade negotiations with the U.S. The breakdown of trade talks will prove devastating if the negotiations do not resume. Trevor Tombe estimates the government’s counter-tariffs are going to cost Canadians at least $4 billion in the coming months. A Deloitte Canada report estimates that if CUSMA is lost, through the next 10 years Canada’s real GDP would fall by 1.6 per cent, or $402 billion, and the country would shed 1,630,000 jobs. Deloitte concludes, “The bottom line is a severe but not cataclysmic impact on Canada’s overall economy, although perhaps cataclysmic for some sectors.” Economist Ian Lee of the Carleton University Sprott School of Business sees the ramifications of the failed trade talks as much more damaging. He has been on multiple news interviews in the past couple of weeks and in an Allan Small interview he stated, “The twin hammer of massive increase in bankruptcies and unemployment and massive increase in capital flight of businesses moving to the States will devastate – devastate – the Canadian economy. We are looking at a deep, deep recession, possibly even a depression if that comes to pass and we don’t have any kind of trade agreement with the United States. It is the worst, the most catastrophically terrible thing that could ever happen.” In a CBC News interview Lee was direct, “Step back and take a look at the big picture. Our economy will go into deep recession if we do not have any kind of a trade agreement with the U.S.” Last word on the Canadian economy this week goes to Jerry Haar, a professor at Florida International University, who provided a frank assessment of the problem with Canada’s economy. (A foreign perspective is often the most insightful). Haar assessed, “The Canadian economy suffers from a lack of dynamism and excessive dependence on American markets.” He said the problem is not Washington, but rather Ottawa, “While the conflict may be widely perceived as a David vs. Goliath match, Canada has only itself to blame for its weakness and vulnerability in trade. The reason? Canada has failed for decades to take sweeping measures to improve competitiveness and diversify exports.” With obvious challenges before the country’s economy, and so much at stake, it is time Canadians snapped out of their state of “vranyo” – uncomfortable as the facts may be.

text: Celebrating India’s Growth Story | Ep. 3 - Mukesh Ambani On 1 September 2016, at a Reliance AGM, voice on a phone network became free. Not cheaper. Free. Data thrown in on a welcome offer that made every other operator rewrite the tariff board. Within a year India went from a back-marker in mobile broadband use to the country that eats the most of it. That is not a branding line. That is what happened to the network in your pocket. Mukesh Ambani did not invent the mobile phone. He spent a decade and a brutal amount of capital building a 4G-only network, missed dates, and then used price as a weapon. The idea, he has said, sat in the house first: Isha home from Yale, internet at home was bad, Akash talking about a world where voice would not be the product. Before that, he was the son who actually poured Jamnagar. Born 19 April 1957 in Aden. Dhirubhai’s elder son. Chemical engineering at the Institute of Chemical Technology, a short Stanford MBA, then home to build plants. The split with Anil in 2005 left him with the refining and petrochemical machine. Anil took the first telecom bet, and it did not become Jio. Mukesh came back to the sector later and did. What the file actually contains: 1. Jamnagar is the unfashionable masterpiece. Late-90s grassroots refinery, then doubled, until one site was among the largest integrated refining-and-petrochem complexes on earth. That cash built the later bets. No Jamnagar, no Jio war chest. 2. He is an operator more than a pitchman. Dhirubhai was the market. Mukesh was the project. People still get that backwards. 3. Jio was a price shock sitting on a greenfield network. Free voice. Cheap data. A stack of apps. Rivals merged or shrank. Users did not ask permission from the old ARPU religion. 4. Retail is the quiet third leg. Thousands of stores, JioMart, a distribution machine that looks boring until you need it in a tier-2 town. 5. The house is not a morality play you can finish in one tweet. Political access, spectrum, and scale are part of Indian telecom. So is the fact that a 4G data plan stopped being a luxury good. You can hold both. We love a founder who “disrupts.” We get shy when the disruptor already owns a refinery. That shyness is not analysis. Jio used hydrocarbon cash to subsidise a digital habit for a country that could not have paid US prices for data. That transfer is the growth story. Settled: Jamnagar made Reliance a global energy node. Settled: 2016 repriced Indian internet. Not settled: that this is only genius, or only capture. A network that large is always both. If your India story starts at a startup dinner in 2018, you are standing on a tower someone else paid for. Next episode tomorrow, 9 PM.

Supply-chain concentration: dependence on a few markets or suppliers increases systemic risk. Constructive Criticism The article's central argument is that India should not respond through panic-driven retaliation, but through structural resilience. At the same time, diversification cannot mean abruptly abandoning cost-competitive energy sources; it must balance affordability, security and geopolitical risk. Strengthen non-dollar and lawful alternative payment mechanisms. Create a permanent economic-security coordination mechanism. Reduce dependence on individual markets through export diversification.
